text: A tornado's wind speeds can exceed 300 mph (480 km/h), making them the most violent atmospheric storms on Earth. The United States experiences more tornadoes than any other country, averaging around 1,200 per year.

Hurricanes, typhoons, and cyclones are the same type of storm — a tropical cyclone — just named differently based on where they form. They are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

The eye of a hurricane is an area of relatively calm weather typically 20–40 miles (32–64 km) wide at the storm's center. Surrounded by the eyewall — a ring of thunderstorms containing the hurricane's most intense winds — the eye is deceptively tranquil.

Lightning strikes Earth's surface approximately 100 times every second, adding up to about 8 million lightning bolts per day. A single lightning bolt can heat the surrounding air to roughly 30,000 K (53,540°F), which is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

Thunder is the sound produced by the rapid expansion of air superheated by a lightning bolt. Because light travels much faster than sound, you can estimate how far away a lightning strike is by counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder and dividing by five to get miles.

The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of wind direction that brings heavy rainfall to large parts of Asia, Africa, and the Americas. The South Asian (Indian) monsoon delivers approximately 80% of India's annual rainfall between June and September.

El Niño is a climate pattern characterized by the unusual warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, occurring every two to seven years. It disrupts normal weather patterns globally, causing droughts in some regions and flooding in others.

La Niña is the counterpart to El Niño, defined by cooler-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. La Niña typically brings increased rainfall to Australia, Southeast Asia, and parts of Africa, while contributing to drier conditions across the southern United States.

The jet stream is a fast-flowing ribbon of air in the upper atmosphere (roughly 6–9 miles altitude) that steers weather systems across the middle latitudes. Polar jet streams can reach speeds of 250 mph (400 km/h) and greatly influence weather patterns in North America and Europe.

A blizzard is defined not just by heavy snow but by sustained winds of at least 35 mph (56 km/h) and visibility reduced to less than a quarter mile for three or more hours. Wind-driven snow creates whiteout conditions that make travel extremely dangerous.

Hailstones form when updrafts in thunderstorms carry water droplets upward into extremely cold regions of the atmosphere, where they freeze and accumulate layers of ice. The largest reliably measured hailstone in U.S. history fell in Vivian, South Dakota, on July 23, 2010, measuring 8 inches (20.3 cm) in diameter.

Fog forms when water vapor condenses into tiny droplets suspended near the ground, reducing visibility to less than 1,000 meters (about 0.6 miles). It most commonly occurs when moist air cools to the dew point, either by radiating heat at night or by moving over a cold surface.

The dew point is the temperature at which air must be cooled (at constant pressure) for water vapor to condense into liquid water. When the dew point matches the air temperature, relative humidity reaches 100% and dew, fog, or precipitation can form.

Frost forms when the temperature of exposed surfaces drops below 0°C (32°F) and water vapor deposits directly as ice crystals without first becoming liquid water — a process called deposition. This differs from frozen dew, which forms when liquid dew subsequently freezes.

A rainbow forms when sunlight enters water droplets and is refracted, reflected inside the droplet, then refracted again as it exits, separating white light into its component colors. The primary rainbow always has red on the outside and violet on the inside, spanning a 42-degree arc from the anti-solar point.

A double rainbow occurs when light reflects twice inside water droplets; in the secondary bow, the colors are reversed, with violet on the outside and red on the inside. The area between the two rainbows, called Alexander's band, appears notably darker because less light reaches that region.

The greenhouse effect is a natural process in which certain atmospheric gases — primarily water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide — absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, keeping Earth's surface about 33°C (59°F) warmer than it would otherwise be. Without this natural effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be around −18°C (0°F).

Earth's atmosphere is divided into five main layers: the troposphere (0–12 km), stratosphere (12–50 km), mesosphere (50–80 km), thermosphere (80–700 km), and exosphere (700–10,000 km). Almost all weather occurs in the troposphere, the lowest and densest layer.

The ozone layer, located in the stratosphere at altitudes of roughly 15–35 km, absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation. Without this protective shield, increased UV radiation would cause higher rates of skin cancer and cataracts and damage ecosystems.

The Antarctic ozone hole is a seasonal thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer that forms each spring over Antarctica, driven by man-made chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). Following the Montreal Protocol (1987), CFC production was phased out and the ozone layer has been slowly recovering.

Global average surface temperatures have risen approximately 1.1–1.2°C (2°F) since the pre-industrial era (1850–1900), driven primarily by the burning of fossil fuels and land-use changes. The last decade (2011–2020) was the warmest on record globally.
Atmospheric CO₂ concentrations crossed 420 parts per million (ppm) in 2023, the highest level in at least 3 million years. The pre-industrial baseline was approximately 280 ppm.

A heat wave is a prolonged period of excessively hot weather, which may be accompanied by high humidity. Definitions vary by region, but heat waves are among the deadliest natural disasters — the 2003 European heat wave caused approximately 70,000 excess deaths.

A dust storm (or sandstorm) occurs when strong winds pick up large amounts of dust and sand from dry, bare surfaces and carry them for hundreds or even thousands of kilometers. The Sahara Desert is the world's largest source of dust, contributing an estimated 800 million tonnes of dust to the atmosphere annually.

A waterspout is a rotating column of air and water mist that forms over a body of water; fair-weather waterspouts are relatively weak and can be found over tropical and subtropical waters, while tornadic waterspouts form from mesocyclones extending onto water. Unlike tornadoes over land, most waterspouts dissipate quickly when they reach shore.

A microburst is a sudden, intense downdraft from a thunderstorm that spreads outward when it hits the ground, producing a brief but dangerous burst of strong diverging winds. Microbursts have caused numerous airplane crashes because the sudden headwind followed by a tailwind dramatically reduces lift at low altitudes.

Cumulus clouds are the classic puffy, white clouds with flat bases that form when rising warm, moist air cools to the dew point. They are generally associated with fair weather when small, but can develop into towering cumulonimbus thunderstorm clouds when conditions are unstable.

Cumulonimbus clouds, often called thunderheads, are the tallest clouds in the troposphere, sometimes reaching heights of 60,000 feet (18 km) or more. They are responsible for thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, hail, lightning, and occasionally tornadoes.

Stratus clouds are low, flat, gray or white sheets that cover large areas of the sky and are often associated with overcast, drizzly weather. They form when a large mass of moist air is cooled uniformly, often producing gray skies but rarely heavy rain.

Cirrus clouds are thin, wispy, feather-like clouds that form at high altitudes (above 20,000 feet / 6,000 m) where temperatures are well below freezing, causing them to be composed entirely of ice crystals rather than water droplets. They often indicate that a weather change — including the approach of a warm front — is on the way.

The Köppen climate classification system, first published in 1884 by Wladimir Köppen, divides Earth's climates into five main groups: tropical (A), dry (B), temperate (C), continental (D), and polar (E), with further subdivisions based on temperature and precipitation seasonality.

Tropical rainforest climates receive more than 2,500 mm (98 inches) of rain per year with no dry season, supporting Earth's most biodiverse biomes. They are found near the equator in regions such as the Amazon Basin, the Congo, and Southeast Asian islands.

The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air surrounding Earth's poles. When the polar vortex weakens or is disrupted, frigid Arctic air can spill southward into mid-latitudes, causing sudden extreme cold snaps across North America and Europe.

The last major ice age peaked approximately 20,000 years ago during the Last Glacial Maximum, when ice sheets covered much of North America, Europe, and Asia. Sea levels were roughly 120 meters (394 feet) lower than today because so much water was locked in glaciers.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The Medieval Warm Period (roughly 950–1250 CE) was a time of relatively warm temperatures across parts of the North Atlantic region, allowing Norse settlers to establish colonies in Greenland and possibly North America. However, this warming was regional rather than global, unlike the current climate change which is warming the entire planet.

The Little Ice Age (approximately 1300–1850 CE) was a period of regional cooling that followed the Medieval Warm Period, featuring colder winters in Europe and North America, advancing glaciers, and disruptions to agriculture. Historical records from this era document harsh winters and crop failures that contributed to famines.

Weather forecasting has been revolutionized by numerical weather prediction (NWP), which uses mathematical models of the atmosphere running on supercomputers to forecast conditions. Modern 5-day forecasts are now as accurate as 1-day forecasts were in the 1980s.

Weather satellites orbiting Earth continuously monitor cloud patterns, sea surface temperatures, and atmospheric moisture. The GOES series of geostationary satellites operated by NOAA provides imagery of the Western Hemisphere every 30 seconds, crucial for tracking rapidly developing severe weather.

Doppler radar measures the velocity of precipitation by detecting shifts in the frequency of reflected radar pulses — the Doppler effect — allowing meteorologists to see wind patterns inside storms and detect rotation that may indicate tornadoes. The WSR-88D (NEXRAD) network of 160 Doppler radars covers nearly all of the contiguous United States.

The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 (74–95 mph winds) to Category 5 (157 mph or higher), based solely on wind speed. Category 5 hurricanes can produce catastrophic damage, destroying most framed homes and snapping or uprooting trees.

The Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale rates tornadoes from EF0 (65–85 mph winds, light damage) to EF5 (over 200 mph winds, incredible damage). It was adopted in the United States in 2007 to replace the original Fujita Scale, incorporating better damage indicators.

Trade winds blow from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and from the southeast in the Southern Hemisphere, converging near the equator in a band called the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). These consistent winds were historically exploited by sailing vessels to cross the oceans.

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), often called the doldrums by sailors, is a belt of low pressure around the equator where the northeast and southeast trade winds meet. This convergence zone features persistent convective thunderstorms and heavy precipitation and migrates seasonally north and south, driving monsoon patterns.

The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. This effect causes hurricanes to spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Arctic sea ice extent has declined dramatically in recent decades, with September (minimum) sea ice averaging about 13% less per decade since satellite records began in 1979. In September 2012, Arctic sea ice reached a record minimum of 3.41 million km², less than half the long-term average.

source.name: NASA National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: Sea level has risen approximately 20 cm (8 inches) globally since 1900, with the rate accelerating since the 1990s. The primary drivers are thermal expansion of warming oceans and the melting of glaciers and ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica.

Snow forms when water vapor in clouds freezes directly into ice crystals that clump together as they fall. Every snowflake is built on a hexagonal lattice structure determined by the molecular geometry of water ice, and while snowflakes share this six-sided symmetry, no two are exactly alike at the microscopic scale.

A nor'easter is a large storm that tracks up the eastern coast of North America and whose winds come from the northeast, battering the coastline with cold, heavy precipitation that can be rain, sleet, or heavy snow. These storms can dump several feet of snow on cities like Boston and New York within 24 hours.

The Hadley Cell is a large-scale atmospheric circulation pattern in which air rises near the equator, flows poleward at high altitude, sinks around 30°N/S latitude, and returns as surface trade winds. This circulation creates the world's major deserts near 30 degrees latitude, including the Sahara, Arabian, and Australian deserts.

The highest reliably recorded surface air temperature on Earth is 56.7°C (134.1°F), measured at Furnace Creek in Death Valley, California, on July 10, 1913. Death Valley holds the record partly due to its low elevation (below sea level) and the bowl-like topography that traps hot air.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The lowest reliably recorded natural surface air temperature on Earth is −89.2°C (−128.6°F), measured at the Soviet Vostok Station in Antarctica on July 21, 1983. A 2010 satellite-based measurement recorded a surface temperature of −93.2°C over the East Antarctic Plateau, though this was a surface temperature, not an air temperature.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Sohra), both in Meghalaya, India, compete for the title of the world's wettest place, each receiving over 11,800 mm (nearly 39 feet) of rain annually on average. This extreme rainfall is driven by moist air from the Bay of Bengal rising abruptly against the Khasi Hills.

The Atacama Desert in South America is one of the driest places on Earth, with some areas receiving less than 1 mm of rain per year. Parts of the Atacama's hyperarid core may go decades without measurable rainfall.

The highest wind speed ever recorded at the Earth's surface (not tornado-related) is 408 km/h (253 mph), measured during Tropical Cyclone Olivia at Barrow Island, Australia, on April 10, 1996. This measurement was verified and accepted by the World Meteorological Organization in 2010.

The Beaufort scale, developed by British Admiral Francis Beaufort in 1805, is an empirical measure that relates wind speed to observed conditions at sea or on land. It ranges from 0 (calm, smoke rises vertically) to 12 (hurricane-force winds that cause widespread damage).

A storm surge is an abnormal rise of water above the predicted astronomical tide generated by the winds and low pressure of a tropical cyclone. Storm surges are the leading cause of hurricane-related deaths; during Hurricane Katrina in 2005, storm surges up to 28 feet (8.5 m) inundated the Gulf Coast.

The Fujiwara effect occurs when two nearby tropical cyclones rotate around each other and may merge into one stronger storm. This interaction was first described by Japanese meteorologist Sakuhei Fujiwhara in 1921.

Permafrost is ground that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years, and it underlies about 25% of the Northern Hemisphere's land surface. As Arctic temperatures rise at more than twice the global average rate, thawing permafrost releases stored methane and carbon dioxide, creating a positive climate feedback loop.

Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream act as the planet's heat conveyor belt, transporting warm tropical water to higher latitudes and significantly moderating climates. The Gulf Stream keeps Western Europe several degrees warmer than it would otherwise be at the same latitudes.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) — of which the Gulf Stream is a part — has slowed significantly since the mid-20th century, likely driven by freshwater input from melting Greenland ice. A significant weakening could cause major shifts in weather patterns and cooling in Western Europe.

The orographic effect (or orographic lift) occurs when air is forced upward over a mountain range, cooling as it rises and often producing rain or snow on the windward side. The leeward (sheltered) side experiences a dry rain shadow, as the descending air warms and its relative humidity drops.

The Chinook wind is a warm, dry foehn wind that descends the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, sometimes raising temperatures by 20–30°C (36–54°F) within minutes. The name 'Chinook' comes from the Chinook people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, and these winds can rapidly melt large amounts of snow.

A haboob is a type of intense dust storm that forms when a collapsing thunderstorm outflow generates powerful straight-line winds that sweep up walls of sand and dust, sometimes reaching 100 km (60 miles) wide and 1.5 km (1 mile) high. They are common in the Sahara, Arabian Peninsula, and the U.S. Southwest.

Ice cores drilled from glaciers and ice sheets in Antarctica and Greenland provide climate records extending hundreds of thousands of years into the past. By analyzing trapped air bubbles, scientists have reconstructed past CO₂ levels, temperatures, and volcanic events with remarkable precision.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Tree rings (dendrochronology) can be used to reconstruct past climate conditions, because trees grow wider rings during warm, wet years and narrower rings during cold, dry years. Long tree-ring chronologies extend climate records back thousands of years before instrumental measurements began.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Ball lightning is a rare, unexplained atmospheric electrical phenomenon described as a luminous, spherical object that varies from pea-sized to several meters in diameter and may last for seconds to minutes. Despite numerous eyewitness reports over centuries, its physical mechanism remains scientifically unresolved.

St. Elmo's Fire is a weather phenomenon caused by a coronal electrical discharge that creates a blue or violet glow around sharp pointed objects — such as ship masts, aircraft wings, or lightning rods — during thunderstorms. It was named by sailors after St. Erasmus (Elmo), patron saint of seafarers.

Sprites are large-scale electrical discharges that occur above thunderstorm clouds, reaching altitudes of 50–90 km in the mesosphere. They appear as reddish-orange columns or jellyfish-like shapes lasting only milliseconds and are triggered by large positive lightning strokes.

The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is a climate pattern involving changes in sea surface temperatures in the western and eastern Indian Ocean that affects rainfall across East Africa, India, and Australia. A positive IOD (warmer west, cooler east) tends to bring drought to Australia and flooding to East Africa.

The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) is a long-lived El Niño–like pattern of Pacific climate variability that shifts between warm and cool phases approximately every 20–30 years. The PDO modulates the frequency and intensity of El Niño/La Niña events and influences climate across North America.

The Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights) and Aurora Australis (Southern Lights) are natural light displays caused by the interaction of solar wind particles with Earth's magnetic field and upper atmosphere. Auroras occur most frequently in oval-shaped zones centered on Earth's magnetic poles at latitudes around 65–72 degrees.

A bomb cyclone (or bombogenesis) is a rapid intensification of a mid-latitude cyclone in which the central pressure drops at least 24 millibars within 24 hours. These powerful storms can produce blizzard conditions, strong winds, and coastal flooding across large areas.

A mesocyclone is a rotating updraft in a severe thunderstorm (supercell) from which tornadoes can develop. Doppler radar can detect mesocyclone rotation, giving forecasters precious warning time before a tornado touches down.

Supercooled water is liquid water that exists below 0°C (32°F) without freezing, possible when it lacks a nucleus around which ice crystals can form. When supercooled water droplets in clouds contact an aircraft surface, they freeze on impact and cause dangerous in-flight icing.

Freezing rain forms when raindrops falling through a shallow subfreezing layer near the surface freeze on contact with cold objects such as roads, trees, and power lines. The resulting glaze ice is extremely dangerous for transportation and can snap tree limbs and power lines under accumulated weight.

Sleet (ice pellets) forms when snowflakes partially melt in a warm layer above ground then refreeze into small ice pellets before reaching the surface. Unlike freezing rain, sleet pellets bounce on impact and accumulate like frozen marbles on surfaces.

The heat index (or 'feels like' temperature) combines air temperature and relative humidity to reflect how hot it actually feels to the human body, since high humidity reduces the evaporation of sweat. A combination of 40°C (104°F) and 75% humidity produces a heat index of about 74°C (165°F), which is life-threatening.

The wind chill factor describes how cold it feels when wind is factored in with low air temperature, because wind accelerates heat loss from exposed skin. At −20°C (−4°F) with a 50 km/h (31 mph) wind, the wind chill is approximately −36°C (−33°F).

An atmospheric river is a narrow corridor of concentrated water vapor in the atmosphere that transports most of the moisture from the tropics toward the poles. When an atmospheric river makes landfall, it can deliver extreme rainfall and flooding equivalent to several months of normal precipitation in just a few days.

The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the largest element of intraseasonal tropical climate variability, representing an eastward-moving pulse of enhanced tropical rainfall and cloudiness that travels around the globe in 30–60 days. The MJO influences hurricane activity, monsoon onset, and weather patterns far outside the tropics.

Graupel (also called soft hail or snow pellets) forms when supercooled water droplets freeze onto a falling snowflake, building up a rounded opaque ice coating. Unlike true hail, graupel is fragile and crumbles when squeezed, and it forms primarily in winter and spring snowstorms rather than summer thunderstorms.

A derecho is a long-lived, widespread wind storm associated with a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms that produces straight-line winds of 93 km/h (58 mph) or more over a continuous path of at least 400 km (250 miles). Unlike tornado damage, derecho damage is primarily from straight-line winds rather than rotation.

The stratospheric warming event known as a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) occurs when temperatures in the stratosphere rise by as much as 30–50°C within a few days, disrupting the polar vortex and often leading to cold outbreaks at the surface weeks later. Major SSW events occur approximately six times per decade.

The Saharan Air Layer (SAL) is a mass of very dry, dusty air that forms over the Sahara and is lofted 1–5 km above the ocean surface as it moves westward across the Atlantic. The SAL suppresses hurricane formation by increasing wind shear and reducing atmospheric moisture.

source.name: NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory

text: Noctilucent clouds (NLCs) are the highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere, forming in the mesosphere at altitudes of about 76–85 km from tiny ice crystals around meteoric dust. They are visible at high latitudes during summer twilight as electric-blue or silver-white wave patterns near the horizon after sunset.

Virga is precipitation that evaporates or sublimates in dry air before reaching the ground. It appears as streaks or shafts of rain or snow hanging beneath clouds in arid regions and can be deceptive to pilots and fire weather forecasters, as lightning strikes may still start wildfires even without rain reaching the surface.

Mammatus clouds are pouch-like protrusions hanging from the underside of a cumulonimbus anvil, formed by sinking pockets of cold, moist air. They are often associated with severe thunderstorms and can signal that extreme weather conditions — such as hail or tornadoes — have occurred or are ongoing nearby.

A fire tornado (or firenado) is a vortex of fire that forms when intense heat from a wildfire and turbulent wind conditions combine to create rotating columns of fire. They can be as tall as several kilometers and move unpredictably, posing extreme dangers to firefighters.

The Dansgaard–Oeschger events were rapid climate fluctuations during the last glacial period in which Greenland temperatures warmed by 10–15°C within decades, followed by gradual cooling, then abrupt returns to cold conditions. Over 25 such events occurred between about 115,000 and 12,000 years ago.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The Younger Dryas was a sudden return to near-glacial conditions about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, interrupting the warming after the last ice age. Greenland temperatures plunged by about 10–15°C within a decade, possibly triggered by a disruption of the Atlantic Ocean circulation due to meltwater flooding.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Milankovitch cycles are periodic changes in Earth's orbital shape (eccentricity), axial tilt (obliquity), and the direction its axis points (precession) that alter how much solar radiation reaches different latitudes. These cycles, with periods of roughly 100,000, 41,000, and 21,000 years respectively, drive Earth's glacial-interglacial cycles.

Acid rain forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides emitted by burning fossil fuels and industrial processes react with water in the atmosphere to produce sulfuric and nitric acids. It damages forests, acidifies lakes, and corrodes buildings and monuments.

Urban heat islands form when cities replace natural land cover with buildings, roads, and other surfaces that absorb and re-radiate heat, making urban areas 1–7°C (1.8–12.6°F) warmer than surrounding rural areas. This effect intensifies heatwaves and raises cooling energy demand in cities.

The Sirocco is a Mediterranean wind originating from the Sahara Desert that can reach hurricane speeds and carry large amounts of dust across North Africa and Southern Europe, particularly Italy, Malta, and Spain. It brings hot, dry conditions to the African coast and becomes hot and humid by the time it reaches the northern Mediterranean.

The Mistral is a strong, cold, dry wind that blows from the north through the Rhône Valley to the Mediterranean coast of France, often exceeding 90 km/h (56 mph) and persisting for days. It is caused by the pressure difference between the high pressure of the French interior and low pressure over the Mediterranean.

The Santa Ana winds are strong, extremely dry offshore winds that originate inland and blow toward the Pacific Coast of Southern California, typically from October through March. These winds create extreme wildfire conditions by lowering humidity, raising temperatures, and fanning flames.

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Los Angeles

text: The Bora is a cold, dry, gusty katabatic wind that blows from the northeast down the Dinaric Alps toward the Adriatic Sea coast of Croatia, Slovenia, and Italy. Wind gusts can exceed 200 km/h (125 mph) in the strongest events and are strong enough to overturn vehicles.

Katabatic winds are gravity-driven winds that form when cold, dense air on high terrain (such as Antarctic ice sheets or mountain plateaus) slides downhill under the force of gravity. In Antarctica, katabatic winds can exceed 300 km/h (186 mph) near the coast, making it one of the windiest places on Earth.

A land breeze and sea breeze are thermally driven coastal winds caused by the different rates at which land and water heat and cool. During the day, the land heats faster than the sea, causing air to rise over land and a sea breeze to blow inland; at night, the land cools faster, reversing the flow into a land breeze.

Solar irradiance — the total amount of solar energy received at Earth's outer atmosphere — varies by roughly 0.1% over the 11-year solar cycle. While solar variability can influence regional climate patterns, the observed warming since the mid-20th century cannot be explained by solar changes alone and is primarily attributed to greenhouse gas emissions.

Relative humidity measures how much water vapor is in the air relative to the maximum amount it could hold at that temperature, expressed as a percentage. Warm air can hold far more water vapor than cold air, which is why tropical regions feel so muggy even at the same relative humidity as cooler climates.

A cold front forms where a cold air mass advances and displaces a warmer air mass, typically producing a narrow band of intense precipitation and a sharp temperature drop after passage. Cold fronts move faster than warm fronts and can trigger severe thunderstorms along their leading edge.

A warm front is the boundary where a warmer air mass gradually advances over and replaces a cooler one, typically producing widespread, steady precipitation ahead of it over a broad area. Warm fronts are associated with low stratus clouds, light rain, and a gradual temperature increase after passage.

An occluded front forms when a fast-moving cold front catches up with a slower warm front, lifting the warm air mass off the surface. Occluded fronts are common in mature mid-latitude cyclones and are usually associated with complex precipitation patterns.

A stationary front is a boundary between two air masses that shows little movement, leading to prolonged periods of cloudiness, wind, and precipitation along the boundary. A stationary front can persist for days and cause significant flooding from persistent rainfall over the same area.

Barometric pressure (atmospheric pressure) at sea level averages about 1,013.25 millibars (hPa). Falling pressure typically indicates an approaching storm, while rising pressure often signals clearing weather — a principle sailors and farmers have used for centuries.

Radiosonde-equipped weather balloons are launched twice daily at hundreds of locations worldwide to measure temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind at heights up to 30 km (18 miles). These upper-air measurements are essential inputs for numerical weather prediction models.

Typhoon Tip (1979) is the largest and most intense tropical cyclone on record, with a diameter of approximately 2,220 km (1,380 miles) — nearly half the size of the continental United States — and a minimum central pressure of 870 hPa, the lowest ever recorded for any tropical cyclone.

The Saffir-Simpson scale only accounts for wind speed; storm surge, rainfall, and flooding are not included in the category rating, which is why lower-category storms like Tropical Storm Allison (2001) can cause more fatalities and damage than higher-category storms that lack these flood components.

Coral bleaching occurs when ocean temperatures rise just 1–2°C above the normal summer maximum for several weeks, causing corals to expel their symbiotic algae and turn white. Mass coral bleaching events have become far more frequent and severe since the 1980s due to climate-change-driven ocean warming.

Ocean acidification is the ongoing decrease in the pH of Earth's oceans caused by the absorption of CO₂ from the atmosphere. Since the industrial revolution, ocean pH has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 — a 26% increase in acidity that threatens shellfish, corals, and marine ecosystems.

Thundersnow is a rare meteorological event in which snowfall is accompanied by lightning and thunder. It requires very unstable atmospheric conditions, typically occurring when a significant amount of lift forces cold, moist air rapidly upward within a winter storm.

Snow squalls are intense but short-lived bursts of heavy snow accompanied by strong gusty winds, causing near-zero visibility and dangerous road conditions. The National Weather Service in the United States issues Snow Squall Warnings for these brief but treacherous events.

A solar flare is an intense burst of radiation from the Sun that can disrupt high-frequency radio communications on the Earth-facing side within minutes. Extreme flares can also produce geomagnetic storms that disrupt power grids and satellite operations.

A geomagnetic storm occurs when energy released by the Sun disturbs Earth's magnetosphere. The strongest geomagnetic storm on record — the Carrington Event of September 1859 — caused telegraph systems worldwide to fail and auroras visible as far south as Cuba.

Altocumulus clouds are mid-level clouds (6,500–20,000 feet / 2,000–6,000 m) consisting of white or gray patches, sheets, or layers and made primarily of water droplets. Altocumulus castellanus (turrets rising from their tops) is a sign of instability at mid-levels that can precede afternoon thunderstorm development.

Lenticular clouds are lens-shaped clouds that typically form on the downwind side of mountains where stable, moist air is lifted over ridges and creates wave patterns in the atmosphere. Because they remain stationary while strong winds blow through them, lenticular clouds are often mistaken for UFOs.

Nacreous clouds, also called polar stratospheric clouds or 'mother-of-pearl' clouds, form in the lower stratosphere at extremely cold temperatures (below −85°C) at altitudes of 15–25 km. They are most commonly seen at high latitudes in winter and play an important role in ozone depletion chemistry.

A supercell thunderstorm is a long-lived, deep, rotating thunderstorm organized around a persistent rotating updraft called a mesocyclone. Supercells produce the majority of significant tornadoes, as well as large hail (greater than 2 inches in diameter) and damaging winds.

A squall line is an elongated line of severe thunderstorms that can extend hundreds of miles and move as an organized system. As the leading edge of cold outflow air undercuts warm moist air, it continuously regenerates new storm cells along the line.

Anvil-shaped cumulonimbus clouds form when a rising thunderstorm updraft reaches the tropopause — the boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere — where temperature inversion prevents further ascent. The cloud then spreads horizontally into the characteristic flat-topped, anvil shape pointing in the direction of upper-level winds.

The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is a major atmospheric pattern based on the pressure difference between the Icelandic Low and the Azores High. During positive NAO phases, northern Europe experiences milder, wetter winters, while negative NAO phases bring colder, drier weather to northern Europe and stormier conditions in the Mediterranean.

The Arctic Oscillation (AO) is a pattern of atmospheric pressure that alternates between positive and negative phases across the Arctic and mid-latitudes. During negative AO phases, the polar vortex weakens, allowing cold Arctic air to spill southward and causing extreme cold outbreaks.

Global average sea surface temperatures have risen approximately 0.9°C (1.6°F) since 1880, with the rate of warming accelerating in recent decades. Warmer sea surfaces provide more energy and moisture for tropical cyclones, contributing to more intense storms.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The global water cycle (hydrological cycle) moves water among the ocean, atmosphere, and land through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff. Climate change is intensifying this cycle — wet regions are getting wetter and dry regions drier — as warmer air holds more moisture and releases it more intensely.

Methane (CH₄) is about 80 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO₂ over a 20-year period, though it breaks down much faster in the atmosphere. Key sources include livestock digestion, rice paddies, fossil fuel extraction, and thawing permafrost.

Aerosols — tiny liquid or solid particles suspended in the atmosphere — can either warm or cool the climate depending on their composition and color. Sulfate aerosols from volcanic eruptions and industrial emissions scatter sunlight and have a net cooling effect, partially masking greenhouse warming.

source.name: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies

text: The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines injected about 20 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, creating a global aerosol layer that lowered global average temperatures by approximately 0.5°C (0.9°F) for about two years. This event provided a natural experiment that confirmed the cooling power of aerosols.

The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia was so massive that it caused 'The Year Without a Summer' in 1816, when global temperatures dropped enough to cause widespread crop failures and famine across North America, Europe, and Asia. It remains the deadliest volcanic event in recorded history.

The Dust Bowl of the 1930s was a period of severe dust storms that devastated the agricultural prairies of the U.S. and Canadian Great Plains, triggered by a combination of prolonged drought and poor farming practices that removed native grasses. Millions of acres of topsoil were blown away, forcing some 3.5 million people to migrate.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The hydrometer (not to be confused with a hygrometer) is an instrument for measuring the density of liquids, while a hygrometer measures atmospheric humidity. The first practical hygrometer was invented by Leonardo da Vinci around 1490, using a ball of wool and wax to detect moisture differences.

Gabriel Fahrenheit invented the mercury thermometer in 1714 and defined the temperature scale still used in the United States. He set 32°F as the freezing point of water and 212°F as the boiling point, creating a scale that remains in common use in the U.S. despite widespread adoption of Celsius globally.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The psychrometric chart (or humidity chart) is a graphical representation of the thermodynamic properties of moist air and is used by meteorologists, engineers, and HVAC professionals to determine dew point, wet bulb temperature, and enthalpy from dry bulb temperature and relative humidity.

Sea ice, unlike land-based glaciers, does not raise sea level when it melts because the floating ice is already displacing its weight in water (Archimedes' principle). However, melting land ice from glaciers and ice sheets does raise sea level.

source.name: NASA National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: Greenland holds enough ice to raise global sea levels by about 7.2 meters (24 feet) if it all melted, while Antarctica's ice sheet holds enough to raise sea levels by approximately 58 meters (190 feet). Both ice sheets are losing mass at accelerating rates due to climate change.

Albedo is a measure of how much solar radiation a surface reflects, ranging from 0 (perfect absorption) to 1 (perfect reflection). Fresh snow has a high albedo of 0.8–0.9, while the open ocean has a low albedo of 0.06. As ice and snow melt due to warming, darker ocean and land surfaces are exposed, absorbing more heat — a positive feedback that amplifies warming.

The wet bulb temperature is measured by a thermometer covered in a wet cloth and cooled by evaporation; it represents the lowest temperature to which air can be cooled by evaporating water into it. A wet bulb temperature of 35°C (95°F) is considered the upper limit of human survivability because evaporative cooling of the skin becomes ineffective.

Hurricane Harvey (2017) stalled over southeastern Texas and dropped more than 60 inches (1,524 mm) of rain in some locations over four days — the largest rainfall event from a tropical system ever recorded in the United States. The catastrophic flooding caused an estimated $125 billion in damage.

The deadliest Atlantic hurricane on record is the Great Hurricane of 1780, which killed approximately 22,000–27,000 people across Barbados, St. Eustatius, and Martinique. It remains the most lethal Atlantic tropical cyclone in recorded history.

The deadliest cyclone in recorded history is Cyclone Bhola (1970), which struck what is now Bangladesh and India's West Bengal, killing between 300,000 and 500,000 people. The combination of storm surge, high tidal flooding, and extremely low-lying land caused catastrophic loss of life.

The Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925 is the deadliest tornado in U.S. history, killing 695 people as it traveled an extraordinary 219 miles (352 km) through Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana at speeds up to 70 mph (113 km/h). It remains the longest tracked tornado on record in the United States.

A thunderstorm is classified as severe when it produces wind gusts of 58 mph (93 km/h) or greater, hail 1 inch (2.54 cm) in diameter or larger, or a tornado. The United States experiences about 100,000 thunderstorms each year, of which roughly 10,000 are severe.

Tornado Alley is an informal term used to describe an area in the south-central United States — particularly Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska — that experiences a disproportionately high frequency of tornadoes due to the frequent clash of cold dry air from the Rockies with warm moist Gulf air. However, a 'Dixie Alley' in the Southeast also sees high tornado frequency.

Funnel clouds are rotating columns of air extending from the base of a thunderstorm toward the ground. A funnel cloud becomes a tornado only when it makes contact with Earth's surface. A large majority of funnel clouds never touch down.

Land tornadoes typically appear gray, tan, or brown because they pick up soil and debris, while tornadoes over water (waterspouts) can appear white or translucent due to condensing water vapor. A tornado's color also depends on the direction of sunlight and the type of terrain it crosses.

The 'Pineapple Express' is a colloquial term for a particularly strong atmospheric river that originates near Hawaii and delivers exceptionally heavy rainfall and high-elevation snow to western North America, particularly the Pacific Coast. These events can last several days and bring several months worth of precipitation.

A polar climate (Köppen E) is defined by the absence of true summer: the warmest month averages below 10°C (50°F). Polar climates are found in the Arctic and Antarctic regions and at high elevations, and they support tundra or permanent ice cap ecosystems.

The Mediterranean climate (Köppen Csa/Csb) is characterized by hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, found in regions around the Mediterranean Sea, coastal California, central Chile, South Africa's Cape region, and southwestern Australia. This climate is ideal for growing olives, grapes, and citrus.

Steppe climates are semi-arid regions that receive 25–500 mm (10–20 inches) of precipitation annually and are too dry to support forest but too moist to be true deserts. They typically surround hot deserts and support grassland ecosystems like the Eurasian steppes and African savannas.

A continental climate (Köppen D) is characterized by large seasonal temperature extremes, with warm to hot summers and cold, snowy winters. Locations far from moderating ocean influence — such as Siberia, central Canada, and the northern U.S. — experience the most extreme versions, with annual temperature ranges exceeding 50°C.

Perihelion — Earth's closest approach to the Sun — occurs in early January at about 147.1 million km, while aphelion — Earth's farthest point from the Sun — occurs in early July at about 152.1 million km. This 3.4% difference in distance means Earth receives about 7% more solar radiation in January than July, demonstrating that seasons are caused by axial tilt, not orbital distance.

Earth's seasons are caused by the 23.5° tilt of its rotational axis relative to its orbit around the Sun, not by its distance from the Sun. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun (June), it receives more direct sunlight and longer days — producing summer. The Southern Hemisphere simultaneously tilts away, producing winter.

The equinoxes (around March 20 and September 22) are the two times per year when Earth's axis is perpendicular to the Sun's rays, resulting in nearly equal hours of daylight and darkness everywhere on Earth. During the solstices (around June 21 and December 21), one hemisphere experiences its longest day and the other its shortest.

Midnight Sun is a natural phenomenon occurring in summer months poleward of the Arctic Circle (66.5°N) and Antarctic Circle (66.5°S), where the Sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours a day. Conversely, these regions experience Polar Night in winter, with the Sun below the horizon for 24 continuous hours.

Sundog (parhelion) is a bright spot that appears on one or both sides of the Sun, produced when sunlight refracts through hexagonal ice crystals in cirrus or cirrostratus clouds. Sundogs are most visible when the Sun is near the horizon and appear as rainbow-colored patches approximately 22° to the left and right of the Sun.

A 22° halo is a ring of light around the Sun or Moon formed when sunlight or moonlight refracts through hexagonal ice crystals in cirrus clouds. The halo appears at exactly 22° from the Sun or Moon, and a halo around the Moon is a traditional indicator of incoming rain or snow.

A glory is a circular rainbow-like optical phenomenon that appears opposite the Sun around an observer's shadow, typically visible when an observer (on a mountain or in an aircraft) looks down on a cloud layer below. It is caused by light diffracting around tiny cloud droplets and is often nicknamed 'The Pilot's Halo' by aviators.

A mirage is an optical phenomenon caused by the refraction of light through heated air layers near the ground, creating an illusion of water or distant objects. In hot deserts, inferior mirages make the sky visible near the horizon, appearing as a shimmering pool of water.

Fata Morgana is a complex, rapidly changing superior mirage found at sea, in polar regions, and occasionally over deserts, in which objects appear stacked, stretched, or inverted due to extreme atmospheric temperature gradients. It can make distant ships appear to float in the air or transform coastlines into fantastical shapes.

Crepuscular rays are shafts of sunlight that stream through gaps in clouds or trees, made visible by dust and moisture particles scattering light. They appear to radiate from the Sun but are actually parallel; they appear to converge due to perspective, the same way railroad tracks seem to converge in the distance.

The Inversion layer in the atmosphere is a layer where temperature increases with height rather than decreasing, trapping pollutants, moisture, and fog near the surface. Los Angeles' notorious smog is partly caused by subsidence inversions that trap polluted air against the mountains and prevent it from dispersing.

The stratosphere extends from about 12 to 50 km altitude and is characterized by temperature increasing with height (due to ozone absorbing UV radiation), which makes it very stable and devoid of convective weather. Jet aircraft cruise in the lower stratosphere to take advantage of smooth, predictable air.

The mesosphere is the atmospheric layer from about 50 to 80 km altitude, where temperatures decrease to as low as −90°C — the coldest temperatures anywhere in Earth's atmosphere. Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere, creating the streaks of light known as 'shooting stars'.

The thermosphere extends from about 80 to 700 km and is where air molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation, causing temperatures to rise to 2,000°C or more. Despite these extreme temperatures, the air is so thin that there are too few molecules per unit volume to transfer significant heat to an object — a spacecraft or astronaut would actually lose heat in this layer.

Lightning can strike the same place more than once — in fact, tall structures like the Empire State Building are struck by lightning about 20–25 times per year. The idea that lightning never strikes the same spot twice is a myth.

Benjamin Franklin proved in 1752 that lightning is electrical in nature by flying a kite in a thunderstorm and conducting charge down a wet string to a Leyden jar. He went on to invent the lightning rod, which protects buildings by providing a low-resistance path for lightning to travel to the ground.

Lightning is actually bidirectional: a faint channel called a stepped leader descends from the cloud, and when it gets close to the ground, a return stroke rushes upward from the ground to the cloud. What we see as a flash moving downward is actually the brighter upward-moving return stroke.

Anemometers measure wind speed, and the cup anemometer — the most common type — uses three or four rotating cups whose rotation rate is proportional to wind speed. The first mechanical wind speed measuring device was created by Leon Battista Alberti around 1450.

The first weather forecast issued to the public was a storm warning telegraphed to ships on the English coast by Vice Admiral Robert FitzRoy of the British Met Office in 1861. FitzRoy coined the term 'forecast' and established the first operational weather service.

Numerical weather prediction was first conceptualized by Lewis Fry Richardson during World War I; he used mathematical equations to calculate a 6-hour pressure change forecast in 1916, though it took him weeks to compute and the result was wrong due to the initial data not being smoothed. Modern computers now perform such calculations in minutes.

The first weather satellite, TIROS-1, was launched by NASA on April 1, 1960, and transmitted the first televised pictures of Earth's cloud cover. This launch revolutionized meteorology, making it possible to observe weather patterns over remote and oceanic areas for the first time.

source.name: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive

text: Ensemble forecasting runs multiple versions of a weather model simultaneously, each starting from slightly different initial conditions to account for uncertainty. By examining the spread of the ensemble's predictions, forecasters can quantify uncertainty and produce probabilistic forecasts rather than single deterministic outlooks.

The chaos theory concept of sensitive dependence on initial conditions is known as the 'butterfly effect', coined by meteorologist Edward Lorenz in the 1960s. He showed that the atmosphere is a chaotic system where tiny differences in initial conditions lead to vastly different outcomes, fundamentally limiting deterministic weather forecasting beyond about two weeks.

Freezing drizzle consists of supercooled drizzle drops that freeze on contact with surfaces at or below 0°C (32°F), creating a thin, clear glaze. Even light freezing drizzle can cause treacherous icy conditions on roads and sidewalks, requiring treatment with sand, salt, or deicers.

In 1816, 'The Year Without a Summer', snow fell in New England in June and July following the eruption of Mount Tambora, destroying crops and causing widespread famine. This climate disaster is also believed to have inspired Mary Shelley to write Frankenstein, as she was confined indoors with Byron and Percy Shelley in the dreary Swiss summer of 1816.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The Great Blizzard of 1888 paralyzed the northeastern United States with snowfall of up to 58 inches (147 cm) and drifts 40–50 feet (12–15 m) high in some areas, killing over 400 people. This disaster led to the construction of New York City's underground subway system to reduce reliance on overland transportation.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The Great Galveston Hurricane of 1900 remains the deadliest natural disaster in United States history, killing between 8,000 and 12,000 people when a Category 4 hurricane's storm surge inundated the Texas barrier island. It led directly to the construction of a 5-meter (17-foot) seawall and the raising of the city's grade.

The Paris Agreement (2015) is an international treaty that aims to limit global average temperature rise to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. It was adopted by 196 parties at the UNFCCC COP21 and entered into force in November 2016.

The WMO defines a climate normal as the 30-year average of a climate variable (such as temperature or precipitation) and updates these normals every 10 years. The current international standard normals are based on the 1991–2020 averaging period, replacing the previous 1981–2010 normals.

A 'blocking pattern' in the atmosphere occurs when a quasi-stationary high-pressure system prevents the normal west-to-east progression of weather systems, sometimes for days or weeks. Atmospheric blocking was associated with the 2003 European heat wave and is linked to extreme weather persistence.

A tropical cyclone requires an ocean surface temperature of at least 26°C (79°F) to depths of around 50 meters to develop and sustain itself. As a cyclone moves over cooler water or land, it weakens because the energy source from warm, evaporating seawater is cut off.

Wind shear — changes in wind speed or direction with height — disrupts the structure of tropical cyclones, preventing or weakening their development. This is why El Niño years, which increase wind shear in the Atlantic, typically produce fewer and weaker Atlantic hurricanes.

source.name: NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory

text: Post-tropical cyclones are former tropical cyclones that have lost their tropical characteristics. When a hurricane becomes extratropical, it can actually expand in size and affect vast areas far north — as occurred with Superstorm Sandy (2012), which transitioned to extratropical status before making landfall in New Jersey.

The heat burst is a rare meteorological phenomenon in which a descending column of rain evaporates completely before reaching the ground, causing the air to warm and rush toward the surface as a sudden blast of extremely hot, dry wind. Temperatures can rise 10–20°C within minutes during a heat burst, occurring at night when conditions are otherwise cool.

Ring of Fire cyclones in the Southern Hemisphere spin clockwise, the opposite of Northern Hemisphere hurricanes, due to the Coriolis effect. Both hemispheres' storms still draw energy from warm ocean water and have low-pressure centers, but their rotation direction is reversed.

The concept of 'feels like' temperature — combining actual temperature with wind chill in winter and heat index in summer — better represents how weather affects the human body than temperature alone. The National Weather Service issues Excessive Heat Warnings when heat index values are expected to exceed 105°F (40.5°C) for two or more hours.

Radiant energy from the Sun travels about 150 million km (93 million miles) and arrives at Earth's outer atmosphere at roughly 1,361 watts per square meter — a value called the solar constant. About 30% of this energy is immediately reflected back to space by clouds, aerosols, and Earth's surface; the remainder is absorbed and drives weather and climate.

Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released by a substance during a phase change (e.g., water evaporating or condensing) without a change in temperature. In the atmosphere, the release of latent heat when water vapor condenses inside thunderstorm updrafts is the primary energy source that powers severe weather.

The ozone layer was discovered in the lower stratosphere by French physicists Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson in 1913. Its role in blocking ultraviolet radiation was described more fully by G.M.B. Dobson in the 1920s, who also invented the Dobsonmeter — the instrument still used to measure total ozone column thickness, expressed in Dobson units.

Global warming is not uniform: the Arctic is warming more than twice as fast as the global average — a phenomenon called Arctic amplification. This accelerated warming is reducing sea ice, thawing permafrost, and altering the temperature gradient that drives the jet stream.

Geoengineering refers to large-scale interventions to counteract climate change, such as stratospheric aerosol injection (seeding the stratosphere with reflective particles to reduce solar radiation) or marine cloud brightening. These techniques are highly experimental, with significant uncertainties about unintended regional effects.

The Beaufort Sea, located north of Alaska and Canada, is one of the fastest-warming ocean regions on Earth. In recent decades, it has experienced dramatic declines in multi-year sea ice — the thickest and oldest type — which has been replaced by thinner, first-year ice that melts more easily.

A flash flood is the most dangerous type of flood, characterized by rapid onset (within 6 hours) and high-velocity water caused by intense, localized rainfall, dam failures, or ice jams. Flash floods kill more people per year in the United States than any other severe weather event, including hurricanes and tornadoes.

The Sahara Desert, the world's largest hot desert, was significantly wetter and greener during the African Humid Period (roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago), when monsoon rains extended into regions that are now hyperarid. This 'Green Sahara' period is well-documented in lake sediments, fossil river channels, and cave art.

The monsoon is actually driven by the differential heating of land and sea: in summer, the land heats faster than the ocean, creating low pressure over land that draws in moist ocean air, bringing heavy rainfall. This reverses in winter when the land cools faster, driving dry air outward from the continent.

Cloud seeding is a weather modification technique that disperses substances (typically silver iodide, dry ice, or liquid propane) into clouds to encourage precipitation. China operates the world's largest cloud seeding program to combat drought and has even used it to ensure dry weather during major events like the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

The Beaufort Scale was extended to include Force 13 through 17 (winds of 72+ knots) by the U.S. Navy in 1955 for use in tropical cyclone situations, though these extensions are rarely used outside of typhoon reporting in the western Pacific. The original 0–12 scale remains the international standard.

Isobar lines on a weather map connect points of equal atmospheric pressure, and their spacing and curvature indicate wind speed and direction: tightly packed isobars indicate strong winds, while widely spaced isobars mean lighter winds. Closed loops of isobars represent high- or low-pressure systems.

Typhoon Haiyan (known locally as Yolanda) struck the Philippines in November 2013 with estimated wind gusts of 315 km/h (195 mph) — among the strongest ever recorded at landfall for a tropical cyclone — and storm surges of up to 7 meters (23 feet), killing over 6,300 people.

The global average precipitation is approximately 990 mm (39 inches) per year, but this is far from uniformly distributed. Oceans receive more precipitation than land on average because more water evaporates from them, and mountains, equatorial regions, and mid-latitude storm tracks receive far more rain than continental interiors and subtropical deserts.

Ice cores drilled from Greenland and Antarctica contain annual layers of compressed snow that preserve air bubbles, dust, pollen, and chemical signatures stretching back 800,000 years. The oldest continuous ice core record — from Antarctica's Dome C — reveals eight complete glacial-interglacial cycles, showing that carbon dioxide concentrations closely tracked global temperature changes across the entire record.

Dendroclimatology — the study of tree rings to reconstruct past climates — works because trees in temperature- or moisture-limited environments produce wider rings in good growth years and narrower rings in bad ones. Tree-ring networks spanning thousands of years have been used to reconstruct Northern Hemisphere temperatures back to 1000 CE, revealing the Medieval Warm Period and the Little Ice Age as significant regional climate variations.

Ocean sediment cores preserve the shells of foraminifera — microscopic marine organisms whose oxygen isotope ratios reflect the temperature of the water they lived in. By analysing foraminifera from thousands of sediment cores worldwide, scientists have reconstructed sea surface temperatures and ice volumes for the past 65 million years, allowing the entire Cenozoic climate history to be mapped.

Speleothem records — growth layers in stalactites and stalagmites in caves — preserve oxygen and carbon isotope signals from ancient rainwater, extending high-resolution climate records in tropical and subtropical regions where ice cores and tree rings are unavailable. Chinese cave records from Dongge and Heshang caves have reconstructed Asian monsoon variability for the past 224,000 years.

The Milankovitch cycles — periodic variations in Earth's orbital eccentricity (100,000 years), axial tilt or obliquity (41,000 years), and precession of the equinoxes (23,000 years) — were proposed by Serbian mathematician Milutin Milankovitch in the 1920s and confirmed by ice core and ocean sediment data in the 1970s as the primary pacemaker of ice age cycles.

The Younger Dryas event (c. 12,900–11,700 years ago) was a rapid return to near-glacial conditions following the initial warming after the Last Glacial Maximum, with temperatures in Greenland plunging by 10°C within decades. It is thought to have been caused by a massive pulse of cold freshwater from melting ice sheets that disrupted the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.

The Holocene Climatic Optimum (c. 9,000–5,000 years ago) was a period when Northern Hemisphere summers were warmer than today — up to 1–3°C above pre-industrial levels in high latitudes — due to orbital forcing with greater summer insolation; the Sahara was green, the monsoon extended further north, and there were hippos in the Rhine. This period is distinct from current human-caused warming.

The Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM), approximately 56 million years ago, saw global temperatures rise 5–8°C within 20,000 years after a massive release of carbon into the atmosphere — possibly from volcanic activity or seafloor methane hydrates. It is considered the closest geological analogue to modern anthropogenic climate change, though it occurred roughly 10 times slower than the current carbon release rate.

source.name: Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences

text: The 'hockey stick' temperature graph — a reconstruction of Northern Hemisphere temperatures over the past 1,000 years by Michael Mann and colleagues published in 1999 — showed relatively stable temperatures before a dramatic 20th-century rise, resembling a hockey stick's blade. Despite intense controversy and multiple attempts to discredit it, the core finding has been reproduced by over a dozen independent research groups using different data and methods.

The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) was established in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and UNEP to synthesise scientific knowledge on climate change for policymakers. Its six Assessment Reports — published in 1990, 1995, 2001, 2007, 2013–2014, and 2021–2022 — each involve thousands of authors reviewing tens of thousands of scientific papers and represent the largest peer-review process in the history of science.

The Keeling Curve — the continuous record of atmospheric CO₂ measured at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, since 1958 by Charles David Keeling — is the longest direct measurement of atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations. It shows an unambiguous upward trend from 315 ppm in 1958 to over 420 ppm in 2023, with a characteristic seasonal sawtooth pattern caused by Northern Hemisphere plant growth.

Solar Radiation Management (SRM) geoengineering proposals aim to cool the Earth by reflecting more sunlight back to space — either by injecting sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere (mimicking volcanic eruptions), brightening marine clouds, or placing sunshades in space. While potentially effective at rapid cooling, SRM does not reduce CO₂ and creates risks of 'termination shock' if suddenly stopped, altered precipitation patterns, and international governance challenges.

Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) methods — the 'other half' of geoengineering — aim to reduce atmospheric CO₂ directly through biological means (afforestation, ocean iron fertilisation, bioenergy with carbon capture, enhanced weathering) or direct air capture (DAC) machines. Current DAC facilities can remove thousands of tonnes of CO₂ per year; to be climatically meaningful, the scale would need to expand to billions of tonnes annually — a factor of a million times larger.

Cloud seeding — the injection of silver iodide, potassium iodide, or liquid propane into clouds to encourage ice crystal formation and precipitation — has been used since Bernard Vonnegut's 1946 discovery and is now deployed commercially in over 50 countries. The United Arab Emirates, with an average rainfall of just 78 mm per year, has the world's most active cloud seeding programme, conducting over 1,000 sorties per year.

Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) occur because cities replace vegetation and soil with dark, heat-absorbing surfaces like asphalt and concrete that store more solar energy; they are also warmed by waste heat from vehicles, air conditioning, and industry. Large cities can be 1–7°C warmer than surrounding rural areas, and the UHI effect intensifies during heat waves, significantly increasing heat-related mortality in dense urban centres.

A microburst is an intense small-scale downdraft produced by a thunderstorm that spreads outward in all directions on reaching the surface, creating sudden extreme wind shear. Wet microbursts, occurring in humid conditions with heavy rain, are associated with the low-altitude wind shear that caused several major aviation disasters in the 1970s–1980s, including Delta Air Lines Flight 191 at Dallas in 1985, which killed 137 people.

A derecho is a long-lived, widespread, straight-line windstorm associated with a band of rapidly moving showers or thunderstorms; to qualify, it must produce a swath of damage extending more than 400 km with wind gusts of at least 93 km/h. The July 1995 Boundary Waters-Canadian derecho is one of history's worst, blowing down over 550,000 acres of timber across Minnesota and Ontario in a single event.

The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air surrounding Earth's poles that exists year-round in the stratosphere and troposphere; when it weakens or becomes distorted, it allows extremely cold Arctic air to spill southward into mid-latitudes. Major polar vortex disruptions — 'sudden stratospheric warmings' — can precede the anomalous cold spells that hit the continental US and Europe, producing temperatures tens of degrees below normal.

Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are narrow corridors of concentrated water vapour in the atmosphere — typically 400–600 km wide but thousands of kilometres long — that transport more than twice the average flow of the Amazon River through the atmosphere. A single strong atmospheric river event striking California can deliver as much as 25–50% of the state's annual rainfall in 1–2 weeks, making them both a critical water resource and a major flood hazard.

The first weather satellite, TIROS-1 (Television and Infrared Observation Satellite), was launched by NASA on 1 April 1960 and returned the first television images of Earth's cloud cover from space; within its 78-day operational life it transmitted over 22,000 cloud images, immediately revolutionising meteorologists' ability to track developing storms. The global satellite network now has over 200 operational meteorological satellites in polar and geostationary orbits.

Doppler weather radar, introduced operationally in the US through the NEXRAD network from 1988 onwards, can detect not only precipitation intensity but also wind velocity by measuring the frequency shift of radar returns from raindrops moving toward or away from the antenna. NEXRAD's ability to detect tornado-producing rotation signatures (mesocyclones) within supercell thunderstorms extended tornado warnings from an average of under 5 minutes to over 13 minutes.

The Beaufort Scale, developed by Royal Navy admiral Francis Beaufort in 1805 to standardise wind observations at sea, ranges from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force). It was adopted internationally in 1838 and extended to 17 on the scale used by Taiwan and China to classify typhoons; Force 12 requires sustained winds of at least 118 km/h (73 mph) sustained for at least 1 minute.

The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates Atlantic and eastern Pacific hurricanes from Category 1 (119–153 km/h sustained winds) to Category 5 (≥252 km/h), based solely on maximum sustained wind speed. It does not account for rainfall, storm surge, or storm size — the deadliest aspects of most hurricanes; Hurricane Katrina in 2005 was a Category 3 at landfall but caused catastrophic flooding from its surge, killing over 1,800 people.

The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, replacing the original Fujita scale in 2007 in the US and Canada, rates tornado intensity from EF0 (65–85 mph winds, minor damage to trees) to EF5 (over 200 mph, total destruction of well-built structures). Actual wind speeds are not directly measured but are estimated from damage indicators on 28 types of structures and vegetation, making tornado rating an inherently indirect forensic science.

The Medieval Warm Period (c. 950–1250 CE) was a time of above-average temperatures in the North Atlantic region, allowing Norse settlement of Greenland and even Vinland (North America). However, proxy data show that this warm episode was regional rather than globally synchronous — different regions warmed at different times — and global mean temperatures during this period were likely lower than today's.

The Little Ice Age (c. 1300–1850 CE) was a period of cooling across much of the Northern Hemisphere characterised by advancing mountain glaciers, severe winters, widespread crop failures, and altered storm tracks; the River Thames froze enough for Frost Fairs — markets on the ice — at least 24 times between 1309 and 1814. Multiple volcanic eruptions (including Tambora 1815) contributed to the coldest decades of this period.

The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia was the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history (VEI 7), ejecting 150 km³ of material and causing the 'Year Without a Summer' in 1816 — crop failures across the Northern Hemisphere, famines in Europe and North America, and the lowest Northern Hemisphere temperatures in 1,400 years. It directly contributed to Mary Shelley writing Frankenstein during a gloomy Swiss summer.

Weather folklore — 'Red sky at night, sailor's delight; red sky in morning, sailor's warning' — has a meteorological basis in mid-latitude weather systems that typically move from west to east. A red sky at sunset indicates dust-laden dry air to the west (fine weather approaching), while red morning sky reflects moisture in eastern air that weather systems have already passed through, suggesting a low-pressure system approaching from the west.

The global climate model (GCM) concept was pioneered by Syukuro Manabe and Richard Wetherald at NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, who in 1967 published the first simulation showing that doubling atmospheric CO₂ would warm the Earth by approximately 2°C — a figure that has remained central to climate science for over 50 years. Manabe shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics for this foundational work.

The Antarctic ozone hole — a seasonal thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer over Antarctica each September–October — was discovered by British scientists at Halley Bay in 1985; by 1987 the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer had been signed, and satellite data now show the ozone hole is gradually recovering, projected to return to 1980 levels by approximately 2066 over Antarctica.

source.name: WMO Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion

text: El Niño events — periodic warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific that occurs irregularly every 2–7 years — disrupt weather patterns worldwide: Australia experiences severe drought, Peru and Ecuador floods, and the Atlantic hurricane season quiets while California and the US Southwest receive above-normal rainfall. The strongest El Niño on record (1997–98) raised global average sea surface temperatures by 3°C above normal in the central Pacific.

Permafrost — permanently frozen ground covering approximately 25% of the Northern Hemisphere's land surface — stores an estimated 1,500 billion tonnes of organic carbon, roughly twice the current total atmospheric carbon. As Arctic temperatures warm at 2–4 times the global average rate, permafrost thaw releases CO₂ and methane (a greenhouse gas 80 times more potent than CO₂ over 20 years), creating a positive feedback loop that climate models increasingly factor into projections.

source.name: NSIDC National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: The Thermohaline Circulation (THC), also called the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), is a global ocean circulation system driven by differences in water temperature and salinity — denser, saltier water sinks in the North Atlantic, pulling in warm surface water from the tropics. This 'conveyor belt' moderates climates in Western Europe; models suggest AMOC is weakening and could collapse this century, potentially cooling Europe by several degrees despite global warming.

The 'Great Oxidation Event' approximately 2.4 billion years ago — when photosynthetic cyanobacteria flooded the atmosphere with oxygen for the first time — was Earth's most dramatic climate shift, causing the 'Huronian Glaciation': the first known global 'Snowball Earth' event. The oxygen catastrophe wiped out most anaerobic life but created the conditions that allowed complex aerobic organisms to evolve.

source.name: Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences

text: Lightning strikes Earth's surface approximately 40–50 times per second, totalling around 1.4 billion flashes per year. A single lightning bolt carries about 1 billion volts and 30,000 amperes, reaching temperatures of 30,000 K (five times hotter than the Sun's surface) for about 30 microseconds; lightning is responsible for an estimated 6,000 deaths per year globally and is a leading cause of wildfire ignition worldwide.

source.name: NASA Global Hydrology and Climate Center

text: The Coriolis effect — the deflection of moving air and water due to Earth's rotation — causes weather systems to rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. This effect is real for large-scale atmospheric and oceanic circulations, but is too weak to reliably determine the rotation direction of water draining from a bathtub; that is dominated by the basin's initial conditions and geometry.

The jet stream — a fast-flowing, narrow band of air in the upper atmosphere roughly 10 km above sea level, moving at 120–400 km/h — acts as a major steering mechanism for mid-latitude weather systems. The polar jet stream has been identified as weakening and becoming more 'wavy' as the Arctic warms disproportionately, potentially trapping weather systems in place longer and causing more persistent heat waves, floods, and droughts.

The 2003 European heatwave killed an estimated 70,000 people across Europe — the deadliest weather event in European history — as temperatures exceeded 40°C in countries without air conditioning infrastructure and with populations unaccustomed to heat. The catastrophe triggered sweeping changes to European public health infrastructure, heatwave early warning systems, and cooling centres, and accelerated research into attribution science linking individual extreme events to climate change.

The Drake Passage between South America and Antarctica — the widest and deepest oceanic passage on Earth, allowing the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to circle the globe — opened approximately 30–34 million years ago. This thermal isolation of Antarctica allowed ice sheets to form, cooling the planet significantly and contributing to the Cenozoic 'icehouse' that we still live in today.

Monsoons — seasonal reversals of wind direction that bring wet and dry seasons to large parts of Asia, Africa, Australia, and the Americas — affect the lives of roughly half the world's population. The South Asian monsoon delivers 70–90% of India's annual rainfall between June and September; a delay or failure of the monsoon can devastate agriculture, and intensification of the monsoon due to climate change is already producing both more intense wet seasons and longer dry spells.

The Paris Agreement (2015) established the goal of limiting global warming to 'well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels' and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. It is the first legally binding international climate treaty to include all nations; the 1.5°C threshold was included at the insistence of small island states and low-lying nations facing existential risk from sea level rise. By 2023, global average temperature was already 1.2°C above the pre-industrial baseline.

Sea level rise is driven by two main factors: thermal expansion of warming seawater (thermosteric rise) and the melting of land-based ice (glaciers and ice sheets). Current global mean sea level rise is approximately 3.7 mm per year — the highest rate in 3,000 years — with the rate accelerating; under high-emission scenarios, IPCC projects sea levels could rise 0.6–1.0 m by 2100, threatening hundreds of millions of coastal inhabitants.

Ocean acidification — the ongoing decrease in ocean pH caused by absorption of excess CO₂ from the atmosphere — has lowered average ocean pH from 8.2 to 8.1 since the Industrial Revolution, representing a 26% increase in hydrogen ion concentration.
