This threatens marine calcifiers (corals, molluscs, echinoderms) by making it harder to build and maintain calcium carbonate shells and skeletons, and is expected to have cascading effects on marine food webs.

The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is a climate pattern driven by the pressure difference between the Icelandic Low and the Azores High; in its positive phase it steers storms toward northern Europe and away from the Mediterranean, while the negative phase brings cold, dry winters to northern Europe and wetter conditions to the Mediterranean. The NAO explains much of the year-to-year variability in European winter weather independent of the long-term warming trend.

The deadliest drought in recorded history was the 1876–1879 Global Drought, which killed an estimated 30–60 million people in a 'Late Victorian Holocide' spanning India, China, Brazil, and Africa; it was driven by an exceptionally powerful El Niño event and was compounded by colonial policies that prioritised grain exports over famine relief. Mike Davis's 2001 book 'Late Victorian Holocausts' documented how colonial structures amplified climate-driven famine.

The Thermohaline Circulation takes approximately 1,000 years to complete one full circuit of the world's ocean basins. Deep water formed in the North Atlantic slowly moves south, around Antarctica, into the Indian and Pacific oceans, before gradually rising and returning as surface water. This slow overturning means that changes in deep ocean chemistry and temperature propagate through the system on millennial timescales.

Noctilucent clouds (NLCs) — electric-blue, filament-like clouds appearing near the poles in summer twilight at altitudes of 76–85 km — are the highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere, forming when water vapour freezes onto meteor dust. Since the 19th century NLCs have been spotted at progressively lower latitudes and have become more frequent, a trend linked to cooling of the upper atmosphere (mesosphere) caused by rising CO₂ — an unexpected climate fingerprint in the stratosphere.

source.name: NASA Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere

text: The Dust Bowl of the 1930s — a decade of severe drought combined with poor farming practices that stripped native prairie grass from millions of acres of Great Plains soil — produced the worst human-made ecological disaster in US history. Black blizzards (massive dust storms) buried farms, forced 3.5 million people from their homes, and reduced sunlight in Chicago to night-time conditions; it directly informed soil conservation policy and the founding of the US Soil Conservation Service in 1935.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Attribution science — determining what fraction of the probability of a specific extreme weather event is attributable to human-caused climate change — has developed rapidly since the 2004 publication of the first such study (on the 2003 European heatwave). By 2023, attribution studies have shown that most observed major heatwaves would have been virtually impossible without human greenhouse gas emissions, fundamentally changing legal and policy discussions about climate liability.

The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines (VEI 6) injected 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, creating a global veil of sulphate aerosols that reflected 2–3% of incoming sunlight and cooled the Earth by about 0.5°C over 1992–1993. Pinatubo's observed cooling provided real-world evidence for proposed stratospheric aerosol injection geoengineering schemes, but also revealed regional disruptions including drought in the Sahel.

Pollen preserved in lake sediments and bogs can be identified to family, genus, and sometimes species level, allowing ecologists to reconstruct changes in vegetation over thousands of years. Palynological studies across Europe have documented the Neolithic replacement of mixed deciduous forest with agricultural grassland and the subsequent reforestation following the post-Roman population collapse of the 6th century — directly linking human demographic history and climate-driven vegetation change.

The global average surface temperature has risen by approximately 1.2°C since the pre-industrial baseline (1850–1900); the past decade (2014–2023) is the warmest in recorded history, and 2023 set a new global record at 1.45°C above the pre-industrial average. The rate of warming has roughly doubled since 1975, primarily driven by CO₂ and methane from fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, and agriculture.

Ball lightning — luminous, floating spheres of plasma ranging from pea-sized to over a metre in diameter, sometimes passing through glass windows or persisting for up to 30 seconds — remains one of meteorology's most debated phenomena despite hundreds of witness reports across history. Proposed explanations include microwave radiation from cloud-to-ground lightning, silicon vapour oxidation, and antimatter annihilation; no scientific consensus has been reached.

Mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) — organised clusters of thunderstorms spanning hundreds of kilometres — produce more rain than any other type of weather system, responsible for over 50% of warm-season rainfall across the central United States and much of tropical Africa. MCSs can persist for 12–24 hours and generate tornadoes, large hail, damaging straight-line winds, and flash flooding simultaneously across an area the size of France.

The 1970 Bhola cyclone that struck East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) on 12 November 1970 is the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history, killing between 300,000 and 500,000 people in storm surges that inundated the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta. The Pakistan government's inadequate response to the disaster fuelled political anger that contributed to the Bangladesh Liberation War and the creation of Bangladesh the following year.

Ice ages — glacial periods within the current Quaternary ice age that began approximately 2.6 million years ago — occur in cycles paced by Milankovitch orbital forcing; during the Last Glacial Maximum (c. 21,000 years ago) ice sheets up to 4 km thick covered all of Canada, northern Europe, and parts of Asia, sea level was 120–130 m lower than today, and global average temperature was about 6°C cooler than the 20th-century average.

The stratospheric 'quasi-biennial oscillation' (QBO) is a regular reversal of equatorial stratospheric winds between easterly and westerly directions with a mean period of about 28 months; it modulates Northern Hemisphere winter weather, tropical cyclone frequency, and the strength of the polar vortex. The QBO disrupted unexpectedly in 2016 for the first time in recorded history, an event that climate scientists linked to tropical convection changes associated with a strong El Niño.

The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is an irregular oscillation of sea surface temperatures between the western and eastern Indian Ocean; a positive IOD brings drought to Australia and Indonesia while producing anomalous rainfall over East Africa and India. The 2019 positive IOD was the strongest on record, contributing to Australia's catastrophic Black Summer bushfires (2019–2020) that burned over 18 million hectares and killed an estimated 3 billion animals.

The diurnal temperature range (DTR) — the difference between maximum daytime and minimum night-time temperatures — has been decreasing globally as a fingerprint of greenhouse warming; minimum temperatures (nights) are warming faster than maximum temperatures (days) because greenhouse gases trap outgoing longwave radiation most effectively at night. This asymmetric warming has important consequences for agriculture, ecosystems, and human health.

The world's first numerical weather prediction (NWP) was calculated by hand in 1922 by Lewis Fry Richardson, who mobilised 64,000 human 'computers' in a theoretical 'forecast factory' that took months to predict six hours of weather — and produced an incorrect result. Modern NWP runs the same equations on supercomputers performing quadrillions of calculations per second and produces global forecasts for the next ten days in under an hour.

source.name: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts

text: The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in Reading, England, produces the world's most accurate weather forecasts, consistently outperforming all national weather services in international competitions. Its model — IFS (Integrated Forecasting System) — assimilates over 40 million observations per day from satellites, weather balloons, aircraft, ships, buoys, and land stations; the ten-day global forecast from 1980 is now as accurate as the three-day forecast was in 1980.

The global radiosonde network — over 800 stations launching weather balloons twice daily at 00:00 and 12:00 UTC — is the backbone of upper-air weather observation. Each balloon carries an instrument package to altitudes of 30–40 km, taking measurements of temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind every second before the balloon bursts and the radiosonde parachutes back to Earth; this global commitment requires over half a million balloon launches per year.

Climate sensitivity — the equilibrium warming expected from a doubling of atmospheric CO₂ — has been estimated in scientific literature since 1979, when a US National Research Council report by Jule Charney suggested a range of 1.5–4.5°C. Despite 40 years of research, this range was only narrowed significantly in 2020 when an international assessment concluded the 'likely range' was 2.5–4.0°C, with 3°C as the central estimate.

Fog forms when air is cooled to its dew point temperature with sufficient moisture and condensation nuclei; advection fog (warm moist air moving over a cold surface) causes the famous fogs of San Francisco Bay, Newfoundland's Grand Banks, and the California coast, while radiation fog forms on clear calm nights over land. London's infamous 'pea souper' fogs were actually a combination of natural fog and coal smoke — 'smog' — last dramatically deadly in the Great Smog of 1952 that killed 4,000 people in four days.

The Indian Ocean Warm Pool — the warmest body of ocean water on Earth, with sea surface temperatures consistently above 28°C — acts as the primary energy source for the global atmospheric circulation and Asian monsoon system. As climate change raises global ocean temperatures, the Warm Pool is expanding eastward into the western Pacific, fundamentally altering the Walker Circulation and monsoon dynamics that sustain the livelihoods of billions of people.

The 1900 Galveston Hurricane — a Category 4 storm that struck Galveston Island, Texas on 8 September 1900 without warning — killed between 6,000 and 12,000 people and remains the deadliest natural disaster in US history. It destroyed 3,600 buildings and 8,000 homes; in response, Galveston built a 17-foot (5.2 m) seawall and raised the entire island's grade by up to 17 feet, in one of the most ambitious coastal engineering projects of the early 20th century.

Wind power has become the cheapest source of new electricity generation in many parts of the world; offshore wind turbines can now reach hub heights of 150 m with blade diameters exceeding 220 m. The global installed wind capacity surpassed 1 terawatt (1,000 GW) in 2023, generating about 7% of global electricity and saving approximately 1.1 billion tonnes of CO₂ annually compared with coal-fired generation.

The 'wet-bulb temperature' — the lowest temperature to which air can be cooled by evaporating water — is the key metric for survivability in humid heat; at a wet-bulb temperature of 35°C (equivalent to 95°C heat index in still air), the human body cannot cool itself even in shade and fatal hyperthermia occurs within hours. Wet-bulb temperatures above 31°C have already been recorded in South Asia and the Persian Gulf, and studies project that parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa will exceed 35°C wet-bulb by 2100 under high-emission scenarios.

The 'albedo effect' describes how Earth's reflectivity affects the energy balance: fresh snow reflects about 80–90% of incoming solar radiation, while the ocean absorbs 94% of it. As Arctic sea ice retreats, dark ocean replaces bright ice, amplifying warming in a positive feedback loop; the Arctic is now warming 3–4 times faster than the global average, a phenomenon called Arctic amplification, fundamentally changing ecosystems and weather patterns across the Northern Hemisphere.

source.name: National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: Flooding is the world's most costly natural hazard, responsible for approximately one-third of all economic losses from natural disasters and affecting more people annually than any other extreme weather event. Global economic losses from floods have risen from an average of $7 billion per year in the 1980s to over $60 billion per year in the 2010s, driven by both climate change intensifying precipitation and growing exposure of assets in floodplains.

The Tri-State Tornado of 18 March 1925 crossed Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana for 352 km (219 miles) in 3.5 hours — the longest continuous tornado track ever recorded — and killed 695 people (possibly over 800), making it the deadliest tornado in US history. It had no warning system, and many residents thought they were seeing a storm cloud rather than a tornado until it was upon them.

Haboobs — intense walls of dust and sand carried by strong thunderstorm outflow winds — can reduce visibility to zero within minutes across vast areas of the Sahara, Arabian Peninsula, Sahel, and southwestern United States. A haboob can stretch 100 km wide, reach 1,500 m high, and travel at 50–100 km/h; the 2011 Phoenix haboob was captured in videos showing an orange wall of dust 1.5 km high engulfing the city, reaching as far as 100 km from its origin.

The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the dominant form of intraseasonal tropical variability — a large-scale coupling of atmospheric circulation and precipitation that propagates eastward around the tropics every 30–60 days. The MJO influences tropical cyclone activity in all ocean basins, affects monsoon onsets and breaks, modulates the frequency of US tornado outbreaks, and can trigger El Niño events by warming the eastern Pacific through a train of warm Kelvin waves.

Whiteout conditions — total loss of contrast and horizon definition caused by diffuse light from an overcast sky reflected by a uniformly snow-covered surface — can cause complete spatial disorientation in polar regions. Aviation and military whiteouts have caused fatal crashes because pilots and drivers lose all sense of altitude and terrain, leading aircraft to fly into white surfaces they cannot distinguish from the white sky.

The 1972 Iran blizzard — the deadliest blizzard in recorded history — dropped up to 8 metres (26 feet) of snow across a 400 km² area of rural southern Iran over 7 days in early February, killing approximately 4,000 people and completely burying entire villages. Rescue operations were hampered because the area was so remote that the extent of the disaster was not known for several days.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: Heat domes — areas of high pressure that trap hot air beneath them like a lid — have become more frequent and intense with climate change; the June–July 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome shattered century-old temperature records in Canada and the US, with Lytton, British Columbia reaching 49.6°C on 29 June — 5°C higher than the previous all-time Canadian record — before burning to the ground the following day.

La Niña events — periodic cooling of the central and eastern tropical Pacific, opposite to El Niño — typically increase Atlantic hurricane season activity, bring drought to the southern US, and deliver above-normal rainfall to eastern Australia. The strong La Niña of 2021–2023 produced the wettest three years on record across eastern Australia, filling the Murray-Darling river system to capacity and causing widespread flooding.

The global average methane concentration has more than doubled since pre-industrial times, reaching 1,923 parts per billion in 2023 — the highest in 800,000 years of ice core records. Methane from fossil fuels, livestock, and wetlands is responsible for about 30% of observed warming to date; unlike CO₂ which persists for centuries, methane breaks down in about 12 years, meaning rapid cuts to methane emissions can produce visible climate benefits within a decade.

The Great Red Spot on Jupiter — an anticyclonic storm larger than Earth that has been observed continuously since the 1830s — is the solar system's longest-lived known storm, though it has been shrinking steadily from 40,000 km wide in the 19th century to about 15,000 km today. Understanding its dynamics helps atmospheric scientists study long-lived high-pressure systems on Earth, including the mechanisms sustaining tropical heat domes.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) 2021 Sixth Assessment Report stated that it is 'unequivocal' (its strongest language) that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land. The report used 234 authors from 66 countries and assessed over 14,000 scientific papers, expressing findings in terms of assessed likelihood levels ranging from 'virtually certain' (>99%) to 'extremely unlikely' (<5%).

Aerosols — microscopic particles in the atmosphere from pollution, sea spray, dust, and wildfires — have a net cooling effect on the climate by reflecting sunlight and seeding cloud formation; they are estimated to have masked approximately 0.5°C of warming that would otherwise have occurred due to greenhouse gases. The 'aerosol masking' effect means that rapidly reducing air pollution in the short term could temporarily accelerate warming, a paradox studied under the concept of 'termination shock'.

The stratospheric polar vortex is a large-scale cyclonic circulation in the stratosphere above each pole; sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) events — when stratospheric temperatures rise by up to 50°C in just days as wave energy from the troposphere disrupts the vortex — can split or displace the polar vortex, steering Arctic air into mid-latitudes weeks later and causing extreme cold outbreaks like those that paralysed Texas in February 2021.

The Atacama Desert in Chile — the driest non-polar desert on Earth, with some areas receiving less than 1 mm of rainfall per year — has weather stations that have recorded no precipitation for decades. Despite this, the Atacama blooms with flowers every few years when exceptionally strong El Niño events bring enough rain; in 2015 and 2017 rare mega-blooms covered the usually barren landscape with millions of flowers.

Cyclone Idai, which struck Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi in March 2019, became the worst tropical cyclone on record in the Southern Hemisphere, killing over 1,300 people, destroying 90% of Beira, Mozambique's fourth-largest city, and flooding an inland area roughly the size of Luxembourg. Attribution studies found the storm's rainfall was made 50% more intense by human-caused climate change.

The Vostok Station in Antarctica holds the world record for the lowest reliably measured natural temperature: −89.2°C (−128.6°F) recorded on 21 July 1983. A satellite-measured temperature of −93.2°C was observed in 2013 over a high plateau near Vostok, but because satellite measurements are indirect and not WMO-certified, Vostok retains the official record. The station is also the site of the Vostok ice core, which extends the climate record back 420,000 years.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: The Foehn — a warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of a mountain range — can raise temperatures by 10–20°C in hours as descending air compresses and warms adiabatically faster than it cooled on the windward side; the Foehn in the Alps, the Chinook in the Rockies ('the snow eater'), and the Santa Ana in California have been blamed for rapid snowmelt floods, wildfires, and psychosomatic effects on human health.

A blue moon — now commonly defined as the second full moon in a calendar month — occurs approximately once every 2.7 years due to the mismatch between the 29.5-day lunar cycle and the 30–31 day calendar month. The expression 'once in a blue moon' has been traced to the Maine Farmers' Almanac of the 1930s, which defined it differently as the third full moon in a season with four full moons, an astronomical rarity that created calendar confusion subsequently adopted by popular culture.

The 'albedo paradox' — sometimes called the 'faint young Sun paradox' — asks why liquid water and life existed on early Earth billions of years ago when the Sun was 30% less luminous; the answer likely involves a much stronger greenhouse effect from high concentrations of CO₂ and methane, and possibly lower surface albedo due to less continental land. The paradox remains one of the foundational puzzles of Earth system science.

source.name: Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences

text: Weather modification programs in the Soviet Union and Russia have included cloud seeding to prevent rain over military parades in Moscow since the 1960s; the practice continues today, with aircraft seeding clouds outside Moscow with silver iodide, cement powder, or liquid nitrogen to induce precipitation before it reaches the city. Russian authorities claim an 80% success rate in preventing rain during state celebrations.

The Ferrel Cell — the mid-latitude atmospheric circulation cell between 30° and 60° latitude — is an indirect, thermally indirect cell driven by interactions between the tropical Hadley Cell and the polar cell. Unlike the Hadley Cell (rising warm air near the equator) and polar cell (sinking cold air at the poles), the Ferrel Cell has surface air moving poleward and rising at 60°N/S, creating the sub-polar low-pressure belts responsible for mid-latitude storms.

The 1993 Storm of the Century (also called the '1993 Superstorm') produced the widest snowfall extent of any Atlantic storm on record, blanketing the entire eastern US from Alabama to Maine with 100–140 cm of snow while generating hurricane-force winds and storm surges that killed 318 people across 26 states and Cuba. It closed every major East Coast airport simultaneously — the only time this has ever occurred.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Graupel — also called 'soft hail' or 'snow pellets' — forms when supercooled water droplets freeze onto a snowflake, riming it with ice until the original shape is entirely obscured. Unlike hail (which forms in thunderstorm updrafts) graupel forms in mixed-phase clouds including winter storms; it is electrically charged and plays a key role in thunderstorm electrification by colliding with ice crystals in updrafts to generate the charge separation that produces lightning.

The concept of 'tipping points' in the climate system — thresholds beyond which self-reinforcing feedback loops drive irreversible change even if warming halts — includes the potential collapse of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (a commitment to 3–4 m of sea level rise), the dieback of the Amazon rainforest, and the thawing of permafrost carbon stores. A 2022 Science paper identified 16 major climate tipping elements, several potentially cascading into each other.

The Sichuan Basin in China and the Po Valley in Italy are among the world's most persistent fog zones because cold, moist air becomes trapped by surrounding mountains under calm anticyclonic conditions; Chengdu averages only 71 sunny days per year, giving it the nickname 'the city that never sees the sun.' The absence of strong ventilation in such basins also concentrates air pollution, creating severe smog events.

The 1970s saw a brief scientific and media discussion of possible 'global cooling' due to sulphate aerosol pollution; a 1975 Newsweek article became the most-cited reference for climate change deniers claiming scientists predicted an ice age. In reality, the scientific literature of that period showed papers on warming outnumbering papers on cooling 6:1, and the cooling hypothesis was never the consensus position of atmospheric scientists.

source.name: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

text: The Subtropical Ridge (also called the horse latitudes) — a belt of high pressure at approximately 30° north and south latitude where descending dry air suppresses cloud formation — is responsible for the location of most of the world's great deserts: the Sahara, Arabian, Namib, Kalahari, Australian, and Atacama deserts all sit beneath the subtropical high. As the Hadley Cell expands poleward with climate change, this dry descending belt is shifting toward the poles, increasing drought risk in Mediterranean climates.

Weather forecasting accuracy has improved dramatically since the 1980s: a modern 5-day forecast is now as accurate as a 1-day forecast was in 1980. This improvement comes from better numerical models, denser observational networks, data assimilation techniques, satellite data, and increased computing power. The economic value of weather forecasting is estimated at over $160 billion per year in the United States alone, as advance warning of severe weather saves lives, infrastructure, and agricultural investments.

source.name: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts

text: The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) — a long-lived pattern of Pacific climate variability shifting between warm and cool phases on 20–30-year timescales — modulates El Niño effects and global mean temperature trends. When the PDO is in its negative (cool) phase, La Niña-like conditions dominate the Pacific and global temperature rise can appear to stall, as happened in the early 2000s 'hiatus'; when the PDO turned positive after 2013, global warming accelerated.

The colour of the sky at different times of day is determined by Rayleigh scattering — the preferential scattering of shorter (blue) wavelengths of sunlight by atmospheric gas molecules. At midday, when sunlight travels a short path through the atmosphere, blue dominates; at sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere, scattering away all blue light and leaving red and orange wavelengths to dominate. Mars's sky appears pink-reddish at midday for the opposite reason: its red dust scatters red wavelengths preferentially.

Ensemble weather forecasting — running the same forecast model tens to hundreds of times with slightly different initial conditions — quantifies forecast uncertainty and provides probability-based predictions ('60% chance of rain') rather than single deterministic forecasts. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts runs a 50-member ensemble twice daily; the spread of ensemble solutions tells forecasters how confident they should be in a forecast, enabling better risk-based decisions for aviation, emergency management, and agriculture.

Tropical cyclone rapid intensification — defined as an increase in maximum sustained wind speed of at least 35 mph (56 km/h) in 24 hours — has become more frequent and extreme due to warmer ocean temperatures. Hurricane Patricia in 2015 achieved the most extreme rapid intensification ever observed in the Western Hemisphere, strengthening from 85 mph to 215 mph in just 24 hours in the Eastern Pacific, reaching the highest wind speed ever recorded in the Americas.

The Walker Circulation — an east-west atmospheric circulation cell over the tropical Pacific driven by the temperature contrast between the warm western and cooler eastern Pacific — was identified by Gilbert Walker in the 1920s. During El Niño events the temperature contrast weakens and the Walker Circulation slows or reverses; since the 1990s it has shown an overall weakening trend that may reflect anthropogenic climate change.

The coldest inhabited place on Earth is Oymyakon, Russia, which holds the Northern Hemisphere record for lowest air temperature at a permanently inhabited location: −67.7°C (−89.9°F) recorded in February 1933. The remote Yakutian village of approximately 500 people experiences temperature swings of over 100°C between summer (up to +37°C) and winter extremes, the largest annual temperature range of any settled place on Earth.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: The Saharan dust plume — an annual phenomenon where 182 million tonnes of Saharan dust are transported across the Atlantic Ocean to fertilise the Amazon rainforest — represents one of the most remarkable long-distance material transfers in Earth's atmosphere. NASA satellites track the plume annually; in 2020 it produced the largest and densest plume in decades, significantly degrading air quality across the Caribbean and southeastern US.

The term 'climate refugee' describes people forced to move due to climate-driven events (sea level rise, desertification, extreme weather), but it currently has no legal status under the 1951 Refugee Convention. The World Bank estimates that without action, 216 million people could be displaced within their own countries by 2050 due to climate impacts; Pacific island nations like Tuvalu and Kiribati are negotiating land purchases in Fiji as part of contingency plans for national relocation.

source.name: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal

text: Lightning detection networks like the US National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN) use sensors that detect the electromagnetic pulses emitted by lightning to triangulate strike locations within 500 metres and in near-real time. The US is struck by lightning about 25 million times per year; the state most frequently struck is Florida, known as the 'Lightning Capital of the US', particularly the Tampa Bay area which averages over 100 lightning days annually.

Ocean heat content (OHC) — the total thermal energy stored in the ocean — is now considered a more reliable indicator of the planet's energy imbalance than air surface temperature because the ocean absorbs over 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. Global OHC records have been set every year since 2017; the top 2,000 metres of the ocean have warmed by approximately 0.1°C since 2005, equivalent to adding the energy of 25 billion atomic bombs per year.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Lenticular clouds — smooth, lens-shaped clouds forming over mountains when moist air flows upward over a peak and cools to the dew point — are stationary relative to the mountain even in strong winds, because new cloud is continuously forming on the upwind side and evaporating on the downwind side. They are frequently misidentified as UFOs due to their smooth, disc-like shape and their uncanny ability to remain motionless while surrounding clouds move.

The 'heat index' (apparent temperature) accounts for the combined effect of air temperature and relative humidity on perceived heat; at 35°C air temperature and 90% humidity the heat index reaches 55°C — potentially fatal. Conversely, the 'wind chill factor' describes how wind accelerates heat loss from exposed skin; at −20°C with 40 km/h wind, exposed flesh can freeze in 10 minutes. Both indices were developed in the mid-20th century as practical meteorological tools for public safety communications.

Lake-effect snow — intense, localised snowfall produced when cold air flows over relatively warm lake water, picks up moisture, and deposits heavy snow on the downwind shore — affects the Great Lakes region annually from October to January. Buffalo, New York, is the most lake-effect-prone major city in North America; the November 2022 lake-effect snowstorm deposited over 180 cm (71 inches) in 72 hours near Buffalo, stranding thousands of motorists and killing 44 people.

source.name: NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory

text: The ENSO cycle's impact on global economic output is substantial: a study published in Science in 2023 estimated that El Niño events since 1960 have cost the global economy $4.1 trillion in lost economic output cumulatively, by reducing agricultural productivity, increasing disease (particularly malaria and cholera), and exacerbating conflict. The damage persists for 5–10 years after the event ends, disproportionately affecting tropical developing nations.

The Bermuda-Azores High — a semi-permanent subtropical anticyclone over the central Atlantic — migrates seasonally: in summer it expands northwestward and steers Atlantic hurricanes away from the US East Coast or into it, while in winter it retreats southeastward. The position of this high-pressure system largely determines whether an Atlantic hurricane tracks into the Gulf of Mexico or curves harmlessly out to sea, making its seasonal position one of the most important factors in hurricane season forecasting.

Fire weather — atmospheric conditions that promote rapid fire spread including low humidity, high temperatures, and strong winds — is quantified by fire weather indices used by wildfire agencies globally. The Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System is the most widely used internationally; with climate change, the number of 'extreme fire weather days' has increased by 14% globally since the 1980s, and the fire season has lengthened by an average of 19% in drylands worldwide.

Rain drops are not tear-shaped: small raindrops (< 1 mm) are spherical due to surface tension, while larger drops (1–4 mm) are flattened on the bottom by air resistance into a shape resembling a hamburger bun, not a teardrop. Drops larger than about 4.5 mm are aerodynamically unstable and break apart into smaller droplets; the largest raindrops ever measured — about 8–9 mm — were observed in Brazil and the Marshall Islands.

The 1988 NASA testimony of James Hansen to the US Senate — delivered during a historic heat wave — is widely credited as the moment climate change entered public consciousness; Hansen stated that it was '99 percent certain' that warming trends were caused by the greenhouse effect, a historically bold scientific statement at the time. The hearing was arranged by Senator Tim Wirth, who opened windows the night before to maximise the room's heat for dramatic effect.

source.name: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies

text: The global ocean covers 71% of Earth's surface and has a mean depth of 3,688 metres; the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at 10,935 metres, is the deepest point. The ocean's enormous heat capacity — it can absorb 1,000 times more heat than the atmosphere for the same temperature rise — makes it the primary buffer slowing surface warming but also commits Earth to centuries of continued warming even if emissions stopped today.

Supercell thunderstorms — the most powerful type of single-cell thunderstorm, characterised by a persistent rotating updraft called a mesocyclone — are responsible for virtually all significant tornadoes (EF2 and above), large hail (>5 cm), and extreme wind gusts in the US. A mature supercell can last for hours, covering hundreds of kilometres, with updrafts exceeding 200 km/h that carry hailstones through repeated growth cycles until they are large enough to fall.

The 2022 Pakistan floods — driven by record monsoon rainfall (over 190% above the 30-year average in Sindh province) combined with catastrophic glacial lake outburst floods from the accelerated melting of Pakistan's 7,000+ glaciers — inundated one-third of the country, killed 1,700 people, and caused $30 billion in damage. Pakistan contributes less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making the disaster one of the starkest examples of climate injustice.

The carbon cycle — the movement of carbon through the atmosphere, ocean, land, and living organisms — includes both fast (biological, years to decades) and slow (geological, millions of years) components. Humans are releasing geological carbon stored over hundreds of millions of years of photosynthesis in just centuries, at a rate approximately 100 times faster than the geological release rate from volcanoes, overwhelming the natural carbon cycle's capacity to absorb the excess.

Hailstones form when updrafts in severe thunderstorms carry water droplets above the freezing level, where they freeze and accumulate layers of ice as they cycle up and down through the storm. The largest hailstone ever officially recorded in the US fell at Vivian, South Dakota, in July 2010: it measured 20 cm (7.9 inches) in diameter and weighed 878 grams (1.94 pounds), with a circumference of 47 cm. The world record is held by a hailstone from Gopalganj, Bangladesh in 1986 that weighed 1.02 kg.

The Sahel — the semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the African savanna — experienced catastrophic drought from the late 1960s through the 1980s that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered mass migration; the drought was partly linked to cooling of the North Atlantic by industrial aerosols reducing rainfall, but since the 1990s a partial 'greening of the Sahel' has occurred as rainfall recovered and land management improved.

Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) — sudden catastrophic floods caused by the failure of moraine or ice dams holding glacial meltwater lakes — are becoming more frequent and larger as glaciers retreat in the Himalayas, Andes, and Central Asia. The 2013 Kedarnath disaster in India, which killed over 5,000 people, was triggered by a glacial outburst combined with extreme monsoon rainfall; over 15 million people in the Himalayas live at risk from GLOF events.

source.name: ICIMOD International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development

text: The 'global dimming' phenomenon — a measured reduction in solar radiation reaching Earth's surface between 1950 and 1990 of approximately 2–3% per decade, caused by increasing aerosol pollution from industry and aviation — partially offset greenhouse warming and has reversed in many regions since the 1990s as air quality improved. The reversal of global dimming in Europe and North America may have contributed to accelerating regional warming over the past 30 years.

The hydrological cycle (water cycle) circulates approximately 577,000 km³ of water annually through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. Climate change is intensifying this cycle: a warmer atmosphere holds about 7% more water vapour per degree Celsius of warming (Clausius-Clapeyron equation), increasing the potential for both heavier rainfall events and more intense droughts as water concentrates in fewer, more intense precipitation events.

The first modern weather forecast was issued by Robert FitzRoy — the captain of Darwin's Beagle — who founded the UK Meteorological Office in 1854 and began issuing daily weather forecasts from 1861 using the telegraph network. FitzRoy coined the term 'forecast' for weather predictions and developed storm warning cones hoisted in harbours to warn sailors; he killed himself in 1865 partly due to public ridicule of his forecasts.

An ice storm occurs when supercooled rain freezes instantly on contact with surfaces below 0°C, creating a layer of glaze ice (freezing rain). The January 1998 North American ice storm deposited up to 100 mm of freezing rain across Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick, and upstate New York over five days, collapsing 120,000 km of power lines and trees, leaving 3–4 million people without power for weeks, and killing 35 people — the most expensive natural disaster in Canadian history at that time.

Coral bleaching — the expulsion of photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) from coral tissues when sea temperatures exceed the corals' thermal tolerance by just 1°C for several weeks — turns corals white and leads to widespread death if the stress persists. The Great Barrier Reef experienced its first mass bleaching event in 1998 and has since had six, with 2022 being the first bleaching during a La Niña (usually a cooling event). Over 50% of the world's coral reefs have been lost since the 1950s.

source.name: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

text: Thundersnow — lightning and thunder occurring during a snowstorm — forms when unstable air exists within a cold winter precipitation system, most commonly over the Great Lakes or in intense nor'easters; the snow's acoustic dampening effect reduces thunder's audibility to within about 3 km, compared to 16 km for summer lightning. Each thundersnow lightning bolt is typically accompanied by an extremely intense snowfall of 5–7 cm per hour immediately beneath the storm.

The Arctic amplification — the disproportionately rapid warming of the Arctic (now warming at 4× the global average rate) — is driven by positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo feedback, water vapour feedback, and changes in cloud cover. Arctic warming has geopolitical implications: it is opening new shipping routes (the Northern Sea Route across Russia is now navigable 3–4 months per year), unlocking fossil fuel reserves, and creating sovereignty disputes over previously ice-locked territories.

source.name: NSIDC National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: The greenhouse effect was first theoretically described by French mathematician Joseph Fourier in 1824, who proposed that Earth's atmosphere acts like the glass of a greenhouse, trapping heat. Irish physicist John Tyndall experimentally confirmed in 1859 that CO₂ and water vapour absorb infrared radiation, and Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius in 1896 calculated that halving CO₂ concentrations would cool the Earth by 4–5°C and doubling CO₂ would warm it by 5–6°C — a surprisingly accurate prediction.

Frost forms when air temperature drops below 0°C and water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals (deposition, bypassing liquid state) on surfaces that have cooled to below freezing; hoarfrost creates beautiful feathery ice crystals on grass and branches. Freezing fog — when tiny supercooled water droplets in fog freeze on contact with surfaces — creates a spectacular phenomenon called 'rime ice', coating everything in white crystalline ice and common near Lake Tahoe, California, in winter.

The 2010 Russian heatwave — the most severe in the country's 130 years of meteorological records — killed approximately 55,000 people, destroyed 25% of Russia's wheat crop (triggering global food price spikes), and drove the Moscow wildfire smog that reduced life expectancy in the capital. Attribution studies calculated it would have been virtually impossible without human-caused climate change, and subsequent analysis identified it as an early example of the new 'climate normal' rather than a rare exception.

Microplastics have been detected in clouds, rain, and snow at the remote Pyrenees mountains at concentrations of up to 365 plastic particles per square metre per day. Researchers have found microplastics in Arctic sea ice, Antarctic snow, in rainwater from the Rocky Mountains, and even in deep ocean sediment cores — indicating that plastic pollution has entered the global atmospheric and hydrological cycle, with unknown implications for cloud formation and precipitation.

The 'wet monsoon' and 'dry monsoon' distinction underlies the agricultural calendar of over 2 billion people in Asia; the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) — the equatorial belt of rising air and intense thunderstorms that migrates seasonally — drives the monsoon by moving northward in summer to bring rain to South and Southeast Asia, then returning south in winter. The precise timing and intensity of ITCZ migration determines crop success for half the world.

Ocean deoxygenation — the loss of dissolved oxygen from the world's oceans driven by warming (warmer water holds less dissolved gas) and increased stratification that reduces ventilation of deep waters — has led to the expansion of 'oxygen minimum zones' (OMZs). Global ocean oxygen content has declined by 2% since 1960; OMZs now cover an area larger than Europe and are expanding, threatening marine life including commercially important fish species.

St. Elmo's Fire — a luminous plasma that appears on pointed objects (ship masts, aircraft wings, church spires, cattle horns) during thunderstorms when the electric field ionises the surrounding air — was named for St. Erasmus of Formia, the patron saint of sailors. It is visible as a blue or violet glow and hissing sound, benign in itself but indicating dangerous conditions nearby; it was observed on SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket fins and inside aircraft cockpits during severe weather.

The 'ozone-climate penalty' describes how ground-level ozone (smog) concentrations are expected to increase with climate change because warmer temperatures accelerate ozone formation from precursor pollutants; ozone is a potent greenhouse gas at the surface and causes 1–2 million premature deaths annually from respiratory disease. Reducing NOx and VOC emissions reduces both ground-level ozone and contributes to climate protection — one of the most powerful 'co-benefits' of climate policy.

The 2011 Thailand floods — the costliest flooding event in Asia's history at the time, causing $45 billion in economic damage — inundated over 13 million people's homes and flooded major industrial estates including hard drive manufacturers that supplied 40% of the world's hard drives, creating a global hard drive shortage that lasted over a year. The disaster highlighted how supply chain disruptions from climate extremes in one country can affect global industries.

Transpiration — the evaporation of water through plant stomata — accounts for roughly 60% of all land evapotranspiration and is a major driver of regional rainfall patterns. The Amazon rainforest generates its own rainfall through 'flying rivers' — massive aerial streams of water vapour transpired by trees that transport moisture from the Atlantic deep into the South American continent, producing rainfall as far west as the Andes and as far south as the Rio de la Plata basin.

The concept of 'climate risk' distinguishes between physical risk (direct exposure to climate hazards like floods, droughts, and heatwaves) and transition risk (economic disruption from decarbonisation policies, stranded fossil fuel assets). The Bank of England's 2019 'climate stress tests' were the first by a central bank; by 2023, 130+ central banks and supervisors in the Network for Greening the Financial System were conducting climate scenario analysis for their financial systems.

Mammatus clouds — rare, pouch-like protrusions hanging beneath anvil-shaped cumulonimbus clouds — form through a mechanism opposite to usual cloud development, with negatively buoyant air sinking through the cloud base. Their name comes from the Latin for breast; they typically appear after a severe thunderstorm has passed, creating an eerie yellow sky in late afternoon, and are associated with — though not indicative of — supercell thunderstorms and tornadoes nearby.

GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) twin satellites, operating from 2002 to 2017, measured tiny variations in Earth's gravitational field caused by mass redistribution, allowing scientists to track groundwater depletion, ice sheet mass loss, and soil moisture from space. GRACE data showed that the Greenland ice sheet was losing mass at an accelerating rate — from 137 billion tonnes per year in 2002–2005 to 286 billion tonnes per year in 2012–2016 — providing the most definitive evidence of ice sheet change.

Wildfire smoke has become a major air quality hazard across North America, Europe, and Australia; in September 2020, wildfires along the US West Coast generated so much smoke that San Francisco's sky turned orange at midday, with PM2.5 particulate levels reaching 200 µg/m³ — 25× above safe levels. Climate models project that wildfire smoke exposure in the western US could increase 4–6× by end of century under high-emission scenarios.

The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, triggered by a 9.1 magnitude undersea earthquake off Sumatra, killed 227,898 people in 14 countries — the deadliest tsunami ever recorded. The disaster exposed the absence of a Pacific-style tsunami warning system in the Indian Ocean; the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning and Mitigation System (IOTWMS) was established in 2006, with buoys, seismographs, and tide gauges now providing real-time warnings across the ocean basin.

The 'Greenhouse Earth' state — when Earth has no permanent polar ice caps, sea levels are 70+ metres higher than today, and tropical forests extend into polar regions — has been the planet's default condition for most of the past 540 million years. The current 'Icehouse Earth' state, with permanent ice at both poles, has existed only for about 2.6 million years (Quaternary) and represents an unusually cold period in Earth's deep climate history.

Hurricane Harvey (2017) produced the most extreme rainfall ever recorded in the United States from a single event — 1,539 mm (60.58 inches) at Nederland, Texas, over four days — and stalled over Houston because the normally steering upper-level winds had weakened due to expanded subtropical high-pressure systems linked to climate change. The storm caused $125 billion in damage, making it the costliest hurricane in US history alongside Katrina.

Snow rollers — naturally occurring cylinders of snow formed when wind rolls a snowball across a flat snowy field, adding concentric layers — are extremely rare because they require a specific combination of wet, sticky snow, a smooth surface, light wind, and temperatures near 0°C. They can range from golf ball to barrel size and have hollow centres because the core layer of snow is less compacted; they are so unusual that many people who see them for the first time believe they are man-made.

Enhanced weathering — spreading pulsite silicate rock (basalt, olivine) on agricultural fields to accelerate natural rock weathering that removes CO₂ from the atmosphere — has potential to remove 2–4 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year globally if deployed at scale. The process also improves soil pH and fertility; pilot projects on UK and US farms have demonstrated CO₂ removal of up to 2.5 tonnes per hectare per year at costs of $50–200 per tonne of CO₂, making it one of the more promising carbon removal approaches.

The 1995 Chicago Heat Wave killed 739 people in five days (14–20 July) when temperatures reached 41°C and heat index values exceeded 52°C; autopsies showed victims had core body temperatures above 41°C. Sociologist Eric Klinenberg's book 'Heat Wave' documented how the disaster disproportionately killed elderly Black residents in high-crime neighbourhoods who feared opening windows; the disaster fundamentally transformed urban heat emergency planning in the US.

The phenomenon of 'night cooling' — lower nighttime temperatures in dry climates allowing passive cooling of buildings without air conditioning — is the foundation of traditional vernacular architecture in the Middle East, Mediterranean, and Southwest US, with thick adobe or stone walls absorbing daytime heat and releasing it at night. As nighttime temperatures rise faster than daytime temperatures under climate change, this ancient building technology becomes less effective, increasing air conditioning demand.

Antarctic sea ice reached its all-time record minimum extent in February 2023 — just 1.79 million km² compared to the previous record low of 1.92 million km² (2022) — a shortfall roughly the size of Greenland below the 1981–2010 average; scientists described the anomaly as 'five standard deviations below the mean', meaning it was statistically extraordinary. The reasons for the sudden sea ice loss remain actively debated.

source.name: National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: A bombogenesis or 'bomb cyclone' — the rapid intensification of a mid-latitude cyclone with central pressure dropping at least 24 millibars in 24 hours — occurs when an intense temperature contrast between cold arctic air and warm ocean air drives an explosive deepening of a low-pressure system. The December 2022 'Christmas Bomb' cyclone across the central and eastern US broke over 60 all-time low temperature records and killed more than 60 people.

Fog stripping — harvesting water from fog by large mesh screens that collect droplets which drip into collecting troughs — has been used in Peru, Chile, Eritrea, Namibia, and Morocco to provide fresh water in areas with negligible rainfall but persistent coastal fog. A single standard fog collector (1 m × 1 m mesh) can yield 5–22 litres per day; Peru's 'fog catchers' in the Lima hills supply 200 families with water from the garúa sea fog.

The Köppen Climate Classification System — developed by German-Russian climatologist Wladimir Köppen in 1884 and updated in 1936 — divides the world into five major climate types (A: tropical, B: dry, C: temperate, D: continental, E: polar) and 30 subtypes based on temperature and precipitation thresholds tied to vegetation boundaries. It remains the most widely used climate classification today; climate change is causing observable 'Köppen type transitions' as zones shift poleward.

The term 'albedo engineering' describes interventions to increase Earth's reflectivity by brightening rooftops, urban surfaces, and croplands; painting roofs white can reduce building cooling costs by up to 40% and lower urban temperatures by up to 2°C in hot climates. A 2023 study estimated that making all suitable urban roofs highly reflective worldwide could avoid up to 0.3°C of global warming, at relatively low cost compared to other climate interventions.

The 'rain shadow effect' occurs on the leeward side of mountain ranges, where descending dry air creates arid or semi-arid conditions immediately behind the mountains. The Atacama Desert exists in the rain shadow of the Andes; Death Valley in California sits in the rain shadow of the Sierra Nevada; the Tibetan Plateau blocks the monsoon from much of Central Asia. Climate change is shifting precipitation patterns, generally intensifying rain shadows on the dry side and increasing orographic precipitation on the wet side.

The 'polar amplification' signal — the disproportionate warming of polar regions — is not unique to Earth's current climate; it is a robust feature of climate change in models because of ice-albedo feedbacks, changes in atmospheric heat transport, and polar-specific cloud feedbacks. Ice core records from past interglacials show that polar regions warmed 2–3× the global average during past warm periods, providing paleoclimate confirmation of the model-predicted polar amplification behaviour.

The Red List of Ecosystems — analogous to the IUCN Red List for species — assesses the collapse risk of major biomes and ecosystem types under climate and other pressures. As of 2023, 7% of assessed global ecosystems are in the two most threatened categories, including Mediterranean forests and shrublands, salt marshes, and tropical dry forests; climate change is identified as a driver in over 70% of threatened ecosystem assessments.

Frost hollows — valley bottoms and depressions where cold dense air pools on calm nights through radiative cooling — can be up to 10°C colder than surrounding hillsides. The Ricketts Point frost hollow in Victoria, Australia, records the lowest temperatures in the Melbourne region despite being far from the mountains; understanding frost hollow dynamics is crucial for aviation (where cold pooling produces valley fog), viticulture, and ecology.

source.name: Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology

text: The Gaia hypothesis — proposed by James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis in the 1970s — suggests that Earth's living organisms collectively regulate the planet's atmosphere, temperature, and chemistry to maintain conditions favourable for life. While rejected in its strong 'purposeful regulation' form, the hypothesis stimulated the field of Earth system science, which now quantitatively models how life modulates climate through carbon and nitrogen cycles, biogenic cloud condensation nuclei, and weathering.

The highest recorded wind speed at the surface is 408 km/h (253 mph), measured at Barrow Island, Australia during Tropical Cyclone Olivia on 10 April 1996, replacing the previous record set at Mount Washington, New Hampshire in 1934. Mount Washington still holds the record for the world's most extreme recorded wind chill — a heat index of −65°C (-85°F), and for its most famous weather station motto: 'Home of the World's Worst Weather'.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: Pineapple Express — the informal name for a particularly strong atmospheric river originating near Hawaii — carries extraordinary amounts of tropical moisture from the warm Pacific into the western United States and Canada, producing extreme precipitation events. The January 2017 California atmospheric river series, nicknamed 'Pineapple Expresses', ended a five-year drought and over-filled reservoirs — but threatened the Oroville Dam (the tallest in the US), causing 188,000 people to be evacuated.

Periglacial environments — those shaped by freeze-thaw cycles in cold climates rather than actual glaciation — cover about 25% of Earth's land surface, including tundra, high-altitude plateaus, and some mountain ranges. Processes like solifluction (slow downslope creep of water-saturated soil over frozen ground), frost heaving, and polygon ground (ice-wedge networks forming hexagonal patterned ground visible from space) are all periglacial phenomena losing their activity as permafrost thaws.

The 2019–2020 Australian Black Summer bushfires — the worst fire season in Australian recorded history — burned 18.6 million hectares (186,000 km²), an area larger than Syria, and killed approximately 3 billion animals. Attribution science found the severe fire weather was made at least 30% more likely by climate change; the smoke plumes circled the globe and reached the stratosphere, where they caused a 4% reduction in Southern Hemisphere sunlight for several months.

source.name: Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements

text: The South Asian heat dome of April–May 2022 — affecting India and Pakistan with temperatures exceeding 49°C and causing widespread mass heat stroke — was described by climate scientists as 'almost impossible without climate change.' Wheat harvests in northwest India fell by 50% in affected districts; with climate models projecting these events occurring every 5 years by 2050 under current emissions trajectories, South Asian food security faces a severe structural challenge.

The 'nitrogen cycle' and climate interact powerfully: nitrous oxide (N₂O) — emitted mainly from agricultural soils fertilised with synthetic nitrogen — is a greenhouse gas 273 times more potent than CO₂ over a 100-year timescale and is the dominant ozone-depleting substance currently emitted. Global N₂O emissions are increasing 30% faster than IPCC projections assumed, driven by expanding agricultural nitrogen use, threatening both climate targets and stratospheric ozone recovery.

Pressure tendency — the change in barometric pressure over the past 3 hours — is one of the most critical short-term weather indicators available to forecasters; a falling pressure of more than 3 hPa per 3 hours indicates a rapidly approaching storm, while rising pressure indicates improving conditions. Traditional mercury barometers, aneroid barometers, and modern digital sensors all measure absolute pressure in hectopascals (hPa), with standard sea-level pressure defined as 1013.25 hPa.

The driest place on Earth is the Atacama Desert's hyperarid core, where the Calama weather station in Chile recorded no measurable rainfall for 14 consecutive years (1903–1917). The Atacama's aridity results from the combined effect of the cold Humboldt Current upwelling (cooling and stabilising coastal air), the rain shadow of the Andes, and its location beneath a subtropical high pressure zone — a triple barrier that makes some areas essentially rainless for centuries.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: Evaporation cooling creates what meteorologists call 'virga' — rain or snow that evaporates completely before reaching the ground, appearing as trailing streaks beneath clouds. In dry climates virga is common; the evaporating precipitation cools the downdraft air, which can descend to the surface as a destructive microburst even though no surface rain fell. This 'dry microburst' phenomenon causes crop damage, dust storms, and aviation hazards in the US Great Plains and Australia's outback.

The global land surface temperature record is maintained by NOAA, NASA GISS, and the UK Met Office Hadley Centre using data from approximately 7,000 surface weather stations; sea surface temperatures add ocean data from ships, buoys, and Argo floats. Satellite temperature records (from 1979) and the surface instrumental record have been independently confirmed by multiple paleoclimate proxies as accurately representing a warming trend unprecedented in at least the past 2,000 years.

The Beaufort Gyre — a large clockwise-rotating ocean circulation in the Arctic Ocean that accumulates freshwater from rivers and sea ice melt — has been accumulating freshwater at an accelerating rate since the 1990s, now storing about 40% more freshwater than in the 1980s. Scientists fear that if the gyre weakens or reverses, it could release a massive pulse of cold freshwater into the North Atlantic, potentially weakening the AMOC circulation that moderates European climate.

Green Flash — an optical phenomenon occurring just as the Sun sets below a clear ocean horizon, when the last sliver of sunlight appears to flash green for a fraction of a second — results from atmospheric refraction dispersing sunlight into its spectral colours; the shorter green wavelengths are refracted slightly more than red, and visible longer, with the blue wavelengths scattered away. Jules Verne romanticised it in his 1882 novel 'The Green Ray', claiming the flash allows you to read others' hearts.

The Paris Agreement's 'Loss and Damage' mechanism — formally established at COP27 in 2022 — creates a fund for developing nations that have suffered irreversible climate impacts they cannot adapt to, such as the complete inundation of low-lying island nations. The first pledges in 2022 totalled only $130 million against estimated needs of $400 billion per year; at COP28 in 2023 the fund was operationalised with over $700 million pledged.

Ice nucleation — the process by which water vapour freezes around a particle (dust, pollen, bacteria, sea salt) to form an ice crystal — is the key step in precipitation formation. Some bacteria, including Pseudomonas syringae, are the most efficient ice nuclei known, triggering freezing at temperatures as warm as −2°C compared to −38°C for pure water; they are found in clouds worldwide and may play a significant role in natural precipitation, raising questions about the role of the biosphere in regulating rainfall.

The Larsen B Ice Shelf — a 3,250 km² section of the Antarctic Peninsula ice shelf — collapsed catastrophically in 35 days in early 2002, disintegrating into thousands of icebergs after being stable for at least 10,000 years; its collapse was driven by an exceptionally warm summer with surface meltwater pooling and fracturing the shelf from above. The event accelerated glaciers behind the shelf, causing them to flow 8× faster into the ocean.

The subtropical jet stream — a band of fast-moving air at about 30° latitude driven by the temperature contrast between the tropics and subtropics — influences the timing of monsoon breaks and onsets across Asia and Africa. The subtropical jet is distinct from the polar jet (at 60°) and more persistent year-round; it affects Mediterranean storm tracks, North African rainfall, and the development of winter precipitation in the southern US.

The 'butterfly effect' — the concept that a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil could trigger a tornado in Texas — was coined by meteorologist Edward Lorenz in a 1972 lecture as a metaphor for sensitive dependence on initial conditions in chaotic dynamical systems. Lorenz's 1963 discovery of chaotic behaviour in simplified weather models established the theoretical limit of deterministic weather predictability at approximately 2 weeks, a horizon that remains robust 60 years later.

The 2021 Central Europe floods — caused by record rainfall of up to 200 mm in 24 hours from a stalled low-pressure system over Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands — killed over 220 people and caused €33 billion in damage, the costliest natural disaster in German history. Analysis found that climate change made rainfall in this type of event 1.2–9× more intense; the disaster reignited European debate about flood risk management and early warning systems.

Aerosol-cloud interactions — the 'Twomey effect' — describe how increasing aerosol pollution creates more but smaller cloud droplets from the same amount of water vapour, making clouds brighter (higher albedo) and longer-lived. This 'first indirect aerosol effect' causes additional cooling estimated at 0.5–2 W/m² — comparable in magnitude to but opposite in sign to CO₂ forcing — but with much larger uncertainty than the greenhouse effect, making it the largest source of uncertainty in climate projections.

The highest point on Earth relative to sea level, Mount Everest (8,849 m), has a temperature that averages approximately −19°C at the summit year-round, with winter temperatures as low as −60°C. Climbers on Everest above 8,000 m operate in the 'death zone' where oxygen partial pressure is only one-third of sea level, and weather windows for summit attempts are typically just a few days in May when the polar jet stream temporarily moves north of the mountain.

Phenology — the study of seasonal timing of biological events (first bloom, bird migration, insect emergence) — provides one of the clearest ecological signals of climate change; across Europe, plant flowering has advanced by an average of 6–8 days per decade since 1980. Phenological mismatch — when species relying on the same seasonal cues advance their timing at different rates (e.g., caterpillar emergence outpacing bird egg hatching) — threatens food webs and biodiversity.

The 1783 Laki volcanic eruption in Iceland — one of history's largest effusive eruptions — released 120 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the troposphere over 8 months, creating an acidic dry fog across Europe that killed livestock, destroyed crops, and likely contributed to 23,000 deaths in the UK alone from respiratory disease. Benjamin Franklin, US Ambassador to France at the time, was the first to link the 'constant fog' to the Icelandic eruption — an early exercise in climate attribution.

Sea spray aerosols — tiny salt particles ejected from breaking ocean waves — are the most abundant aerosol type by mass in the marine atmosphere; they act as cloud condensation nuclei, scatter sunlight directly, and influence the chemistry of marine air. The Southern Ocean's exceptionally clean 'baseline atmosphere' (very few anthropogenic aerosols) allows cloud condensation nuclei to come almost entirely from sea spray and biogenic dimethylsulphide (DMS) produced by phytoplankton.

The 'Mayflower Anomaly' — the fact that the Mayflower arrived in Plymouth, Massachusetts in November 1620 during the Little Ice Age, experiencing extreme cold and storms — was part of a pattern of severe winter weather unusual even for New England. Tree ring studies of that period show 1620 was an anomalously cold year across North America; the hardships of the first winter, which killed half the colonists, were partly attributable to this climatic context.

The global temperature anomaly for 2023 surpassed 1.45°C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline for the first time, with every single month from June to December setting a new global monthly temperature record. The combination of the El Niño that began in 2023 and the long-term background warming trend produced a year that, by year's end, was assessed by WMO as 'almost certain' to be the warmest in recorded history.

The Dry Line — a sharp boundary in the US Great Plains separating moist Gulf air to the east from hot, dry continental air to the west — is the primary initiation mechanism for supercell thunderstorms and tornadoes across Tornado Alley. The convergence along the dryline focuses intense solar heating on the dry side while providing fuel (moist, unstable air) on the wet side; it migrates eastward by day and can shift 300 km between morning and afternoon.

Biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) — molecules like isoprene emitted by vegetation on hot summer days — react with nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere to form ground-level ozone and secondary organic aerosol. Forests emit roughly 700 million tonnes of isoprene per year, comparable in scale to all human VOC emissions; climate change is increasing BVOC emissions as temperatures rise, creating a positive feedback loop through enhanced ozone production and aerosol formation.

The 1970 Super Outbreak — 148 tornadoes in 13 US states over 16 hours on 3–4 April 1974 — killed 330 people and was the largest tornado outbreak ever recorded until it was surpassed by the April 2011 Super Outbreak (364 tornadoes in 72 hours across 21 states), which killed 324 people in the largest, most destructive tornado outbreak in world history and caused $11 billion in damage.

Psychrometrics — the study of the thermodynamic properties of air-water vapour mixtures — underpins both weather forecasting and building climate control; relative humidity (the ratio of actual to maximum possible water vapour) is measured with a hygrometer or calculated from wet-bulb and dry-bulb thermometer pairs. The 'comfort zone' for most humans is 40–60% relative humidity; above 70% (high humidity) the body's ability to cool through sweating diminishes significantly.

source.name: American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers

text: The 1979 Red River of the North catastrophic flood in North Dakota and Minnesota — when 100-year flooding inundated Grand Forks, causing $3.5 billion in damage — was exacerbated by the city's overconfidence in its dike system rated for a 500-year flood that the actual event exceeded by 2 feet. The disaster transformed North American flood risk communication, emphasising that no flood control system eliminates risk and that probabilistic language (100-year flood) misleads the public.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The Tibetan Plateau — the world's highest plateau at a mean elevation of 4,500 m — acts as a giant heat pump for the Asian monsoon, with its elevated surface absorbing solar radiation and heating the overlying troposphere much more than surrounding lowlands at the same latitude. This 'elevated heat source' intensifies the Asian summer monsoon by creating a strong pressure differential between the hot plateau and the cooler Indian Ocean — making the plateau a critical node in global atmospheric circulation.

The 'urban breathing' phenomenon — CO₂ concentrations measurably decreasing within cities during lockdowns in 2020, as traffic stopped and industry slowed — allowed atmospheric scientists to directly attribute local CO₂ to traffic and industry in near-real-time for the first time. The 2020 global lockdown produced the largest single-year emissions drop on record (7%), yet atmospheric CO₂ still increased by 2.6 ppm, illustrating how large the natural carbon cycle's internal variability is.

Frost flowers — clusters of ice ribbons that extrude from plant stems or sea ice under specific cold, calm conditions as supercooled moisture is 'wicked' outward and freezes — are both visually spectacular and scientifically important. Sea ice frost flowers are extremely salty and act as highly efficient cloud condensation nuclei; they also concentrate organic matter and sea surface bacteria, potentially affecting polar atmospheric chemistry and cloud formation above the Arctic Ocean.

The strongest thunderstorm updraft ever measured — 83 m/s (nearly 300 km/h) — was recorded inside a severe supercell thunderstorm by a NOAA research aircraft over the central US. Such extreme updrafts are powerful enough to suspend grapefruit-sized hailstones, hurl objects several kilometres upward, and carry insects, pollen, and bacteria from the surface into the upper troposphere, potentially affecting the chemistry and biological content of the upper atmosphere.

The 'heat in the pipeline' — also called committed warming — refers to warming that will occur even if all greenhouse gas emissions stopped immediately today, due to the thermal inertia of the ocean absorbing heat slowly. Current estimates suggest Earth is committed to at least 0.3–0.5°C of additional warming above current levels regardless of future emissions; this irreducible commitment to further warming is a strong argument for prioritising adaptation alongside mitigation.

Rime ice — the opaque, granular ice formed when supercooled fog droplets freeze instantly on contact with surfaces below 0°C — is distinct from glaze ice (clear, formed by freezing rain) and is the most common form of aircraft icing in clouds. The accretion of rime on aircraft wings alters their aerodynamic profile, reducing lift and increasing drag; anti-icing systems (bleed air, electrothermal heating, or pneumatic boots) are standard equipment on commercial aircraft operating in icing conditions.

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) moves seasonally following the overhead sun; over land it migrates more widely than over oceans because land heats faster. The ITCZ's current mean position is slightly north of the equator because more land mass in the Northern Hemisphere provides stronger heating; climate models project the ITCZ will shift further northward as the Northern Hemisphere warms faster than the Southern, altering precipitation distributions for billions of people in tropical regions.

The 2012 Hurricane Sandy — which made a rare left-turn into New Jersey rather than recurving out to sea — caused catastrophic flooding of the New York subway system, $65 billion in damage, and 233 deaths in 24 countries. The storm's unusual track was caused by a blocking high pressure over Greenland (itself linked to recent Arctic sea ice loss) that prevented the normal recurvature; attribution studies found that climate change raised Sandy's storm surge by approximately 0.4 m through sea level rise alone.

The concept of 'planetary boundaries' — nine Earth system processes within which humanity can safely operate — was proposed by Johan Rockström and colleagues in 2009 in Nature. As of 2023, six of the nine boundaries have been transgressed, including climate change (atmospheric CO₂ above 350 ppm safe boundary), biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, and novel entities (synthetic chemicals and plastics) — with only three boundaries (ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone, atmospheric aerosol loading) remaining within safe limits.

The first comprehensive global climate agreement — the UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change), signed at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 by 154 nations — established the principle that countries have 'common but differentiated responsibilities' for addressing climate change, reflecting the fact that developed nations are historically responsible for most cumulative emissions. The UNFCCC framework underpins all subsequent climate treaties including the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement.

The global average surface pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hPa (101,325 Pa or 1 atmosphere), but this varies enormously: the highest reliably recorded sea-level pressure was 1083.8 hPa in Agata, Siberia in December 1968 (extreme cold dense air), while the lowest was 870 hPa in Typhoon Tip in October 1979 — a pressure difference of 214 hPa that reflects the vast atmospheric energy differential driving Earth's weather systems.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: The South Asian monsoon onset date — defined in India as the day monsoon rain reaches Kerala — typically falls around 1 June but can vary by several weeks; predicting the onset date 3–4 weeks in advance is the Indian Meteorological Department's most important annual challenge. Monsoon onset prediction has improved dramatically with coupled ocean-atmosphere models, but the precise date still carries a ±4 day uncertainty that has major implications for agricultural planning.

The 'global conveyor belt of ocean circulation' transports heat poleward and carbon downward on thousand-year timescales; bottom water formed in the Weddell Sea, Antarctica, is the world's coldest ocean water (-1.8°C) and densest, sinking to abyssal depths and spreading northward into all ocean basins. The Weddell Sea polynya — an open water hole that occasionally forms in winter sea ice — is a crucial ventilation point where surface water sinks to the abyss.

Sun dogs (parhelia) — bright spots of light appearing at 22° on either side of the sun, often with halos — are caused by hexagonal plate ice crystals in cirrus clouds that refract sunlight at the same angle as a glass prism. They are most visible when cirrus clouds are below eye level — such as from mountain tops or aircraft — and are among the most common atmospheric optics phenomena, visible multiple times per year at mid-latitudes if you know where to look.

Radiative forcing — the change in net energy flux at the tropopause caused by a change in atmospheric composition or surface albedo — is the fundamental metric by which scientists compare the warming or cooling effect of different climate drivers. CO₂ has caused approximately +2.2 W/m² of forcing since pre-industrial times; all greenhouse gases together contribute about +3.3 W/m², partially offset by aerosols (−0.5 to −1.5 W/m²), giving a net human forcing of about +2.7 W/m².

The Beaufort Sea — the Arctic Ocean section north of Alaska and western Canada — experienced its largest recorded open water extent in September 2012, when sea ice retreated 550 km north of its average position, opening the Northern Sea Route along Russia and the Northwest Passage through the Canadian Arctic simultaneously. September Arctic sea ice extent has declined approximately 13% per decade since satellite observations began in 1979.

The 'carbon budget' concept — the total amount of CO₂ that can be emitted while staying within a given temperature target — has become central to climate policy; the IPCC AR6 estimated the remaining budget for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5°C was approximately 500 billion tonnes of CO₂ as of January 2020, equivalent to about 10–12 years of current global emissions. The budget shrinks by roughly 1 billion tonnes every 10 days.

Cumulonimbus clouds — the 'kings of clouds' — can extend from near the surface to above 15 km altitude (the tropopause), with anvil-shaped tops that spread horizontally as the rising air hits the temperature inversion at the tropopause. A mature cumulonimbus contains updrafts and downdrafts moving at over 100 km/h, an estimated 300,000 tonnes of water in various phases, and electrical energy equivalent to several atomic bombs, released through the lightning it produces.

The 'ITCZ anchoring' mechanism — by which deforestation in the Amazon shifts the ITCZ southward, potentially drying the African Sahel — illustrates how regional land use change can affect distant climate systems.
