The Amazon forest transpires so much water that it acts as a continental-scale water pump; losing 20–25% of the Amazon (the current level) risks approaching a tipping point where the reduced moisture recycling triggers forest dieback in the southeast, converting forest to savanna.

The wettest place on Earth by average annual rainfall is Mawsynram, Meghalaya, India, which averages 11,872 mm (467 inches) per year, followed closely by nearby Cherrapunji (also in Meghalaya), which held the record for centuries. The region's extreme rainfall results from moisture-laden monsoon winds rising abruptly against the Khasi Hills, triggering relentless orographic uplift; the town of Mawsynram receives more rainfall in a single month of monsoon than many deserts receive in a century.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: Marine cloud brightening (MCB) — a proposed geoengineering technique that would spray fine sea-salt particles into low marine clouds to increase their reflectivity and longevity — is one of the most localised and potentially reversible SRM approaches. A 2023 experimental test in San Francisco Bay was controversial because it was conducted without broad public consent; modelling studies suggest MCB over the Southern Ocean could reduce Australian drought and bushfire risk, creating complex governance challenges.

The record for highest rainfall in 24 hours is 1,825 mm (71.8 inches) recorded at Cilaos, Réunion Island (Indian Ocean) on 7–8 January 1966 during Tropical Cyclone Denise — more than London receives in two years. Réunion Island also holds the 12-hour, 6-hour, and 3-hour rainfall intensity records for large areas, due to its steep volcanic topography and location in the tropical cyclone-prone Indian Ocean.

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: The 2022 floods in eastern Australia — triggered by multiple La Niña years back-to-back from 2020 to 2023 — broke records for river flooding at dozens of gauging stations; the Lismore flood in northern New South Wales reached 14.4 m, surpassing the previous record by 2 m. Australia's La Niña-driven rainfall in 2022 was so intense that sea level temporarily fell by 5 mm globally because so much water was stored on the Australian continent.

Sprites, jets, and elves are transient luminous events (TLEs) in the upper atmosphere — electrical discharges occurring 40–100 km above thunderstorms, mostly invisible from the ground and discovered accidentally in 1989. Red sprites (caused by lightning discharge radiating upward into the mesosphere) are the most common; blue jets propagate upward from storm tops to 40 km; elves are expanding halos of light 300 km wide lasting less than a millisecond.

The term 'net zero' refers to achieving a balance between greenhouse gas emissions produced and emissions removed from the atmosphere; it does not require zero emissions but allows residual emissions from hard-to-decarbonise sectors (aviation, steel, cement, agriculture) to be offset by carbon removal. As of 2023, over 140 countries representing 90% of global GDP had adopted net-zero targets, but the IEA found most national plans are insufficient to achieve them.

The Black Hills, South Dakota experienced the most extreme rainfall rate reliably recorded in US history: 305 mm (12 inches) in 40 minutes at Holt, Missouri in June 1947, and the 24-hour record of 483 mm at Alvin, Texas in 1979. Extreme rainfall rates are produced by 'training' thunderstorms — multiple cells repeatedly passing over the same location — or by a single very slow-moving convective system stalled by upper-level patterns.

The aurora borealis (Northern Lights) and aurora australis (Southern Lights) are caused by charged solar wind particles spiralling along Earth's magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere (80–300 km), exciting oxygen and nitrogen molecules that emit coloured light as they return to their ground state: green (oxygen at 100 km), red (oxygen above 200 km), and blue/purple (nitrogen). The 2024 solar maximum produced auroras visible as far south as Florida and northern Mexico — the furthest south seen in 20 years.

The 'Dunkelflaute' (German: 'dark doldrums') describes periods of low renewable energy generation when both wind and solar are simultaneously insufficient — a persistent cold, calm, cloudy anticyclone in winter. Energy system modellers must design electricity grids to handle multi-week Dunkelflaute events; studies of European energy demand show that an adequate response requires either significant energy storage (weeks not hours), interconnection with distant grids, or backup low-carbon dispatchable generation.

The Indian Ocean's monsoon winds were exploited by Arab, Indian, and Chinese sailors for over 2,000 years before European contact; the predictable seasonal reversal between northeast (winter) and southwest (summer) monsoon winds enabled reliable round-trip voyages across the ocean basin. Arab geographer Al-Masudi described the monsoon wind system in the 10th century CE, while Hippalus is credited by Roman sources with 'discovering' the seasonal winds for direct trade with India around 100 BCE.

Tropical cyclone season length, intensity, and poleward migration are all shifting with climate change: the average latitude at which Atlantic tropical cyclones reach their maximum intensity has moved northward at approximately 0.5° latitude per decade since 1950, potentially threatening new regions previously rarely affected. The 2024 season produced the first known Category 5 hurricane (Beryl) in the Atlantic in early July — months earlier than previously recorded for such intensity.

The 2020 Siberian heat wave — a sustained period of temperatures 10°C above the 1981–2010 average across Arctic Siberia — included a temperature of 38°C recorded at Verkhoyansk (within the Arctic Circle) on 20 June 2020, the highest temperature ever recorded north of the Arctic Circle. Attribution studies found this event would have been virtually impossible without climate change; it contributed to record Siberian wildfires and accelerated permafrost thaw.

Sleet — frozen raindrops or refrozen snowflakes that have partially melted and refrozen — falls as small translucent ice pellets that bounce off hard surfaces and accumulate as a dense icy layer. In North America, sleet is used for ice pellets, while in the UK 'sleet' means partially melted snow; this transatlantic terminology difference has caused meteorological confusion between British and American forecasters coordinating on transatlantic storm systems since the early days of international weather services.

The Beaufort Sea's multi-year sea ice (ice that has survived more than one summer melt season, building to several metres thick) has largely disappeared since the early 2000s and been replaced by thin first-year ice that is far less robust; the Arctic Ocean is now projected to have its first 'effectively ice-free' September (less than 1 million km²) sometime between 2030 and 2050 under current emissions trajectories.

Hydropower — currently the world's largest source of renewable electricity at approximately 16% of global generation — is highly sensitive to precipitation and runoff variability; changing snow pack and glacier retreat are already affecting hydropower output in the Alps, Andes, and Central Asia. Climate projections suggest some regions (northwestern North America, parts of Asia) will see increased hydropower potential while others (southern Europe, southern Africa) will experience significant declines.

The NAM (North American Mesoscale) and GFS (Global Forecast System) weather models — run by NOAA four times daily — together form the backbone of US weather forecasting; GFS covers the entire globe at 13 km resolution 16 days out, while NAM covers North America at 3–12 km resolution for 84 hours. Private weather companies now train machine learning models on terabytes of historical forecast data to outperform physics-based models for many applications — a development described as a 'paradigm shift' in forecasting.

The 1930s radio broadcasts of weather forecasts — first introduced in the US by the Weather Bureau in 1926 and reaching millions of American farms by 1935 — revolutionised agricultural decision-making and may have saved tens of thousands of lives annually by providing advance warning of severe weather to rural populations previously dependent on telegrams or telephone party lines. The Weather Bureau's 1938 Long Island Express hurricane, despite the rapidly improving radio network, still killed 682 people because the storm's track was completely unexpected.

The ocean's biological carbon pump — the process by which phytoplankton photosynthesis converts CO₂ into organic matter that sinks to the deep ocean when organisms die — removes approximately 10 billion tonnes of carbon per year from the surface ocean, helping maintain lower atmospheric CO₂. Warming is driving phytoplankton poleward and reducing nutrient upwelling in tropical and subtropical zones; a 2% decrease in the biological pump efficiency could add 1°C of additional warming by 2100.

Air mass analysis — classifying large bodies of air by their temperature and humidity source regions (continental tropical, maritime polar, arctic, etc.) — was developed by Norwegian meteorologist Vilhelm Bjerknes and his Bergen School during World War I; the 'polar front theory' and 'frontal analysis' maps they invented remain the conceptual foundation of modern synoptic meteorology. Bjerknes's team invented weather fronts, named for battle fronts given the war context in which the theory was developed.

source.name: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

text: Freezing level — the altitude at which atmospheric temperature passes 0°C — is a critical parameter for aviation, avalanche prediction, and precipitation type; at the freezing level, rain turns to snow, and icing conditions begin for aircraft. In the Alps and other mountain ranges, the freezing level has risen approximately 100–150 metres per decade since 1960, reducing snowpack at lower elevations and threatening ski resorts; by 2100 the freezing level in the Alps could rise a further 400–600 m above current levels.

The 'teleconnection' concept — the idea that weather patterns in one region can be statistically associated with patterns in remote parts of the globe through atmospheric wave patterns — was established by Jacob Bjerknes in 1969, who linked El Niño to the Southern Oscillation. Major teleconnections include the PNA (Pacific-North American), NAO (North Atlantic Oscillation), AO (Arctic Oscillation), and SAM (Southern Annular Mode), all of which influence weather predictability at seasonal timescales.

The 2023 Mediterranean wildfires — spreading across Greece, Italy, Spain, Algeria, and Morocco during an extreme summer heat wave — burned over 800,000 hectares in Europe alone, the worst wildfire season since EU satellite records began. Attribution science found that the Rhodope Mountains fires in Greece were made 40× more likely by climate change; smoke from these fires reduced solar energy generation in southern Europe by up to 18% during peak fire periods.

Solstices and equinoxes are not the same as the hottest and coldest days of the year; the seasonal temperature lag (approximately 4–6 weeks in mid-latitudes) means that the hottest average temperatures occur in late July/August and coldest in late January/February in the Northern Hemisphere, due to the thermal inertia of the ocean and land warming up slowly after the solstice. This lag is smaller near the coast and larger in continental interiors.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Cloud radiative effects — the difference in radiative flux at the top of the atmosphere between a world with clouds and a hypothetical cloud-free world — show that clouds have a net global cooling effect of approximately −18 W/m², because the reflective cooling effect of low clouds exceeds the warming effect of high cirrus clouds. Low tropical marine clouds are the most uncertain aspect of climate sensitivity; a small increase in low cloud coverage would significantly slow warming, while a decrease would accelerate it.

The 2017 Hurricane Maria, a Category 4 hurricane that devastated Puerto Rico, caused approximately 2,975 deaths (the official estimate revised upward from 64 in 2018) — the deadliest US natural disaster in a century — and $90 billion in damage. The storm destroyed 80% of Puerto Rico's power grid; some residents went without electricity for up to 11 months, making it the longest sustained power outage in US history and exposing systemic vulnerabilities in island infrastructure.

The stratosphere — the atmospheric layer from 12 to 50 km altitude, just above the weather-producing troposphere — is actually warming slightly at its lower boundary due to ozone recovery but cooling in its upper levels due to CO₂ increase, a distinct fingerprint of greenhouse gas forcing that distinguishes it from solar-driven warming. Stratospheric cooling is one of the most robust 'smoking gun' signatures confirming the anthropogenic origin of observed global warming.

The 1816 'Year Without a Summer' (following the 1815 Tambora eruption) caused widespread crop failures in Europe and North America that coincided with the last great famine in western Europe; in New England, frost was recorded in every month of the year, and a cold July snowstorm destroyed crops in upstate New York. The famine, combined with the disruption of the Napoleonic Wars, is estimated to have killed 200,000 people and triggered massive European emigration to the Americas.

The concept of 'heat stress' encompasses the combined effects of heat and humidity on human physiology; at 35°C and 100% relative humidity, the wet-bulb temperature of 35°C represents the physiological limit — the body can no longer cool itself. Recent research suggests that wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), which also accounts for radiant heat and wind speed, is a more complete metric; worker productivity in outdoor occupations in tropical regions is already declining measurably due to heat stress.

The mesosphere — the atmospheric layer between 50 and 80 km — is the coldest part of Earth's atmosphere, reaching −90°C at its upper boundary (the mesopause); it is also where most meteors burn up. Despite being warmer than 99% of the atmosphere's mass is below it, the mesosphere is poorly observed because it is too high for weather balloons and too low for satellites; it is studied mainly by meteor radar, lidar, and rocket soundings.

source.name: NASA Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere

text: The 'extreme heat urban escalator' — the compounding of background global warming, urban heat island intensification, and increased frequency of heat waves — has been calculated to raise the effective summer temperature experienced by urban residents by 2–5°C above the rural warming rate. Heat-related mortality studies in 726 cities worldwide found that 37% of heat deaths are already attributable to climate change, with this fraction rising steeply as warming continues.

Groundwater depletion — driven by agricultural irrigation extracting water faster than recharge — has begun to register in global sea level rise; a 2023 study found that groundwater pumping contributed 6.24 mm to sea level rise between 1993 and 2010, approximately 10% of the total rise in that period. India and the US are the world's largest groundwater users; the North India Aquifer system is being depleted at an average of 54 cubic kilometres per year, unsustainably exceeding recharge.

The 1950 discovery of the jet stream by wartime fighter pilots in the Pacific, who encountered extreme tailwinds at high altitude, led to significant fuel savings for high-altitude commercial aviation; a flight from Los Angeles to New York typically saves 45 minutes riding the eastward jet stream, while the return flight, flying against it, takes longer. The jet stream's strengthening or weakening affects commercial aviation fuel costs by hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

The 'wet globe bulb' measurements used in heat stress assessment are standardised globally by ISO 7243; the WBGT (Wet Bulb Globe Temperature) combines dry-bulb temperature, globe thermometer (radiant heat), and natural (non-ventilated) wet-bulb temperature. The International Olympic Committee requires WBGT monitoring at all outdoor Olympic events and mandates rest breaks when WBGT exceeds 28°C, a threshold already exceeded regularly at summer Games venues — driving discussion of moving the Summer Olympics to autumn.

The GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite) system — operated by NOAA from 35,786 km altitude over the equator — provides continuous full-disk images of the Western Hemisphere every 10 minutes (every 30 seconds during severe weather). The latest GOES-16 and GOES-18 satellites, launched in 2016 and 2022, carry a 16-channel imager versus 5 channels on previous satellites, dramatically improving detection of fires, volcanic eruptions, fog, and storm development.

Polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) — iridescent, nacreous 'mother of pearl' clouds forming in the lower stratosphere at altitudes of 15–25 km at temperatures below −78°C — are beautiful but chemically destructive; the surfaces of PSC ice particles catalyse ozone-destroying reactions between chlorine compounds, making them a key mechanism amplifying the Antarctic ozone hole each spring. Climate change cooling the stratosphere is expected to increase PSC frequency.

Hurricane Ian (September 2022) made landfall in southwestern Florida as a Category 4 storm with a 5.3 m (17.4 foot) storm surge — the highest ever recorded in Florida — causing $113 billion in damage (the third costliest US hurricane on record). The storm rapidly intensified by 45 mph in the 24 hours before landfall as it tracked over exceptionally warm Gulf of Mexico waters that were 1–3°C warmer than the historical average.

The concept of 'dangerous climate change' first entered international policy in the 1992 UNFCCC, which set its objective as avoiding 'dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system', but left 'dangerous' undefined. Twenty years of negotiation produced the 2°C global mean temperature threshold as a policy goal at the 2010 Cancún Conference; the 1.5°C limit added at Paris in 2015 came from scientific evidence showing significantly higher risks — to coral reefs, glaciers, extreme events, and small island states — between 1.5°C and 2°C.

Deep-sea sediment cores from the Caribbean provide continuous climate records spanning over 5 million years; by analysing benthic foraminifera oxygen isotopes from these cores, scientists can reconstruct the onset of Northern Hemisphere glaciation around 2.7 million years ago and the global cooling trend of the Pliocene that ultimately created the Ice Ages we know today. The Caribbean records show that glacial-interglacial cycles switched from 41,000-year (obliquity-paced) to 100,000-year (eccentricity-paced) cycles around 900,000 years ago.

Snowflakes — aggregates of ice crystals — obey a strict rule: they always have 6-fold (hexagonal) symmetry because water molecules form a hexagonal lattice when they freeze. The enormous variety of snowflake shapes (plates, columns, dendrites, needles) is determined by the temperature and humidity at the altitude where they form; Wilson Bentley (Snowflake Bentley) photographed over 5,000 individual snowflakes through a microscope between 1885 and 1931 and found no two identical.

The Hadley Cell expansion — the poleward expansion of the tropical circulation cell at approximately 0.5–1° latitude per decade — is driven by climate change and is causing the subtropical dry zone to extend toward the poles. The Mediterranean basin, southern Africa, southwestern Australia, California, and southern South America are all located in the regions most likely to experience reduced rainfall as the Hadley Cell expands, and all have already shown multi-decadal drying trends consistent with model projections.

The WMO's World Weather Watch — the international system of weather observation, data exchange, and forecast dissemination established in 1963 — coordinates the meteorological infrastructure of 193 member states, sharing all basic weather data freely and in real time across national borders. This unprecedented international scientific cooperation, maintained even during the Cold War, is one of the most successful examples of global scientific collaboration and has directly saved millions of lives through improved weather warnings.

The 'heat stress threshold' for crops is well-defined: rice fails to produce viable grain when night temperatures exceed 26°C, maize pollen is killed above 35°C, and wheat's filling stage is impaired above 30°C. Global mean yield losses per degree of warming are estimated at −6% for wheat, −7% for maize, −3% for rice, and −3% for soybean — and these effects are compounding with ozone pollution that reduces photosynthesis, threatening the food security of billions.

The Pacific Ring of Fire — the belt of seismically and volcanically active crust surrounding the Pacific Ocean — is responsible for approximately 90% of the world's earthquakes and 75% of its volcanoes. Major volcanic eruptions from Ring of Fire volcanoes (Pinatubo, Krakatoa, El Chichón) inject sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, causing temporary global cooling of 0.1–0.5°C lasting 1–3 years; these events provide natural experiments that help calibrate climate models.

Heat waves are killing more people globally than any other weather extreme, yet they are the least visible — leaving no dramatic physical destruction. A 2021 Lancet study found that between 2000–2019, an average of 489,000 heat-related deaths occurred globally per year; with each additional degree of warming, heat-related mortality could increase by 4–10% in temperate regions and 3–5% in tropical regions already near the physiological limits of human tolerance.

The concept of 'climate overshoot' — exceeding the 1.5°C or 2°C targets before eventually returning below them through massive carbon removal — is now considered likely in most emission scenarios; temporary overshoot could trigger irreversible tipping points (coral reef die-off, ice sheet collapse) that persist even after temperatures return below the target. The feasibility of relying on future carbon removal technology to 'draw down' the overshoot is a major area of scientific and policy debate.

The Aurora — visible most frequently from within the 'auroral oval' between 65° and 72° geomagnetic latitude — is produced by energetic solar wind electrons and protons precipitating into the ionosphere during geomagnetic storms. The Carrington Event of 1–2 September 1859 was the most intense geomagnetic storm ever recorded, producing auroras visible at tropical latitudes including Cuba and Hawaii; if such an event struck today's electrical grid infrastructure, damage estimates range from $600 billion to $2.6 trillion.

The Indian Ocean has warmed faster than any other ocean since the 1950s — approximately 1°C over 60 years — driven by increased greenhouse gas forcing and reduced aerosol cooling in South and East Asia. Faster Indian Ocean warming is intensifying the South Asian monsoon variability, increasing cyclone intensity in the Arabian Sea (historically rare for intense storms), and driving the Indian Ocean Dipole oscillations that bring extreme weather to Africa and Australia.

Ceilometers — automated lidar instruments that direct a laser beam upward to measure the altitude of cloud bases — replaced human cloud observers at most major airports from the 1990s onward. Modern ceilometers also detect aerosol layers, volcanic ash, smoke, and fog, providing continuous boundary layer structure data that feeds into numerical weather prediction models; a network of 120+ ceilometers across Europe now produces hourly profiles of aerosol transport that transformed understanding of dust and smoke events.

The 1963 eruption of Mount Agung in Bali — which killed approximately 1,900 people — injected sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere and cooled global temperatures by about 0.3°C over 1963–1965; scientists studying the Agung eruption made the first modern quantitative estimate of volcanic climate forcing and provided early evidence that stratospheric aerosols have a measurable global cooling effect, laying groundwork for later proposals to mimic volcanic eruptions through geoengineering.

The 'double ITCZ' problem — the persistent tendency of most global climate models to produce excess rainfall south of the equator in the Pacific, creating a symmetric double ITCZ rather than the observed asymmetric single band — is one of the most long-standing biases in climate modelling. After 40 years of effort, the 2023 CMIP6 model ensemble has substantially reduced but not eliminated this bias, illustrating how subtle errors in convective parameterisation propagate into large systematic errors in simulated tropical rainfall.

Snow covers approximately 46 million km² of the Northern Hemisphere at peak (January), and its high albedo (60–90%) reflects most incoming solar radiation, helping to regulate winter temperatures; the annual Northern Hemisphere snow cover extent has decreased by approximately 8% since 1970, with spring snow cover declining faster than autumn cover. Reduced snow cover extends the growing season in some Arctic and boreal regions but is reducing the spring runoff that replenishes rivers and aquifers in snow-fed agricultural regions.

Phenological 'spring advancement' — the earlier arrival of spring warmth, earlier plant flowering, and earlier insect emergence documented across the Northern Hemisphere — is proceeding at approximately 2–6 days per decade at middle latitudes. However, not all species advance at the same rate: plants tend to be more responsive to warming than the birds that eat their insects, and insects more responsive than the fish that eat them, creating 'phenological mismatches' that disrupt food chains and reduce ecosystem stability.

Monsoon depressions — low-pressure systems that form over the Bay of Bengal during the Indian monsoon season and move northwestward over land — are responsible for 40–50% of India's summer rainfall; they are distinct from tropical cyclones (weaker and larger), but can cause devastating flooding in central India. Climate models suggest monsoon depressions may decrease in frequency but increase in intensity under climate change, producing more extreme but less frequent rainfall events.

The 2010 Haiti earthquake — a 7.0 Mw earthquake on 12 January 2010 — killed approximately 200,000–300,000 people, the deadliest earthquake in the Western Hemisphere in 200 years; the disaster was compounded by the fact that it struck in a country severely weakened by a history of deforestation, political instability, and extreme poverty. Attribution researchers linked the earthquake's death toll partly to inadequate building construction exacerbated by chronic underdevelopment, illustrating how natural hazard impact is determined by social vulnerability as much as physical hazard intensity.

The Argo float programme — 3,900+ autonomous profiling floats deployed across the global ocean that drift at 1,000 m depth, dive to 2,000 m measuring temperature and salinity every 10 days before surfacing to transmit data — has provided the most comprehensive ocean heat content record ever assembled. Argo data have transformed understanding of interannual ocean heat storage variability and sea level rise contributions; the programme was extended to include biogeochemical sensors measuring oxygen, pH, and nitrate.

The 'Bergeron process' (or Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen process) explains why precipitation forms most efficiently in mixed-phase clouds (containing both ice crystals and supercooled liquid water droplets): ice crystals have a lower saturation vapour pressure than supercooled water, so water vapour deposits on ice while the liquid drops evaporate, rapidly growing large ice crystals that fall as precipitation. This process is why rain can originate as ice, even in tropical clouds where it begins as snowflakes at altitude.

The concept of 'climate debt' — the accumulated greenhouse gas emissions from developed nations since industrialisation that have consumed the majority of the 'safe' atmospheric carbon budget — underpins much of the equity debate in international climate negotiations. Cumulative US emissions since 1850 represent approximately 25% of total historical emissions, Europe 22%, and China 13%; per capita cumulative emissions show an even starker disparity between industrialised and developing nations.

The Saffir-Simpson Wind Scale's limitation — addressing only wind speed and ignoring storm surge, size, and inland flooding — led to the development of the 'integrated kinetic energy' (IKE) metric for tropical cyclones, which accounts for the entire windfield's destructive potential rather than the maximum sustained wind in a small area. Under the IKE metric, large but slower storms like Sandy (2012) rank far higher in destructive potential than faster but compact storms like Patricia (2015), better reflecting their actual economic impacts.

source.name: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

text: The global average temperature increase in the 20th century of approximately 0.74°C was not uniform: land areas warmed more than oceans (by approximately 40%), high latitudes warmed more than tropics, and nighttime minimums warmed more than daytime maximums — all consistent with the physical predictions of greenhouse gas theory and clearly distinguishable from the patterns of warming expected from solar variability or urban heat island bias.

The 2004 Southeast Asia tsunami's death toll was dramatically higher in Aceh, Indonesia (c. 170,000) than in Thailand's Khao Lak (c. 5,000) — not only because Aceh was closer to the earthquake epicentre but also because extensive coastal mangrove forests that had buffered wave energy in Khao Lak had been cleared in Aceh for shrimp farming. Subsequent studies quantified that intact mangroves reduce tsunami wave height by 50–90%, triggering global efforts to restore mangrove buffers.

The deepest point measured in the atmosphere — in terms of physical depression below average sea level — is Death Valley, California, at −86 m; but atmospheric pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench (11 km under sea) is over 1,000 times sea-level air pressure. For climate science, the interesting 'depths' are in ocean sediment cores: the deepest borehole climate records penetrate over 5,000 m below the seafloor and contain climate signals 100+ million years old.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The 'climate attribution' movement has expanded from academic research to legal action: as of 2023, over 2,000 climate-related lawsuits had been filed in 65 countries against governments and corporations. Attribution science has been cited in successful climate litigation including the Netherlands' Urgenda case (2019), which used attribution studies to argue the government was failing to protect citizens from climate change, and Shell's 2021 Dutch court order to cut emissions 45% by 2030.

source.name: Sabin Center for Climate Change Law

text: The highest temperature ever recorded on Earth is 56.7°C (134°F), measured at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, California, on 10 July 1913. Its status has been debated by climate historians who note that nearby stations recorded far lower temperatures that day, but the WMO archive continues to recognise it. Death Valley's extreme heat results from its basin shape (trapping hot air), dark volcanic soil, lack of vegetation, and low elevation (−86 m sea level).

source.name: WMO World Weather & Climate Extremes Archive

text: Ocean freshening — the dilution of seawater salinity due to increased glacial melt and Arctic/Antarctic runoff — is measurable and has widespread consequences: freshwater is less dense than saltwater, reducing the density difference that drives deep water formation and AMOC overturning. Satellite GRACE data shows that ice sheet meltwater input to the ocean has increased 60% in 30 years; salinity profiling by Argo floats confirms statistically significant freshening in the North Atlantic since the 1990s.

The phenomenon of 'false spring' — an unseasonably warm period in late winter that triggers early plant flowering and insect emergence, followed by a return to freezing temperatures that kills the vulnerable new growth — has become more common as climate variability increases. False springs are particularly damaging for fruit trees: the 2012 US false spring event killed approximately $500 million worth of fruit crops in Michigan and other Great Lakes states after plants broke dormancy 3–4 weeks early.

The tropical tropopause layer (TTL) — the transition zone between 14 and 18.5 km altitude where air is 'freeze-dried' to its lowest water vapour content before entering the stratosphere — acts as the primary control on how much water vapour (a powerful greenhouse gas) reaches the stratosphere. Even a 1 K change in the average TTL temperature significantly changes stratospheric water vapour concentrations, creating a potentially important feedback mechanism in climate change.

Coastal flooding from sea level rise is already the most expensive form of climate adaptation globally; the Netherlands has spent over €16 billion on Delta Works flood protection since 1958, including the Maeslant Barrier — a pair of 210 m steel hollow arms that rotate on ball-and-socket joints to close Rotterdam's harbour entrance during North Sea storm surges. The Dutch system protects a country where 26% of land is below sea level and 60% would flood without protection.

AI weather models like Google DeepMind's GraphCast (2023) and Huawei's Pangu-Weather, trained on 40 years of ECMWF reanalysis data, can produce 10-day global forecasts at 0.25° resolution in under 60 seconds on a single GPU — versus hours for ECMWF's physics-based IFS model. In systematic benchmark evaluations, GraphCast outperformed ECMWF's operational IFS model on 90% of forecast targets at 6-hourly resolution out to 10 days — a significant milestone that may fundamentally reshape operational meteorology.

The thermocline — the oceanic layer of rapid temperature decrease from warm surface to cold deep water, typically between 200 and 1,000 m depth — separates the well-mixed, oxygenated surface ocean from the deep ocean and acts as a barrier to vertical mixing. Warming strengthens the thermocline by making surface water less dense relative to deep water, reducing nutrient upwelling that sustains surface phytoplankton and decreasing the ocean's biological productivity — a positive feedback on atmospheric CO₂.

The 1938 New England Hurricane (the Long Island Express), which struck without warning on 21 September 1938 as a Category 3 storm, killed 682 people and destroyed 57,000 homes; at the time the only US weather radar was in New Jersey and could not have detected the storm over the ocean. The disaster prompted rapid expansion of the US weather observation network, demonstrating that in meteorology as in public health, disasters often drive the most significant advances in protective infrastructure.

Thermal stratification of lakes — the formation of distinct layers of warm and cold water separated by a thermocline — is intensifying as climate change warms surface waters faster than deep waters. Many mountain lakes globally have shifted from 'dimictic' (mixing twice a year, spring and autumn) to 'monomictic' (mixing once), reducing bottom water oxygenation, changing nutrient cycling, and threatening cold-water fish species. Lake Tanganyika, warming since the 1900s, has shown a 20% decline in algal productivity.

The 'glory' — a circular rainbow visible at the antisolar point (the shadow of your head) when viewing downward through cloud from an aircraft or mountain peak — is caused by backscattering and diffraction of light by uniform-sized cloud droplets. It appears as concentric coloured rings (innermost red, outer blue) and is essentially a 3D rainbow specific to the observer's viewpoint; it can only be seen by the individual whose head casts the shadow, making each observer's glory unique to them.

The 'great Pacific garbage patch' — a gyre of concentrated plastic debris in the North Pacific subtropical gyre approximately the size of Texas — affects climate at a micro-scale: plastics floating on the surface absorb more solar radiation than clear ocean water, minutely raising local sea surface temperatures and potentially affecting overlying atmospheric convection patterns. More significantly, plastic degradation produces microplastics that now appear in cloud water and rain globally.

The 'climate change feedback parameter' describes how strongly the climate system responds to warming — high feedback means small forcings produce large temperature changes. Key feedbacks include: water vapour (+1.7 W/m²/°C, positive), lapse rate (−0.8, negative), albedo (+0.4, positive), and clouds (approximately +0.42, positive but uncertain). Together they produce a total feedback of approximately +1.7 W/m²/°C, meaning Earth is significantly more sensitive to forcing than it would be without feedbacks.

Windshear — the change in wind speed or direction over a short distance — is aviation's most significant meteorological hazard; low-level windshear during approach and departure causes sudden loss of airspeed and lift. The US Federal Aviation Administration's Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWAS), installed at major airports after several fatal crashes, uses a network of anemometers to detect windshear in real time and warn pilots; combined with onboard windshear detection radar, it has reduced windshear-related accidents to near zero since the mid-1990s.

The Hadley cell strengthens in summer when equator-pole temperature gradients are steepest; its upwelling limb over the ITCZ produces the wettest belt on Earth, while its descending limb at 30°N and 30°S creates the driest. The 'precipitation minus evaporation' (P-E) signal in the oceans — fresh regions getting fresher (more rainfall) and salty regions getting saltier (more evaporation) — is a direct confirmation from the ocean's salinity record that the global water cycle is intensifying with warming.

The Dansgaard-Oeschger (D-O) events — 25 rapid climate oscillations during the last ice age characterised by warming of 10–15°C in Greenland within decades followed by slow cooling — provide dramatic evidence that the climate can change far faster than orbital forcing would suggest. The trigger mechanism is believed to be abrupt changes in AMOC linked to freshwater forcing from ice sheets; D-O events affected climate worldwide and are studied as analogues for potential future abrupt climate changes.

The globally averaged precipitation is not expected to increase in direct proportion to temperature — instead, global average rainfall increases at only about 2% per degree of warming because it is limited by atmospheric energy balance, not moisture content. However, individual extreme precipitation events increase at the Clausius-Clapeyron rate of approximately 7% per degree — meaning more intense downpours separated by longer dry periods, the 'intensification of the water cycle' that characterises climate change.

The 2019 Polar Vortex disruption that sent Arctic air over the Midwest US in late January 2019 produced the coldest temperatures in some locations since the 1980s; Chicago reached −29°C (−20°F), colder than the South Pole on that day. The event illustrated the paradox of Arctic warming enabling more frequent cold outbreaks into the mid-latitudes: as the Arctic warms and the temperature contrast between the Arctic and mid-latitudes decreases, the polar vortex becomes weaker and more susceptible to disruption.

Biosphere-atmosphere feedbacks through 'ecosystem respiration' — the CO₂ released by soil microbes decomposing organic matter — currently balance roughly half of all photosynthetic carbon uptake; as soils warm, microbial activity accelerates, potentially releasing more CO₂ than forests and grasslands absorb, flipping the terrestrial biosphere from a carbon sink to a carbon source. Model studies suggest this tipping could occur globally at around 2°C of warming if soil warming outpaces plant growth enhancement.

The world's largest snowflake ever recorded was reportedly 38 cm (15 inches) wide at Fort Keogh, Montana on 28 January 1887 — documented in the Guinness Book of Records but not independently verified. More scientifically reliable is the understanding that very large snowflakes are aggregates of many smaller crystals clumping together at temperatures near 0°C with low wind; at lower temperatures snow is drier and crystals do not readily aggregate, explaining why the wettest, heaviest snowfalls occur closest to freezing.

The 2018 Kerala floods — the worst flooding in India in nearly a century, killing over 400 people and displacing 1.5 million in August 2018 — were produced by a combination of unusually intense monsoon rainfall (42% above average) and simultaneous opening of 35 dams whose reservoirs had been filled to capacity, raising questions about dam management protocols during extreme rainfall events and the need to pre-release water before storms.

The 'black body' concept — a theoretical object that absorbs all electromagnetic radiation falling on it and emits radiation according to Planck's law based solely on its temperature — is fundamental to understanding Earth's energy balance. Earth absorbs solar radiation primarily in the visible spectrum (5,778 K solar blackbody peak) and emits longwave (infrared) radiation at its own temperature (~255 K effective blackbody temperature); greenhouse gases absorb this emitted infrared, warming the surface to 288 K rather than the −18°C expected without atmosphere.

The Pacific Northwest heat dome of June 2021 broke the all-time temperature record of Canada (Lytton, BC: 49.6°C) and killed an estimated 1,400 people in British Columbia alone, along with over 1 billion intertidal marine creatures along the Pacific Coast that were boiled alive at low tide. The event was so statistically extreme that the World Weather Attribution team initially struggled to quantify how much more likely climate change made it — eventually concluding it was 'virtually impossible' without climate change.

Ice albedo feedback amplifies Arctic warming through a particularly powerful mechanism: as sea ice melts, dark ocean absorbs 94% of solar radiation rather than reflecting 90%, converting a reflection surface into an absorption surface. The global average effect of losing summer Arctic sea ice is equivalent to adding approximately 25 years of current CO₂ emissions — an enormous feedback that is already playing out and contributing to the observed acceleration of Northern Hemisphere warming.

The 2010 Pakistan 'super floods' — driven by an exceptionally intense monsoon amplified by La Niña — inundated one-fifth of the country over three months from July to September, killing nearly 2,000 people, displacing 20 million, and causing $43 billion in damage. The flooding was partly attributed to anomalous atmospheric blocking patterns linked to the simultaneous 2010 Russian heat wave, which diverted the monsoon jet stream southward, a teleconnection between two extreme events on opposite sides of Asia.

Weather modification using explosive artillery was attempted by American scientist Charles Hatfield in the early 1900s, who claimed to produce rain by firing shells into clouds; the city of San Diego contracted him in 1915–16 to end a drought, and an unexpectedly severe rainstorm followed that killed 20 people and caused massive flooding — but the legal and scientific question of whether Hatfield caused the rain was never resolved, and his contract was not paid.

The Coriolis-driven subtropical gyres — five large rotating ocean circulation systems driven by the interaction of surface winds with Earth's rotation — concentrate heat in their western boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas, East Australian) while producing cold upwelling on their eastern sides. These gyres are accelerating as climate change intensifies surface winds; a faster East Australian Current has shifted marine heat southward, bleaching Tasmanian kelp forests and changing marine species distributions.

The WMO Global Climate Observing System (GCOS) identifies 54 Essential Climate Variables (ECVs) — including surface temperature, precipitation, sea level, sea ice extent, and ocean heat content — that must be monitored with sufficient accuracy, length, and spatial coverage to detect climate change. Maintaining these observation systems requires continuous international cooperation; instrument changes, station relocations, and data gaps all require careful homogenisation to produce reliable long-term trends.

The 2023 El Niño — the strongest since 1997–98 — drove global sea surface temperatures to the highest ever recorded by March 2024 (0.95°C above the 1982–2011 average), with equatorial Pacific temperatures more than 2°C above normal. The event's interaction with the background of human-caused warming pushed 2023 global mean temperature to a level that scientists in the 1990s projected would not be reached until the 2040s under business-as-usual emissions, illustrating how natural variability interacts with underlying anthropogenic trends.

The Earth's climate is ultimately powered by two energy sources: solar radiation (1,361 W/m² at the top of the atmosphere) and Earth's internal geothermal heat (0.087 W/m²) — the former is approximately 15,000 times stronger than the latter. However, anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing has added approximately 2.7 W/m² to the energy imbalance — equivalent to 30× Earth's entire geothermal heat flux — meaning humans have become, in energy terms, a force comparable to Earth's interior heat flow in driving the climate system.

The global average sea level has risen approximately 20 cm (8 inches) since 1900, with the rate accelerating from about 1.4 mm/year in the early 20th century to over 3.6 mm/year today. Thermal expansion of warming ocean water accounts for roughly half of observed sea-level rise, with melting glaciers and ice sheets contributing the rest.

Cloud seeding is a weather modification technique that disperses substances such as silver iodide or liquid propane into clouds to encourage precipitation. China operates the world's largest cloud-seeding program, aiming to alter weather over an area of 5.5 million km² — roughly 1.5 times the size of India.

The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air surrounding the Earth's poles; when it weakens or becomes distorted, it can send tongues of Arctic air plunging into mid-latitudes. A weakened polar vortex was linked to the February 2021 Texas freeze, which killed over 200 people and caused an estimated $195 billion in damage.

Haboobs are massive dust storms driven by the outflow of downdrafts from collapsing thunderstorm cells; the storm wall can reach heights of 1.5 km (5,000 ft) and advance at speeds exceeding 100 km/h. They are common in the Sahara, Arabian Peninsula, and the American Southwest, particularly around Phoenix, Arizona.

The Younger Dryas was an abrupt climate reversal approximately 12,900–11,700 years ago that plunged much of the Northern Hemisphere back into near-glacial conditions within just a few decades. It is thought to have been triggered by a massive pulse of cold, fresh meltwater from glacial Lake Agassiz into the North Atlantic, which disrupted thermohaline circulation.

The heat dome phenomenon occurs when a high-pressure system traps hot air under it like a lid, preventing it from escaping and allowing temperatures to build day after day. The June 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome shattered records across Canada and the United States, with Lytton, British Columbia, reaching 49.6°C (121.3°F) — nearly 5°C above the previous Canadian record.

St. Elmo's Fire is a weather phenomenon in which luminous plasma is created by a corona discharge from a sharp-pointed object in a strong electric field during a thunderstorm. Sailors historically viewed the bluish-white glow on ship masts as an omen, and it is named after the patron saint of sailors.

Ball lightning is a rare and poorly understood atmospheric phenomenon appearing as a luminous, spherical object that ranges in size from a pea to several metres across and can persist for seconds to minutes. Despite thousands of eyewitness accounts, no fully accepted scientific explanation exists, and researchers are still debating whether it involves plasma, microwave radiation, or other mechanisms.

The stratosphere contains the ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation, and is heated from above unlike the troposphere where temperature decreases with altitude. The discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole in 1985 by British scientists at Halley Research Station led directly to the Montreal Protocol, often called the world's most successful environmental treaty.

Noctilucent clouds (NLCs) are the highest clouds in Earth's atmosphere, forming at altitudes around 76–85 km (47–53 miles) in the mesosphere and visible only during twilight when they catch sunlight from below the horizon. They have been observed more frequently and at lower latitudes in recent decades, a trend thought to be related to increasing methane emissions, which produce water vapor in the upper atmosphere.

The trade winds are steady easterly winds blowing toward the equator from the subtropical high-pressure belts in both hemispheres; they were the primary route for European sailing ships crossing the Atlantic during the Age of Exploration. Their consistent direction is produced by the combination of the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis effect.

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a belt of low pressure near the equator where trade winds from the Northern and Southern hemispheres meet, rising and creating the tropics' heavy rainfall. Sailors historically called it the 'doldrums' because its light and unpredictable winds could leave sailing ships becalmed for weeks.

The global conveyor belt, also called thermohaline circulation, moves water around the entire globe taking roughly 1,000 years to complete one full cycle. It redistributes heat from the tropics to the poles and plays a key role in regulating Earth's climate by transporting nutrients and oxygen to deep ocean ecosystems.

Graupel, also called soft hail or snow pellets, forms when supercooled water droplets freeze onto snowflakes in a process called riming, creating fragile, rounded pellets up to 5 mm in diameter. Unlike hailstones, which form in thunderstorms, graupel typically falls from convective clouds and disintegrates easily on impact.

The concept of 'wet-bulb temperature' measures the cooling effect of evaporation; a wet-bulb temperature of 35°C (95°F) represents the theoretical upper limit of human survivability even in the shade with unlimited water, because the body can no longer cool itself through sweating. Climate models project that parts of South Asia and the Persian Gulf will regularly exceed this threshold by mid-century.

Fog occurs when water vapor condenses into tiny droplets suspended in the air near the ground, reducing visibility to less than 1 km (0.62 miles). Advection fog — formed when warm moist air moves over a cool surface — is responsible for the iconic fog of San Francisco Bay and the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, one of the world's foggiest regions.

The global surface temperature anomaly for 2023 was 1.45°C above the pre-industrial average, making it the warmest year in recorded history by a substantial margin. For the first time, every single day of a calendar year was at least 1°C warmer than the pre-industrial baseline.

Virga is precipitation that evaporates or sublimates before reaching the ground, appearing as streaks or wisps hanging beneath clouds. It is particularly common in arid regions such as the American West and can be visually striking against a sunset backdrop, though the evaporation of virga can cool air rapidly and sometimes trigger dangerous microbursts.

The stratospheric polar vortex in the Southern Hemisphere is stronger and more persistent than its Northern Hemisphere counterpart because of the absence of large mountain ranges that disrupt atmospheric circulation. This stronger vortex allows Antarctic temperatures to plunge lower in winter, which is why the Antarctic ozone hole is far more severe than any Arctic equivalent.

A piezometer network beneath Greenland's ice sheet has revealed that the bedrock under the ice is still rebounding upward from the last Ice Age — a process called glacial isostatic adjustment — at rates up to 4 cm per year. As the ice sheet loses mass faster due to climate change, this rebound is accelerating and will eventually affect sea-level calculations.

Katabatic winds are gravity-driven flows of cold, dense air that rush downslope, sometimes reaching extreme speeds. Antarctica's katabatic winds regularly exceed 300 km/h in places, and the Bora wind of the Adriatic coast is a notable European example, while the Foehn of the Alps and the Chinook of North America are warm equivalents driven by orographic descent.

The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the largest element of tropical weather variability on 30–90 day timescales, characterized by an eastward-propagating region of enhanced rainfall and cloudiness. The MJO modulates hurricane activity, monsoon onset, and mid-latitude weather patterns, making it one of the most important targets for extended-range weather forecasting.

Permafrost thaw lakes (thermokarst lakes) form when permafrost melts and the ground collapses, allowing water to pool in depressions; from above they give the Siberian tundra a polka-dot appearance. These lakes are significant methane sources: methane bubbles up from decomposing organic material on their beds year-round, even in winter through the ice.

source.name: USGS National Climate Change and Wildlife Science Center

text: Lightning contains enough energy to power a 60-watt light bulb for approximately six months, yet the massive voltage difference (roughly 300 million volts) is discharged in a fraction of a second — so fast that harnessing it is not currently practical. The typical lightning bolt carries around one billion joules but releases it across such a tiny area and time that efficient capture remains an engineering challenge.

The Köppen climate classification system, developed by German-Russian climatologist Wladimir Köppen in 1884 and refined in 1936, divides the world into five major climate groups (A–E) based on temperature and precipitation. It remains the most widely used climate classification system in education and research.

The 'Little Ice Age' was a period of regional cooling between roughly 1300 and 1850 CE, most pronounced in the North Atlantic region, during which European winters were harsher, alpine glaciers expanded, and the Thames River in London regularly froze solidly enough to hold 'Frost Fairs.' Its causes remain debated but likely involved a combination of reduced solar activity, volcanic eruptions, and ocean circulation changes.

Pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb) clouds form above intense wildfires when heat and moisture from burning vegetation rise rapidly and create towering thunderstorm-like clouds that can generate their own lightning, downdrafts, and fire whirls, spreading the fire. The 2019–20 Australian Black Summer fires generated over 30 pyroCb events, injecting smoke into the stratosphere where it can persist for months.

Thermoclines are distinct layers in the ocean or a lake where temperature drops rapidly with depth, separating warm surface water from colder, denser deep water. In tropical oceans, the thermocline lies at approximately 200 metres depth, and during El Niño events its position shifts dramatically across the Pacific, affecting fisheries and climate patterns worldwide.

Windshear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance and is one of the greatest hazards to aviation during takeoff and landing. Microbursts — intense, localized downdrafts from a thunderstorm — can produce windshear strong enough to overwhelm aircraft lift; understanding this phenomenon followed the 1985 Delta Air Lines crash in Dallas, which killed 137 people.

The Sahara Desert was green and substantially wetter during the African Humid Period (approximately 11,000–5,000 years ago), supporting hippos, crocodiles, and extensive human settlements in what is now barren desert. This 'Green Sahara' ended abruptly due to changes in Earth's orbital parameters that reduced summer solar radiation over the Northern Hemisphere, altering monsoon patterns.

Dust from the Sahara Desert regularly travels across the Atlantic Ocean and fertilizes the Amazon rainforest with phosphorus and other minerals, compensating for the nutrients washed out by heavy tropical rain. NASA satellite data show that about 22,000 tonnes of phosphorus arrives in the Amazon from the Sahara each year — roughly the same amount the forest loses annually from rainfall leaching.

Snowflakes are hexagonal (six-sided) because water molecules form a hexagonal lattice when they freeze, and every arm of a snowflake grows under identical atmospheric conditions — producing remarkable symmetry. Despite the oft-quoted claim that no two snowflakes are alike, identical snowflakes have been found in laboratory settings when very simple crystals form under controlled conditions.

The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 (119–153 km/h sustained winds) to Category 5 (≥252 km/h), but the scale measures only wind speed and says nothing about storm surge, rainfall, or flooding — which often cause more deaths. Hurricane Camille (1969) and Hurricane Dorian (2019) both made landfall as Category 5 storms.

The Mediterranean climate — characterised by hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters — is found in only five regions worldwide: the Mediterranean Basin, California, central Chile, southwestern Australia, and South Africa's Cape region. These areas are biodiversity hotspots and cover less than 2% of Earth's land surface but support about 20% of all vascular plant species.

The 1883 eruption of Krakatau in Indonesia produced global temperature drops of about 1.2°C for several years by injecting sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it formed a reflective aerosol veil. The vivid red and orange sunsets it caused around the world may have inspired Edvard Munch's famous 1893 painting 'The Scream.'

Albedo is the fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface, ranging from nearly 0 (perfect absorber) to 1 (perfect reflector). Fresh snow has an albedo of 0.80–0.90, while open ocean has an albedo of just 0.06 — which is why sea ice loss creates a powerful positive feedback loop as darker ocean absorbs far more solar energy than the ice it replaced.

Weather balloons, known as radiosondes, are launched twice daily from over 900 stations worldwide to measure temperature, humidity, pressure, and wind throughout the atmosphere up to about 35 km altitude. The data they collect, standardised since the mid-20th century, form the backbone of numerical weather prediction models.

The anticyclone, a region of high atmospheric pressure around which winds circulate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere (anticlockwise in the Southern), typically brings clear, settled weather. Blocking anticyclones can stall in place for weeks, deflecting storm tracks and causing prolonged droughts in summer or persistent cold spells in winter.

The global average precipitation is approximately 990 mm (39 inches) per year, but its distribution is extremely uneven — some tropical regions receive over 10,000 mm annually while polar deserts receive less than 100 mm. Land receives slightly less precipitation than it evaporates on a global average, with the deficit compensated by river runoff from the wetter ocean-influenced areas.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Atmospheric rivers are long, narrow corridors of intense water vapor transport in the mid-latitude atmosphere, typically 400–600 km wide and 2,000 km or more long. A single atmospheric river can transport as much water as 7.5 times the average flow of the Mississippi River; they account for 30–50% of the annual precipitation on the US West Coast.

Sea fog forms when warm, moist maritime air moves over cold ocean water and is cooled to its dew point; it can be extremely dense and persistent, with visibility near zero. The Grand Banks off Newfoundland and the coast of Northern California are renowned for their persistent summer sea fogs, which provided the ideal conditions for San Francisco's iconic fog banks.

Arctic amplification refers to the phenomenon whereby the Arctic warms at more than twice the global average rate; between 1979 and 2021, the Arctic warmed about 3–4 times faster than the global mean. This differential warming is driven by positive feedbacks including sea-ice loss, changes in snow cover, and shifts in atmospheric and ocean heat transport.

Cyclogenesis is the development or intensification of cyclonic circulation in the atmosphere; extratropical cyclogenesis typically occurs along fronts where warm and cold air masses meet. The bomb cyclone phenomenon — also called explosive cyclogenesis — occurs when a low-pressure system deepens by at least 24 millibars in 24 hours, producing violent winds and heavy precipitation over a very short period.

The global average temperature is now approximately 1.2°C above the pre-industrial average (1850–1900 baseline), but this warming is not uniform — land areas have warmed about twice as fast as ocean areas, and the Arctic has warmed three to four times faster than the global mean. The warming trend has accelerated since the 1970s, with each of the last four decades being successively warmer than any previous decade.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers

text: The Cryosphere — all frozen water on Earth including sea ice, ice sheets, glaciers, snow cover, and permafrost — is shrinking on nearly every front. Since 1979, Arctic sea ice minimum extent has declined by about 13% per decade; the Greenland ice sheet is losing mass at a rate six times faster than in the 1990s.

Ice cores extracted from Antarctica and Greenland contain air bubbles that preserve ancient atmospheric samples, allowing scientists to reconstruct CO₂ and methane concentrations going back 800,000 years. The Vostok and EPICA Dome C ice core records show that current atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (~420 ppm) are higher than at any point in at least 800,000 years — and likely 3–5 million years.

Soil moisture plays a crucial role in weather because wet soil promotes evapotranspiration that cools the surface and produces cloud cover, while dry soil absorbs more heat and suppresses convection. The drying of soils under climate change is creating a positive feedback: hotter temperatures dry soils, which reduces rainfall, which dries soils further.

The concept of 'planetary boundaries' identifies nine Earth system processes within which humanity can safely operate; climate change is one, quantified by atmospheric CO₂ concentration with a proposed boundary of 350 ppm — a level we already exceeded around 1988 and have now surpassed by over 70 ppm. This framework, introduced by Johan Rockström and colleagues in 2009, has become influential in sustainability science and policy.

El Niño years tend to suppress Atlantic hurricane activity while enhancing Pacific hurricane activity, because the warmer central and eastern Pacific aloft increases wind shear over the Atlantic, inhibiting hurricane formation. Conversely, La Niña years — with cooler Pacific waters — typically reduce Atlantic wind shear and produce more active Atlantic hurricane seasons.

The Keeling Curve, a continuous record of atmospheric CO₂ concentrations measured at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, since 1958, is one of the most important datasets in climate science. Charles David Keeling began the measurements and the curve he produced showed for the first time an annual oscillation (Northern Hemisphere plants absorbing CO₂ in summer) superimposed on a steady long-term rise from fossil fuel burning.

source.name: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory Mauna Loa CO2

text: Supercell thunderstorms are the most organised and dangerous type of thunderstorm, characterised by a rotating updraft called a mesocyclone that can produce large hail, severe winds, and the majority of violent tornadoes. They form when there is strong wind shear — a significant change of wind speed and direction with height — in the lower atmosphere.

The Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events were rapid climate fluctuations during the last glacial period, in which Greenland temperatures rose by 10–15°C within decades, then cooled slowly back over centuries. Twenty-five such events occurred between about 115,000 and 11,700 years ago, and understanding their cause — thought to involve shifts in Atlantic Ocean circulation — remains an active area of research.

Wind direction is conventionally described by where the wind comes from, not where it is going — so a 'northerly' wind blows from north to south. This convention dates from meteorological tradition and can lead to confusion with ocean current naming, where a 'northward' current moves towards the north.

The ozone layer's recovery is one of the great success stories of international environmental governance: since the Montreal Protocol came into force in 1989, production of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) has been cut by over 99%, and the Antarctic ozone hole is projected to return to 1980 levels by approximately 2065–2070. Without the Protocol, the ozone layer over the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes could have been destroyed by 67% by 2065.

The Azores High is a semi-permanent subtropical anticyclone over the North Atlantic that plays a critical role in steering weather systems across Europe. Its position and intensity influence the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and thus the severity of European winters and the supply of Atlantic moisture to the Sahel.

The most intense rainfall ever recorded in a single minute was 31.2 mm (1.23 inches) at Unionville, Maryland, USA, on July 4, 1956. The world record for 24-hour rainfall is 1,825 mm (71.9 inches) at Foc-Foc on Réunion Island during Tropical Cyclone Denise in January 1966.

Lake-effect snow forms when cold, dry air masses move over warmer unfrozen lake surfaces, picking up moisture and heat, then depositing intense narrow bands of snow on the downwind shore. The Great Lakes of North America produce some of the world's most prolific lake-effect snowstorms; Buffalo, New York, has received over 1.5 metres of snow in a single storm.

The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) is a long-lived El Niño-like pattern of Pacific climate variability that shifts between warm and cool phases on timescales of 20–30 years. The PDO modulates the impact of ENSO — during a positive (warm) PDO phase, El Niño effects on North American precipitation are amplified, while during a negative phase they are muted.

Morning glory clouds are rare, low-level, roll-shaped clouds — solitary atmospheric waves — that form in the Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia each spring, often occurring in sequences of up to 10 waves and extending for hundreds of kilometres. Local Aboriginal people of the region have observed them for generations, and glider pilots travel from around the world to ride their updrafts.

Acid rain, caused by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides released from burning fossil fuels reacting with atmospheric moisture, was a major environmental problem through the 1970s–1990s, damaging forests and lakes across North America and Europe. The 1990 US Clean Air Act amendments led to an SO₂ cap-and-trade programme that reduced acid rain-causing emissions by 76% over 20 years, restoring many affected ecosystems.

The Mei-yu (Chinese: 梅雨, 'plum rain') is a stationary frontal system that brings weeks of persistent rain to central and eastern China, Korea, and Japan from June to July, typically timed with the ripening of plums. The front forms at the boundary between the cold, dry continental air mass retreating northward and the warm, moist air flowing north from the tropics.

The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is the dominant pattern of atmospheric variability in the North Atlantic region, defined by the pressure difference between the Azores High and the Icelandic Low. A strongly positive NAO brings mild, wet winters to northern Europe and cold, dry winters to the Mediterranean; a negative NAO reverses this pattern, bringing frigid Arctic air to Europe.

Waterspouts are rotating columns of air over water — essentially tornadoes over the sea or large lakes. Fair-weather waterspouts, the most common type, develop from the surface upward and are generally weaker than tornadic waterspouts, which are true tornadoes that have moved from land over water.

The 'urban heat island' effect causes cities to be significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas — sometimes by 1–7°C — due to dark pavement and rooftops absorbing heat, reduced vegetation and evapotranspiration, concentrated human activity, and altered airflow. Cities effectively create their own local climates and can trigger convective rainfall downwind.

The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is a coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon in which the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean alternately warm and cool relative to each other, affecting monsoon strength. A strongly positive IOD — with warm western and cold eastern Indian Ocean — enhanced rainfall over East Africa and India while contributing to the catastrophic 2019–20 Australian bushfire season.

Isobar maps — weather maps with lines connecting points of equal atmospheric pressure — were first developed by Francis Galton in 1875 and became the foundation of modern synoptic meteorology. The spacing of isobars indicates the pressure gradient force: closely spaced isobars mean strong winds, while widely spaced ones indicate gentle breezes.

Photochemical smog, first identified in Los Angeles in the 1940s, is formed when sunlight drives chemical reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from vehicle exhausts, producing ground-level ozone and other irritants. Unlike London's pea-soup sulfur smog, LA's photochemical smog required sunlight and was not understood until chemist Arie Haagen-Smit identified its mechanism in 1952.

The Santa Ana winds of Southern California are hot, dry, downslope winds originating from high-pressure systems in the Great Basin and Mojave Desert; they can exceed 100 mph and reduce relative humidity to less than 5%. These conditions are highly conducive to rapid wildfire spread — the 2018 Woolsey Fire was driven by Santa Ana winds and destroyed over 1,600 structures.

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Los Angeles

text: The Tambora volcanic eruption of April 1815 was the most powerful eruption in recorded history (VEI 7), killing approximately 71,000 people directly and triggering 1816's 'Year Without a Summer,' which caused crop failures and famine across North America and Europe. The atmospheric cooling from Tambora's sulphur injection also indirectly inspired Mary Shelley to write 'Frankenstein' during the famously wet and gloomy Swiss summer of 1816.

Precipitation efficiency in clouds ranges from less than 1% for light cumulus to around 50% for thunderstorms; most of the water in a cloud evaporates before it reaches the ground. Warm rain processes (coalescence) dominate in the tropics, while cold rain processes (ice crystal growth via the Bergeron-Findeisen mechanism) are more important at mid-latitudes.

The Hadley Cell is a tropical atmospheric circulation in which air rises near the equator, moves poleward in the upper troposphere, descends at about 30°N and 30°S, and returns toward the equator as the trade winds. The zone of descent at about 30° latitude corresponds to the world's major desert belts — the Sahara, Arabian Desert, and Australian outback.

Weather prediction has improved dramatically over recent decades: a 5-day forecast today is as accurate as a 3-day forecast was in the 1980s. Modern numerical weather prediction models ingest data from satellites, aircraft, ships, buoys, and radiosondes and run on some of the world's most powerful supercomputers; ECMWF's model, often considered the world's best, runs on a 100-km global grid and makes predictions up to 15 days ahead.

The stratospheric sudden warming (SSW) event is a dramatic phenomenon in which the polar stratosphere warms by 30–50°C within a few days, reversing the normal cold polar vortex. Major SSW events disrupt the polar vortex and often lead to cold snaps at the surface over North America, Europe, or Asia 2–6 weeks later.

The global electric circuit connects thunderstorms (acting as generators), the ionosphere (a reservoir), and fair-weather regions (leaky capacitor) in a continuous electrical system. At any given moment, about 2,000 thunderstorms are active around the globe, collectively maintaining the ionosphere at a potential of roughly 250,000 volts above Earth's surface.

The word 'hurricane' derives from Huracán, the Taíno and Carib god of storms; 'typhoon' likely comes from the Cantonese 'dai fung' (big wind) or the Greek 'Typhon,' a monstrous wind giant. These different names for the same phenomenon reflect the different cultures that first encountered and named tropical cyclones in different ocean basins.

Transpiration by forests contributes significantly to regional precipitation through the 'biotic pump' mechanism: trees release water vapor that drives moisture-laden air from the coast inland, sustaining rainfall far from the ocean. Studies of the Amazon basin suggest deforestation not only removes trees but also suppresses the moisture recycling that sustains rainfall across continental interiors.

The Ferrel Cell is a thermally indirect atmospheric circulation cell at mid-latitudes (30°–60°) in which air flows from the poles toward the equator at the surface and from the tropics toward the poles aloft — the opposite of the Hadley and Polar cells. It is maintained not by heating differences but by the momentum imparted by eddies from extratropical storm systems.

The 'Butterfly Effect' in meteorology, articulated by mathematician and meteorologist Edward Lorenz in 1972, describes the sensitive dependence on initial conditions in chaotic systems: a tiny change (metaphorically, a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil) could in principle alter large-scale weather patterns weeks later. This fundamental sensitivity imposes an intrinsic limit of about 2 weeks on deterministic weather forecasting, regardless of computing power.

The Walker Circulation is a zonal (east-west) atmospheric circulation over the tropical Pacific, driven by the sea-surface temperature gradient: warm water in the west causes rising air, which flows east aloft and descends over the cold eastern Pacific. During El Niño, this circulation weakens or reverses as the temperature gradient flattens, with profound consequences for rainfall across the tropics.

The earliest known weather records were made by Chinese scholars around 1000 BCE, who documented rainfall and snowfall on oracle bones. Modern systematic meteorological observations began in Europe around the 17th century; the invention of the barometer by Evangelista Torricelli in 1643 and the thermometer by Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1714 provided the first instruments for quantitative weather measurement.

The global average temperature in 2024 crossed the 1.5°C above pre-industrial threshold for the first time on an annual basis, breaching the aspirational limit set in the Paris Agreement of 2015. Scientists emphasise that crossing this threshold for one year does not mean the Paris goal is permanently lost — that depends on the long-term trend.

Sea ice extent in the Arctic reached its lowest September minimum since satellite observations began in 1979, set in September 2012 at 3.41 million km². While records have been approached but not broken since, the long-term trend is unambiguously downward; climate models project the Arctic could be effectively ice-free in September (below 1 million km²) before 2050.

Radiant cooling at night occurs when Earth's surface emits infrared radiation to space and the surface temperature drops below the dew point, forming dew, frost, or radiation fog. Ground frost can form even when official air temperature at screen height (1.2 m) is above freezing, because the surface itself can cool several degrees below the measured air temperature through radiative heat loss.

The Sahel region of Africa — the semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara and the savanna — experienced a catastrophic drought from the late 1960s through the 1980s that killed hundreds of thousands of people and drove millions into famine. Research has linked the drought to a complex interaction between land degradation, reduced vegetation, and shifts in Atlantic sea surface temperatures driven partly by industrialised countries' aerosol emissions.

The jet stream was discovered during World War II when US B-29 bombers encountered unexpected strong headwinds over Japan at altitude, reducing their ground speed. Wartime meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby had theorised the existence of such upper-level winds; the post-war development of transatlantic aviation made jet stream forecasting commercially vital.

Droughts are defined not just by a lack of rainfall but relative to what is normal for a given region and season; a 'drought' in Seattle involves less rainfall than a normal year in Los Angeles. The Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), developed in 1965, is one of the most widely used measures, combining temperature and precipitation data to estimate soil moisture deficit.

source.name: NOAA National Integrated Drought Information System

text: The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) measures the difference in atmospheric pressure between Tahiti and Darwin, Australia, and is the classic indicator of El Niño/La Niña events. A sustained strongly negative SOI indicates El Niño conditions; a strongly positive SOI indicates La Niña; the coupled ocean-atmosphere system it measures was named the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) by Jacob Bjerknes in 1969.

Ground-level ozone (O₃), unlike the beneficial stratospheric ozone layer, is a pollutant and respiratory irritant formed by photochemical reactions. It reduces crop yields significantly — an estimated 10–35% reduction in wheat, soybean, and maize production in polluted regions — and costs the global economy billions of dollars annually in agricultural losses.

The Dead Sea is the lowest point on Earth's land surface at approximately 430 metres below sea level, and its extreme depth below sea level means the air column above it contains about 10% more oxygen than at sea level — making it a destination for people with respiratory conditions.
