However, the Dead Sea is shrinking at about 1 metre per year as the Jordan River is diverted for agriculture.

Chinook winds on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains can cause spectacular temperature rises: during a January 1972 Chinook event in Loma, Montana, the temperature rose from −48°C to 9°C (−54°F to 49°F) in just 24 hours — a rise of 57°C (103°F), which remains the most rapid temperature change ever recorded. The Chinook's warming is caused by adiabatic compression as air descends the leeward slope.

The first weather satellite, TIROS-1 (Television and Infrared Observation Satellite), was launched by NASA on April 1, 1960, and transmitted the first satellite images of clouds and weather systems. Within the first 78 days of operation it transmitted 22,952 useable photographs, transforming meteorologists' ability to observe large-scale weather patterns.

The Silk Road dust corridor transports Central Asian and Gobi Desert dust eastward across China, Korea, and Japan each spring in events known as Asian Dust (Kosa in Japanese, Hwangsa in Korean), affecting air quality across populated regions. The dust contains iron, phosphorus, and other nutrients that fertilise Pacific Ocean ecosystems, but also carries soil pathogens and pollutants.

Frost hollow formation demonstrates cold air drainage: on a still, clear night, cold dense air flows downhill and collects in low-lying areas and valleys, making them significantly colder than nearby hillsides — sometimes by 10°C or more. This phenomenon is why vineyards in hilly terrain are often planted on slopes rather than in valley bottoms.

The global hydrological cycle moves approximately 505,000 km³ of water through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation each year. Evaporation from the oceans accounts for about 86% of total global evaporation, and the residence time of water in the atmosphere is only about 9–10 days, meaning the entire atmospheric moisture reservoir is recycled approximately 40 times per year.

source.name: NOAA National Integrated Drought Information System

text: The term 'climate change' was first used in a scientific context by oceanographer Roger Revelle and chemist Hans Suess in a 1957 paper that described the ocean's limited ability to absorb all the CO₂ being released by fossil fuel burning. Revelle famously described humans as conducting a 'large-scale geophysical experiment' on the atmosphere.

Glaze ice (black ice) forms when supercooled rain (freezing rain) falls on surfaces below 0°C, coating everything in a clear, transparent layer of ice that is extremely difficult to see on roads. A single freezing rain event can deposit hundreds of tonnes of ice on power lines, causing them to snap; the January 1998 North American ice storm knocked out power to 4.7 million customers in Canada and the northeastern US.

The boreal forest (taiga) — the world's largest land biome, stretching across Russia, Canada, and Scandinavia — plays a dual role in climate: it absorbs CO₂ as a carbon sink, but its dark canopy also reduces albedo, absorbing solar radiation that would otherwise be reflected by snow. Whether the net climate effect of the boreal forest is warming or cooling at high latitudes remains an active area of scientific debate.

The Sirocco is a hot, dry, dust-laden wind that blows from the North African interior northward across the Mediterranean, often reaching Italy and Spain with temperatures above 40°C. As the Sirocco crosses the Mediterranean, it picks up moisture and can arrive as a humid, hot, oppressive wind on the northern shores, depositing red Saharan dust that colours the rain and coats surfaces.

The concept of 'weather versus climate' is captured in the aphorism 'Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get,' attributed in various forms to meteorologists including Robert Heinlein and Mark Twain. Climate represents the statistical behaviour of weather over 30-year standard periods (the current WMO reference period is 1991–2020), while weather describes the instantaneous state of the atmosphere.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was established in 1988 by the WMO and UNEP to provide policymakers with regular scientific assessments of climate change. Its Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), completed in 2021–2022, involved over 700 scientists from 90 countries and drew on more than 14,000 peer-reviewed studies.

Polar mesospheric clouds (PMCs), also known as noctilucent clouds, are composed of ice crystals that form at the very edge of space at temperatures below −120°C. They are visible from Earth's surface only during summer twilight at latitudes between 50° and 70°, and their increasing frequency and brightness over recent decades is used as a sensitive indicator of upper atmospheric change.

The Missoula Floods of the last Ice Age were catastrophic glacial outburst floods that swept across eastern Washington State approximately 40 times between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago, carving the Channeled Scablands. Each flood released an estimated 2,000 km³ of water in a matter of days — a flow rate greater than the combined discharge of all the world's rivers.

The diurnal temperature range (DTR) — the difference between daily maximum and minimum temperatures — has been decreasing globally as minimum (nighttime) temperatures warm faster than maximum (daytime) temperatures. This asymmetric warming is partly caused by increased cloud cover and atmospheric moisture trapping outgoing longwave radiation more effectively at night.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The term 'derecho' (from Spanish for 'straight ahead' or 'direct') describes a widespread, long-lived wind storm associated with a band of rapidly moving showers or thunderstorms, producing straight-line winds rather than the rotating winds of a tornado. The August 2020 Midwest derecho produced wind gusts exceeding 140 mph across Iowa, causing an estimated $7.5 billion in agricultural damage.

Clouds play a critical and uncertain role in climate; low-level clouds generally cool the planet by reflecting sunlight, while high-altitude cirrus clouds warm it by trapping outgoing infrared radiation. The net effect of clouds on Earth's energy balance (cloud radiative forcing) is currently a net cooling of about 20 W/m², and how this will change as the climate warms is one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate projections.

The dust bowl of the 1930s was the worst drought in American recorded history, turning vast areas of the Great Plains into a dust wasteland after decades of overplowing broke down the natural grassland that had held soil in place. During the 'Dirty Thirties,' enormous dust storms known as 'black blizzards' buried farms and towns under meters of dirt, forcing an estimated 3.5 million people to migrate from the region.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The world's deepest lake, Lake Baikal in Siberia, contains approximately 23,615 km³ of water — about 22% of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water. The lake has warmed faster than the global ocean average since 1946, and ice cover has declined by more than three weeks in the past century, affecting the unique Baikal seal and other endemic species.

Supercooled water droplets can remain liquid well below 0°C — pure water can be cooled to about −38°C before it freezes spontaneously. This supercooled state is common in mid- and high-level clouds, and encountering these clouds causes severe aircraft icing as the droplets instantly freeze on wings and fuselage, disrupting airflow and potentially causing crashes.

The global average atmospheric pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hPa (hectopascals), also expressed as one atmosphere or 1013.25 millibars. The lowest sea-level pressure ever recorded was 870 hPa in Typhoon Tip in the western Pacific on October 12, 1979 — a full 143 hPa below average, comparable to the pressure drop of ascending 1,300 metres in altitude.

Dendroclimatology uses the width, density, and isotopic composition of tree rings to reconstruct past climates; ring width generally tracks growing season temperature and rainfall. The famous 'hockey stick' graph of Northern Hemisphere temperatures over the past 1,000 years, published by Michael Mann and colleagues in 1999, relied heavily on tree ring data and showed an unprecedented warming spike in the 20th century.

The Circumpolar Deep Water (CDW) is a warm, salty water mass circulating around Antarctica that is being pushed onto the continental shelf by strengthening westerly winds, melting the undersides of Antarctic ice shelves from below. This ocean-driven melting is considered more dangerous than surface melting because it can trigger marine ice sheet instability — a potential runaway collapse scenario.

The global average ocean surface temperature has risen by about 0.88°C since 1850; the ocean has absorbed over 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases since pre-industrial times, buffering land warming but suffering devastating consequences including coral bleaching, deoxygenation, and shifts in marine ecosystems. The ocean's vast heat capacity means this stored energy will continue to affect sea levels and weather for centuries even if emissions stopped today.

source.name: IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere

text: Sprites and elves are large-scale electrical discharges that occur above thunderstorms, in the mesosphere at altitudes of 40–90 km, and were only confirmed scientifically in 1989 after accidental capture on video. Sprites appear as red jellyfish or carrot shapes lasting mere milliseconds, while elves are flattened, disc-shaped luminous expansions up to 400 km across that last less than a millisecond.

The Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC) is the world's largest and most powerful ocean current, carrying approximately 165 million cubic metres of water per second — more than 100 times the combined flow of all the world's rivers. It encircles Antarctica and acts as a thermal buffer, isolating the continent from warmer waters.

Frozen precipitation takes many forms depending on temperature profiles through the atmosphere: snow (ice crystals aggregated aloft), sleet (rain that refreezes before reaching the ground), freezing rain (supercooled rain that freezes on contact with surfaces), and hail (ice pellets grown in thunderstorm updrafts). Distinguishing these types is critical for safety, as freezing rain creates the most treacherous travel conditions.

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Winter Weather

text: Coral bleaching occurs when ocean temperatures remain just 1°C above the normal summer maximum for as little as four weeks, causing corals to expel their symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) and turn white. The Great Barrier Reef experienced its worst recorded bleaching event in 2022, when a third consecutive La Niña year failed to cool warm waters enough to prevent mass bleaching across 91% of surveyed sites.

The global conveyor belt circulation is driven by the sinking of cold, dense, salty water in the North Atlantic (particularly around Iceland and Greenland) and the Southern Ocean — the so-called 'deep water formation' process. When this dense water sinks, it forms North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) and Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW), which fill the deep ocean and slowly spread toward all other ocean basins.

The Harmattan is a dry, dusty trade wind blowing from the Sahara Desert across West Africa toward the Gulf of Guinea between November and March. It is so laden with fine dust that it dramatically reduces visibility — sometimes to less than 200 metres — causing flight cancellations and respiratory problems, while simultaneously providing welcome relief from humidity.

The global mean radiative forcing from all human activities combined was assessed at 2.72 W/m² (1750–2019 baseline) in the IPCC AR6, with CO₂ alone contributing 2.16 W/m² and methane 0.54 W/m². This imbalance — more energy entering than leaving the Earth system — is the fundamental thermodynamic driver of global warming.

The first known weather forecast was published by Robert FitzRoy, captain of HMS Beagle on Darwin's famous voyage and later head of the UK Meteorological Office, in The Times newspaper on August 1, 1861. FitzRoy coined the term 'forecast' for weather prediction and developed the first synoptic weather maps, pioneering modern meteorology.

Marine heatwaves — periods when ocean surface temperatures exceed the 90th percentile for a given location and time of year for at least five consecutive days — have become more frequent, longer, and more intense since the 1980s. The 2013–2016 'Blob' of anomalously warm water in the Northeast Pacific contributed to massive harmful algal blooms, fishery collapses, and sea bird die-offs across the US West Coast.

Evapotranspiration — the combined water loss through evaporation from soils and transpiration from plants — transfers more energy from the land surface to the atmosphere than any other process, including sensible heat transfer. In the Amazon, over 50% of rainfall is recycled back to the atmosphere through evapotranspiration, sustaining the forest's own rainfall regime.

The Beaufort Sea polynya — a persistent area of open water surrounded by sea ice in the Canadian Arctic — is maintained by offshore winds that push ice away from the coast and allow the ocean surface to remain exposed. Polynyas are hotspots of biological productivity, serving as essential feeding, calving, and wintering areas for narwhals, beluga whales, polar bears, and migratory birds.

Flash droughts are rapidly developing droughts that can intensify within weeks, driven by a combination of low precipitation, high temperatures, and strong winds that rapidly deplete soil moisture. Unlike slow-onset droughts that develop over months to years, flash droughts can devastate crops before farmers and emergency managers have time to respond; they are projected to become more frequent as temperatures rise.

source.name: NOAA National Integrated Drought Information System

text: Ice-albedo feedback is the most powerful positive feedback mechanism in the Arctic climate system: when sea ice melts, it exposes darker ocean water that absorbs about 6 times more solar radiation than ice, warming the ocean further and melting more ice. This self-reinforcing loop is a primary reason the Arctic is warming so much faster than the global average.

The Drake Passage — the waterway between South America and Antarctica — is the world's most treacherous sea route, infamous for its extreme storms, giant waves up to 20 metres, and powerful currents. The opening of the Drake Passage roughly 30–34 million years ago as Antarctica and South America separated allowed the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to develop, thermally isolating Antarctica and triggering the growth of the Antarctic ice sheet.

The dew point temperature is the temperature to which air must be cooled (at constant pressure and moisture content) for saturation to occur and dew to form. A dew point above 21°C (70°F) is considered uncomfortable for most people, and above 26°C (79°F) it feels oppressive; dew points above 30°C are extreme and have been recorded in the Persian Gulf region.

The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines was the second-largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century, injecting 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. The resulting aerosol veil cooled the global mean surface temperature by about 0.5°C for approximately two years and provided scientists with a natural experiment validating climate models' ability to simulate aerosol forcing.

Anabatic winds are upslope winds driven by the heating of mountain slopes by solar radiation; they rise during the day as the heated air over slopes becomes less dense than the surrounding atmosphere. In contrast to katabatic winds (which flow downhill at night due to radiative cooling), anabatic winds are typically gentle breezes that can carry moisture upslope and trigger afternoon thunderstorms over mountains.

Microplastics have been found in cloud water collected from mountain peaks in Japan and the French Pyrenees, suggesting plastic particles are becoming part of the hydrological cycle and may influence cloud formation and atmospheric chemistry. Researchers have detected microplastics at high altitudes in remote locations including the Pyrenees and the Tibetan Plateau, thousands of kilometres from any source.

The annual 'breathing' of the Keeling Curve — the seasonal oscillation in atmospheric CO₂ — is driven primarily by the Northern Hemisphere's forests and grasslands absorbing carbon in spring and summer (April–October) and releasing it as vegetation dies in autumn and winter. The amplitude of this seasonal cycle has increased by about 15% since the 1960s, reflecting the response of land ecosystems to warming.

The Mistral is a strong, cold, northwesterly wind that blows through the Rhône valley in southern France toward the Gulf of Lion, sometimes exceeding 100 km/h. It forms when a depression over the Gulf of Genoa draws cold continental air southward; it is responsible for the crystal-clear skies of Provence but can devastate crops and was immortalised in the letters of Vincent van Gogh who painted in Arles.

Ocean acidification is caused by the absorption of CO₂ from the atmosphere into seawater, forming carbonic acid, which dissociates to release hydrogen ions and lower pH. Since industrialisation, ocean pH has decreased from about 8.2 to 8.1 — a shift of 0.1 pH units that represents a 26% increase in ocean acidity — with potentially devastating effects on shell-forming organisms such as oysters, mussels, and pteropods.

The 'stratospheric aerosol injection' (SAI) — also called solar geoengineering — is a proposed method to reflect sunlight by releasing sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere, mimicking the cooling effect of large volcanic eruptions. While computer models suggest it could offset some warming quickly and cheaply, concerns include 'termination shock' (rapid warming if deployment stopped), shifts in regional precipitation, and geopolitical governance challenges.

Snow is an excellent thermal insulator because of the large amount of trapped air; the temperature inside a snow cave or igloo can be as much as 40°C warmer than the outside air. This insulating property is vital for Arctic animals like lemmings, voles, and ground squirrels that overwinter in the subnivean space beneath the snow surface.

source.name: National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: The Tibetan Plateau, often called 'the roof of the world,' exerts a massive influence on Asian climate by acting as a giant heat source in summer — its elevated surface absorbs solar radiation and warms the atmosphere, driving the Asian monsoon. The plateau's average elevation of 4,500 metres also acts as a mechanical barrier that deflects the westerly jet stream and influences weather patterns across Eurasia.

The Clausius-Clapeyron relation describes how the water-holding capacity of the atmosphere increases by about 7% for every 1°C of warming — meaning a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapour, intensifying precipitation when it does occur. This physical relationship explains why extreme rainfall events have become more intense with global warming, even in regions experiencing overall drying.

Frost flowers are intricate ice crystals that form on young sea ice when extremely cold air meets relatively warm, moist surface water; they can grow several centimetres tall and concentrate sea salt and biological material. These delicate structures are important geochemically — they may seed Arctic clouds with sea salt aerosols and contribute to atmospheric bromine chemistry that destroys ozone.

The 2003 European heatwave killed approximately 70,000 people across the continent, with France alone accounting for nearly 15,000 excess deaths in August. Attribution science — which quantifies the role of climate change in specific events — concluded this event was made at least twice as likely by human-caused warming; such heatwaves are now expected to occur every 2–5 years under current conditions.

The water cycle is accelerating as the climate warms: evaporation rates are increasing, the atmosphere holds more moisture, and rainfall events are becoming more intense when they occur. Studies estimate the global hydrological cycle has intensified by about 2–3% per degree of warming, which simultaneously increases drought risk in already dry regions and flooding risk in wet regions.

The global mean Earth Energy Imbalance (EEI) — the excess of incoming solar radiation over outgoing radiation due to greenhouse gas forcing — was approximately 0.87 W/m² over the 2005–2019 period according to IPCC AR6. This imbalance, if continued, would warm the planet's surface by roughly 0.8°C even if greenhouse gas concentrations were somehow held constant today.

The Svalbard archipelago in the high Arctic (77°–81°N) has warmed by approximately 7°C since 1971 — roughly seven times the global average rate — making it one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. This extreme warming has caused year-round average temperatures to cross 0°C for the first time in millennia, fundamentally altering precipitation patterns from snow to rain-dominant.

Anthropogenic aerosols — primarily sulphate particles from burning coal and biomass — have had a significant cooling effect on climate, masking some of the warming from greenhouse gases. The IPCC AR6 estimated aerosol forcing at −1.1 W/m² (partially offsetting the +2.7 W/m² from greenhouse gases); rapid declines in coal burning could temporarily accelerate warming by removing this aerosol 'mask.'

The tropopause is the boundary between the troposphere (where weather occurs) and the stratosphere, typically at about 12 km altitude in mid-latitudes and 18 km in the tropics. It acts as a 'cold trap' for water vapor — rising air cools to the tropopause temperature and loses most of its moisture as ice before entering the stratosphere, keeping the stratosphere extremely dry.

The Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcanic eruption of January 2022 was the most powerful explosion recorded since modern instruments were available, heard 10,000 km away in Alaska. Uniquely, it injected an estimated 150 million tonnes of water vapour — itself a potent greenhouse gas — into the stratosphere, temporarily raising global stratospheric water vapour by 10% and potentially contributing a small additional warming over the following years.

Heinrich events were episodes during the last glacial period when massive fleets of icebergs calved from the Laurentide Ice Sheet and drifted into the North Atlantic, depositing layers of debris on the ocean floor (Heinrich layers) as they melted. These events are detected by coarse rock fragments from North America found in deep-sea sediment cores across the Atlantic; they caused dramatic cooling and disruption of ocean circulation.

Snowfall measurements are tricky: the standard measurement is the depth of snow at a point in time, but wind and settling can significantly affect the reading. The water equivalent of fresh snow is typically a 10:1 ratio (10 cm of snow melts to 1 cm of water), but 'champagne powder' dry snow in cold, dry climates can have ratios of 20:1 or more, while wet, dense snow near 0°C may be 5:1.

The Brewer-Dobson circulation is a slow, overturning circulation in the stratosphere that transports air and ozone from the tropics — where it is produced by solar UV radiation — toward the poles, where it accumulates at lower altitudes. Paradoxically, the springtime Antarctic ozone hole appears over the region farthest from the tropics, because polar stratospheric clouds catalyse ozone destruction in conditions absent at lower latitudes.

Climate scientists use the Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity (ECS) — the equilibrium global warming expected from a doubling of atmospheric CO₂ — as a benchmark metric. The IPCC AR6 assessed the likely range as 2.5–4°C, with a best estimate of 3°C; pinning down this number more precisely has been one of the central challenges of climate science for 50 years because it depends critically on uncertain cloud feedbacks.

The world's first national weather service was established in the United States in 1870, under the direction of the Army Signal Corps, responding to a Congressional resolution recognising the need for meteorological observations on the coasts and interior. It was restructured as the civilian Weather Bureau in 1890 and became the National Weather Service in 1970.

Precipitation pH in unpolluted regions is about 5.6, not 7.0 (neutral), because CO₂ in the atmosphere dissolves into falling raindrops, forming carbonic acid. Acid rain is defined as precipitation with pH below 5.0, caused by sulphur and nitrogen oxides reacting with rainwater; the most acidic rain ever recorded had a pH of 2.2 in Wheeling, West Virginia in 1978.

The global wind speed has increased by about 7% over land since around 2010, reversing a 30-year trend of 'global terrestrial stilling' when surface winds weakened. This 'global reversal' has been linked to changes in large-scale circulation patterns and has significant implications for wind energy generation.

The concept of 'weather attribution' — linking specific weather events to climate change — has rapidly matured as a scientific discipline since the early 2000s. The World Weather Attribution initiative now publishes rapid analyses within days of major extreme weather events; studies have consistently found that climate change made events like the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome at least 150 times more likely.

The Beaufort Gyre is a large rotating ocean circulation feature in the western Arctic Ocean that accumulates and stores enormous quantities of fresh water from river runoff and sea ice melt. It has been spinning faster and accumulating more fresh water in recent decades; if this fresh water were to be suddenly released into the North Atlantic, it could significantly weaken the AMOC circulation.

The Etesian winds (called 'Meltemi' in modern Greek) are strong, dry northerly winds that blow across the Aegean Sea each summer, driven by the pressure difference between a thermal low over the heated continental interior of Asia and high pressure over the northern Mediterranean. They provided favourable sailing conditions for ancient Greek and Minoan maritime trade.

Methane (CH₄) is approximately 80 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO₂ over a 20-year period, though it breaks down in the atmosphere in about 12 years compared to CO₂'s centuries-long persistence. Atmospheric methane concentrations reached 1,923 parts per billion in 2023 — nearly three times the pre-industrial level of ~700 ppb — with agriculture (especially livestock) and fossil fuel extraction as the largest human sources.

The planetary boundary layer (PBL) is the lowest part of the troposphere, typically 1–3 km deep, directly influenced by friction and heat exchange with Earth's surface. Within the PBL, turbulence mixes pollutants, moisture, and heat; its height — the boundary layer top — is a critical parameter for air quality forecasting, because pollutants emitted at the surface are diluted across the whole PBL depth.

The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching 2,300 km along Australia's northeast coast; it can be seen from space. Rising ocean temperatures are its primary threat: the five mass bleaching events since 1998 (1998, 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020) have killed significant portions of the reef, with 2016 being the most devastating, killing approximately 50% of the reef's shallow-water coral.

A mesoscale convective system (MCS) is an organised complex of thunderstorms that covers hundreds of kilometres in area and lasts for hours; MCSs account for the majority of warm-season rainfall over much of the world's grain-growing regions, including the US Midwest and the Sahel. Their behaviour under climate change is uncertain — there is evidence they are intensifying in some regions.

The Paris Agreement of 2015 set a goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. The Agreement represented a landmark shift to nationally determined contributions (NDCs) — voluntary pledges by each country — rather than binding targets; current NDCs, even if fully implemented, are projected to result in around 2.5–2.9°C of warming by 2100.

Zonda is a hot, dry foehn-type wind that descends from the Andes onto Argentina's Cuyo region, particularly affecting Mendoza. Temperatures can rise 20°C in hours during Zonda events, relative humidity drops to near zero, and the combination is highly dangerous for wildfires; the Zonda is also the Spanish name for foehn winds in other parts of Argentina.

Upwelling brings cold, nutrient-rich water from depth to the ocean surface along continental coasts where winds push surface water offshore. The California, Humboldt, Benguela, and Canary Current upwelling systems are among the world's most productive fisheries, supporting large populations of sardines, anchovies, and their predators; El Niño disrupts this upwelling, causing fishery collapses.

The concept of 'climate tipping points' refers to thresholds in the climate system where small changes can trigger self-reinforcing feedbacks leading to qualitatively different states. A 2018 analysis identified nine major tipping elements — including the Greenland ice sheet, West Antarctic ice sheet, and Amazon dieback — and warned that they may form a 'tipping cascade' capable of pushing Earth into a 'Hothouse' state even at 2°C warming.

source.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

text: The stratospheric quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO) is a regular oscillation of equatorial stratospheric winds that alternate between westerlies and easterlies roughly every 28 months. The QBO influences tropical cyclone activity, the Northern Hemisphere polar vortex, and ENSO's impact on weather, and it interacts with other modes of climate variability in complex ways that are still being understood.

The record for the highest recorded temperature in Africa is 55°C (131°F), recorded in Kebili, Tunisia, on July 7, 1931. More recently, the town of Ouargla in Algeria recorded 51.3°C (124.3°F) on July 5, 2018 — the hottest temperature ever reliably recorded on the African continent — as part of a record-breaking North African heatwave.

The Black Sea is one of the world's most isolated seas, with only a narrow connection to the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus. Its deep waters below about 200 m are permanently anoxic (devoid of oxygen), a condition preserved because the dense saltwater from the Mediterranean that flows along the bottom cannot mix with the lighter, fresher surface water — creating one of Earth's largest and deepest anoxic environments.

Night-time urban temperature records consistently exceed nearby rural records by the largest margins, because city heat is stored in buildings and pavements during the day and radiated at night without the radiative cooling experienced by rural surfaces. This asymmetric urban warming — affecting mostly nighttime minimums — inflates city-based temperature records and requires careful adjustments when assessing regional climate change.

The global snow cover extent on Northern Hemisphere land has decreased by approximately 7% since 1970, with June snow cover showing the largest decline at around 15–20% since satellite records began. Earlier spring snowmelt shifts river flood timing, reduces summer water availability in mountain-fed rivers, and alters the albedo feedback contributing to Arctic amplification.

Phytoplankton — microscopic photosynthetic organisms drifting near the ocean surface — produce approximately half of Earth's oxygen and absorb roughly the same amount of CO₂ as all terrestrial forests combined. Their distribution and abundance is tightly linked to sea surface temperature and upwelling; warming oceans are expanding subtropical oxygen minimum zones, reducing phytoplankton habitat.

The Azimov–Manabe numerical climate model — the first computerised general circulation model (GCM) to realistically simulate Earth's climate — was developed by Syukuro Manabe and Kirk Bryan at NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory in the 1960s. Manabe's work on climate sensitivity and CO₂ was central to his being awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2021.

The 'cold blob' or North Atlantic warming hole is an area of anomalous cooling in the subpolar North Atlantic south of Greenland, caused by the influx of freshwater from the melting Greenland ice sheet weakening the AMOC. This feature has persisted and intensified over recent decades and is considered one of the clearest 'fingerprints' of AMOC weakening in the observational record.

The Sahara Desert, while predominantly rocky or gravelly (not sandy), does contain vast seas of sand dunes called ergs — the largest being the Rub' al Khali ('Empty Quarter') spanning 650,000 km² across the Arabian Peninsula. Sand dunes form when wind-blown sand accumulates behind obstacles; the orientation of dune ridges provides a record of prevailing wind directions over geological time.

Thundersnow is a rare phenomenon in which thunder and lightning occur simultaneously with snowfall, typically occurring in intense lake-effect snowstorms or strong winter cyclones where there is sufficient instability and vertical lift to generate lightning. The heavy snowfall associated with thundersnow can rapidly accumulate at rates of 5–10 cm per hour.

The Great Oxidation Event, approximately 2.4 billion years ago, was the most dramatic climate event in Earth's history: photosynthetic cyanobacteria began producing oxygen as a metabolic byproduct, flooding the atmosphere with a gas that was toxic to most existing life. The resulting collapse of atmospheric methane triggered a global glaciation called the Huronian Glaciation — Earth's first recorded 'Snowball Earth' event.

Wind roses are circular diagrams showing the frequency and strength of wind from different directions at a specific location. They are essential tools for site planning for airports, wind turbines, and buildings. A location's wind rose develops over years of observations and reveals dominant wind directions driven by synoptic climate patterns and local topography.

The Polar Jet Stream (also called the Polar Front Jet) separates cold Arctic air from warmer mid-latitude air and flows eastward around the Northern Hemisphere at speeds typically 130–225 km/h. A warming Arctic reduces the temperature contrast that drives the jet stream, causing it to meander in larger waves — a phenomenon that can trap weather patterns and cause extended extreme weather events.

Reactive nitrogen (primarily NOₓ from combustion and NH₃ from agriculture) deposited from the atmosphere is now the dominant driver of eutrophication — nutrient overloading — in many coastal ecosystems and freshwater lakes. The reactive nitrogen cascade means one nitrogen atom emitted from a vehicle exhaust can successively damage the ozone layer, form smog, contribute to acid rain, and eutrophy a coastal estuary.

Sea spray aerosols, produced when wind and waves break ocean surface bubbles, are among the most abundant aerosols over the ocean by mass and play important roles as cloud condensation nuclei and ice nuclei. They also transfer organic matter, pathogens, and heavy metals from the sea surface microlayer to the atmosphere, linking ocean biogeochemistry to atmospheric chemistry.

The highest reliable surface air temperature ever recorded in Asia is 53.9°C (129°F) at Sulaibiya, Kuwait, on July 21, 2016, surpassing the previous Asian record of 53.8°C also in Kuwait. Iraq regularly records temperatures above 50°C in summer — conditions that are becoming more common as the Persian Gulf region experiences some of the most intense warming on Earth.

The Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, and Screaming Sixties are nicknames for the strong westerly winds that sweep the Southern Ocean at latitudes 40°, 50°, and 60° South respectively, where there is almost no land to impede them. Before the Panama Canal, these winds drove sailing ships on the clipper route from Europe to Australia; today they drive the powerful Antarctic Circumpolar Current.

The Tibetan Plateau's glaciers, often called the 'Third Pole' or 'Asia's water tower,' feed 10 of Asia's largest rivers — including the Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong, Ganges, and Indus — which supply water to over 1.4 billion people. These glaciers are retreating rapidly under warming; while some rivers will temporarily benefit from increased meltwater, mass loss will ultimately reduce dry-season flow on which hundreds of millions depend.

Evaporative cooling is the basis of traditional passive cooling techniques used for millennia — the Egyptian porous clay jar, the Indian 'matka,' the Persian windcatcher (badgir), and the yakhchal ice-house. Modern 'passive cooling' design uses the same principle, using evaporation of moisture from rooftop plants or fountains to reduce building temperatures without electricity.

Sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆), used as an insulating gas in high-voltage electrical equipment, has a global warming potential 23,500 times that of CO₂ over 100 years — making it the most potent greenhouse gas assessed by the IPCC. Although emitted in small quantities relative to CO₂, its atmospheric lifetime exceeds 3,200 years, meaning SF₆ released today will be a forcing agent for millennia.

The Great Flood of 1931 in China, caused by simultaneous flooding of the Yangtze, Yellow, and Huai rivers after an exceptionally wet spring following severe winter storms, was one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history. Estimates of the death toll range from 400,000 to 4 million people; widespread cholera, typhus, and famine followed the inundation.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The South Asian monsoon is driven by the intense heating of the Tibetan Plateau and the Indian subcontinent in spring, which draws moisture-laden air from the Indian Ocean northward. The monsoon onset date — when steady rains begin over Kerala, southwestern India — is one of the most closely monitored annual meteorological events, typically occurring around June 1 and affecting agriculture for over a billion people.

The winter of 1816–17 saw Europe suffer extraordinary cold and crop failures following the 1815 Tambora eruption, leading to massive food shortages and the last great subsistence crisis in the Western world. Grain prices rose 400% in parts of Europe; bread riots broke out in France, Germany, and Britain; and the ensuing famine displaced tens of thousands and contributed to large-scale emigration to North America.

Sea level rise is not globally uniform: regional variations of up to ±50% from the global mean arise due to differences in ocean circulation, gravitational effects of melting ice sheets, land subsidence, and changes in Earth's rotation. The US East Coast is a 'sea level rise hotspot' experiencing rise two to three times faster than the global mean due to weakening AMOC and groundwater extraction causing land sinking.

The 2019–20 Australian Black Summer bushfires burned approximately 18.6 million hectares — an area larger than Cambodia — killing an estimated 3 billion animals and releasing around 830 million tonnes of CO₂. The smoke plumes circled the Southern Hemisphere and were still detectable a year later; the fires were preceded by Australia's hottest and driest year on record.

The Pleistocene Ice Age, which lasted from about 2.6 million to 11,700 years ago, was characterized by repeated glacial cycles in which massive ice sheets advanced over North America, Europe, and Asia. At the Last Glacial Maximum (~21,000 years ago), global sea levels were approximately 120 metres lower than today, and ice sheets up to 3–4 km thick covered what is now Chicago and London.

Water vapour is by far the most abundant greenhouse gas by concentration, contributing about 50% of the total greenhouse effect; CO₂ contributes about 20%, clouds about 25%, and other gases the rest. However, water vapour is a feedback, not a forcing: it amplifies the warming from CO₂ but cannot itself initiate warming because its atmospheric lifetime is only ~9 days.

The North American Monsoon — also called the 'Arizona Monsoon' — is a dramatic seasonal shift in wind direction that brings intense but brief afternoon thunderstorms to the American Southwest and northwestern Mexico from July through September. About half of Arizona's annual precipitation falls during the monsoon months, and the system is driven by heating of the Mexican Plateau drawing in moisture from the Gulf of California and the Gulf of Mexico.

A 'perfect storm' in meteorological parlance refers to the rare convergence of multiple weather systems that amplify each other to produce extreme conditions; the 1991 Perfect Storm that inspired Sebastian Junger's book was an extratropical cyclone energised by remnant Hurricane Grace, producing waves over 30 metres high. The term has since entered popular language to describe any rare convergence of adverse factors.

Bioaerosols — airborne particles of biological origin including pollen, fungal spores, bacteria, and viruses — are ubiquitous in the atmosphere and influence cloud formation. Viable bacteria have been found at altitudes of 12 km in the upper troposphere, and some researchers propose that they may serve as efficient ice nuclei, accelerating precipitation — the concept of 'bioprecipitation.'

The Southern Annular Mode (SAM) is the dominant mode of atmospheric variability in the Southern Hemisphere, describing the north-south migration of the westerly wind belt around Antarctica. A positive SAM — with the westerlies shifted poleward — has been trending since the 1970s, driven by ozone depletion and greenhouse gas increases, bringing less rainfall to southern Australia and South America.

Cyclone Idai, which struck Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi in March 2019, was the deadliest tropical cyclone on record in the Southern Hemisphere, killing over 1,300 people and affecting 3 million. It devastated the port city of Beira and demonstrated that climate change is increasing the intensity of tropical cyclones that make landfall in regions with limited capacity to withstand them.

The 'breathing' of terrestrial ecosystems in the global carbon cycle is demonstrated by land ecosystems absorbing approximately 3.1 GtC/year as a net sink, slightly more than the ocean sink (2.6 GtC/year); together they remove nearly half of human CO₂ emissions. However, this land sink is vulnerable — droughts, fires, and permafrost thaw could transform it into a source, significantly accelerating climate change.

Dust devils are small, rotating updrafts of warm air made visible by the dust, sand, or debris they pick up; they form on hot, dry days when the ground heats air near the surface to temperatures well above the overlying atmosphere, creating instability. Unlike tornadoes, dust devils are not associated with thunderstorms; they form in clear conditions and typically last only a few minutes.

The Caspian Sea — the world's largest inland body of water — has been shrinking dramatically due to a combination of climate change-driven increased evaporation and reduced river inflow, falling approximately 1.5 metres between 2005 and 2018. Projections suggest it could lose 9–34 metres of depth and 23–74% of its volume by 2100 under different emissions scenarios.

Transpiration by a single large tree can release hundreds of litres of water vapour into the atmosphere daily; a mature oak, for example, may transpire 160–450 litres on a warm summer day. Urban trees thus provide significant cooling not only through shading but through evapotranspiration, with studies finding urban trees reduce nearby surface temperatures by 1–5°C.

The tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) and tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S) mark the poleward limits of the Sun's direct overhead position, at the June and December solstices respectively. The tropics — the belt between these two lines — receives more solar radiation per unit area than any other zone, driving the Hadley circulation and forming the climate engine that powers much of the planet's weather.

Rayleigh scattering, the scattering of sunlight by gas molecules in the atmosphere, is responsible for the blue colour of the sky. Shorter (blue) wavelengths scatter more strongly than longer (red) wavelengths; at sunset, light travels through more atmosphere to reach the observer, scattering away most of the blue and leaving the warm reds and oranges.

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is not so much a solid island of trash as a massive concentration zone of microplastics driven by the North Pacific Gyre's circular current; it spans approximately 1.6 million km² — three times the size of France. These concentrated plastics enter the marine food web as they are mistaken for food by fish, seabirds, and marine mammals.

The thermal expansion of seawater — 'steric sea level rise' — is currently contributing about 40% of observed global mean sea level rise. As the ocean warms, water volume increases; the deep ocean has been slowly warming for decades, and the committed thermal expansion from heat already absorbed by the ocean guarantees continued sea level rise for centuries even if emissions stopped today.

Rime ice forms when supercooled water droplets in fog or clouds instantly freeze on contact with surfaces at temperatures below 0°C, building up delicate white feathery deposits on the windward side. Unlike glaze ice (which is clear), rime ice is opaque and white; heavy rime accumulations can snap tree branches and power lines.

The tropical Hadley circulation has been expanding poleward — widening the tropical belt — at a rate of about 0.5° latitude per decade since 1979. This expansion is shifting the subtropical dry zones poleward, contributing to the drying of southern Australia, the Mediterranean, and parts of South America and southern Africa — regions that host some of the world's most productive agricultural areas.

The ancient Chinese term for the monsoon was 'Nanbali' (南埔利), and farmers across Asia have timed planting cycles to monsoon onset for thousands of years. The reliability of the monsoon — and crop timing — has been disrupted in recent decades as changing atmospheric circulation has made monsoon onset more variable, with profound implications for food security.

The Antarctic ice sheet contains approximately 26.5 million km³ of ice — enough to raise global sea levels by about 57 metres if entirely melted. Current rates of ice loss average approximately 150 billion tonnes per year; the most vulnerable portion, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, rests largely on bedrock below sea level, making it potentially susceptible to rapid marine ice sheet instability.

The Beaufort Wind Scale force 12 — a hurricane — is defined as winds exceeding 64 knots (119 km/h) that cause widespread structural damage and produce exceptionally large waves at sea. At sea in a Force 12 storm, the wave crests blow into streaks of foam and the air is filled with driving spray; visibility is near zero.

Lenticular clouds (Altocumulus lenticularis) are stationary lens-shaped clouds that form in the wave of air flowing over mountains. Because they don't move despite strong winds inside them, they have frequently been mistaken for UFOs. Glider pilots seek them out because the updrafts that form them can carry aircraft thousands of metres in altitude.

The Ogallala Aquifer, which underlies about 450,000 km² of the Great Plains of the United States, is the world's largest underground freshwater reservoir. Overpumping for agriculture has caused water levels to fall dramatically — in some areas by more than 60 metres — and the aquifer is being depleted roughly 10 times faster than it is naturally recharged.

Omega blocks are large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns in which a strong high-pressure ridge flanked by two low-pressure troughs creates an 'Ω'-shaped pattern in the upper-level flow, locking weather systems in place for days to weeks. Omega blocks are responsible for prolonged heatwaves, droughts, and floods; the 2010 Russian heatwave that killed over 50,000 people was driven by a persistent omega block.

The Siachen Glacier in the Karakoram range of the Himalayas is the world's highest battlefield, where India and Pakistan have fought since 1984 at altitudes above 6,000 metres. Extreme weather — with temperatures dropping to −50°C and winds exceeding 160 km/h — has killed more soldiers than enemy action. The glacier is also retreating significantly due to climate change.

Phosphine (PH₃) detected in the Venusian cloud layers by radio astronomy in 2020 sparked intense debate about whether it was a biosignature or an abiotic chemical product; phosphine on Earth is primarily produced by anaerobic microorganisms. Subsequent analyses suggested measurement errors and abiotic atmospheric sources could explain the signal, but the episode highlighted how atmospheric chemistry can reveal or mislead about planetary conditions.

The first weather radio broadcast in the United States was transmitted by the US Weather Bureau in 1940 in Cincinnati, Ohio. Today, NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards broadcasts 24 hours a day on 162 MHz from over 1,000 transmitters, covering 95% of the US population, serving as the 'voice of NOAA' for weather warnings and other emergencies.

The Aral Sea in Central Asia was once the world's fourth-largest lake; Soviet irrigation projects that diverted its feeder rivers beginning in the 1960s caused it to lose over 90% of its volume. The exposed seabed — now called the Aralkum Desert — generates toxic dust storms containing salt, pesticides, and heavy metals that affect the health of millions of people in the region.

The 'Silk Road' heat teleconnection links warm-season heatwaves from the Middle East and Central Asia eastward to East Asia via a stationary atmospheric wave propagating along the subtropical jet. This mechanism was identified as contributing to simultaneous 2010 heatwaves in Russia and Pakistan's catastrophic floods by altering the jet stream and downstream atmospheric circulation patterns.

The Koppen climate type 'BWh' — hot desert — covers roughly 14.2% of Earth's land area and is found in the Sahara, Arabian Desert, and Australian interior. By contrast, the most common climate type is 'BSh' (hot semi-arid steppe) at about 14.9%, while tropical rainforest ('Af') covers only about 5% of land but contains the greatest biodiversity of any terrestrial ecosystem.

The world's most tornado-dense region outside the USA is Bangladesh, which experiences violent tornadoes produced by the collision of dry northerly winds with moist southerly air during pre-monsoon season. The April 1989 Daulatpur-Saturia tornado is considered the deadliest tornado in world history, killing approximately 1,300 people.

The Pacific Ring of Fire — a horseshoe-shaped belt of volcanic and seismic activity around the Pacific Ocean — influences climate through episodic volcanic eruptions that inject aerosols into the stratosphere. The 'volcanic weather' that followed the 1991 Pinatubo eruption cooled global temperatures by 0.5°C and temporarily reduced agricultural productivity worldwide.

Continental drift has shaped Earth's climate history profoundly: the opening and closing of ocean gateways altered thermohaline circulation, and the uplift of mountain ranges changed atmospheric circulation. When India collided with Asia approximately 50 million years ago, the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau rose, fundamentally changing the Asian monsoon and drawing down atmospheric CO₂ through accelerated rock weathering.

The Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission — a joint NASA/JAXA satellite — measures precipitation across the globe every three hours using a dual-frequency precipitation radar and a multichannel microwave imager, providing data critical for weather forecasting, flood warnings, and tracking how the water cycle is changing. It succeeded the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM, 1997–2015).

Wetlands — including marshes, swamps, bogs, fens, and mangroves — cover approximately 12.1 million km² globally and store enormous quantities of carbon; northern peatlands alone hold about 500 GtC, roughly twice the amount of carbon in the atmosphere. When wetlands are drained and their organic matter decomposed, this stored carbon is released; wetland restoration is considered one of the most cost-effective climate mitigation strategies.

Firestorms — self-sustaining conflagrations that generate their own wind system, drawing in surrounding air and creating hurricane-force inward winds at the periphery — can occur in extreme wildfires. The 1871 Peshtigo Fire in Wisconsin produced a firestorm that killed an estimated 1,500–2,500 people on October 8, 1871 — the same night as the more famous Great Chicago Fire.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: The Pacific Ocean covers approximately 165 million km² — more than all of Earth's land surface combined. Its heat content and circulation patterns dominate global climate variability, and the La Niña events of 2020–2023, the triple-dip La Niña, were among the longest in recorded history, contributing to significant flooding in Australia and drought in parts of South America and East Africa.

The Venturi effect — the drop in fluid pressure as it speeds up through a constriction — is why winds are funnelled and accelerated through mountain passes and urban canyons. This principle is exploited in wind energy siting and urban wind engineering; downtowns of cities like Chicago earn their 'Windy City' reputation partly from wind funnelled through densely packed skyscraper corridors.

Ground-level humidity has been increasing as global temperatures rise, consistent with the Clausius-Clapeyron relation. However, relative humidity over land has actually slightly decreased in recent decades because temperatures are rising faster than dew points — meaning air feels drier and vegetation stress increases, even though the absolute amount of water vapour in the atmosphere is growing.

Ice nucleating particles (INPs) — substances that trigger ice crystal formation in supercooled cloud droplets — are remarkably diverse: mineral dust from desert soils, biological particles (bacteria, pollen, fungal spores), sea spray, and anthropogenic aerosols all serve as INPs. The most efficient natural INP known is a protein from the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae, which nucleates ice at temperatures as warm as −2°C.

The Beaufort Sea gyre has accumulated about 8,000 km³ of fresh water — more than the total fresh water in all the Great Lakes combined — forming a large lens of buoyant fresh water that resists mixing with saltier Atlantic waters. The freshwater accumulation has accelerated in recent decades with increased sea ice melt and strengthened wind-driven Ekman pumping.

The diurnal pressure wave — a regular twice-daily oscillation in surface atmospheric pressure of about 1–2 hPa amplitude — is driven primarily by the absorption of solar radiation by ozone in the stratosphere. It produces a barometric pressure maximum near 10:00 and 22:00 local solar time, a phenomenon so reliable it was used as an atmospheric 'clock' by early meteorologists.

Wildfires have increased dramatically in both frequency and intensity globally due to the combination of climate change-driven drying and warming, changes in land management, and increased human ignition sources. The global area burned annually has declined over decadal timescales due to agricultural expansion suppressing savannah fires, but fire intensity and the burned area in forests and temperate regions have significantly increased.

Aerosol optical depth (AOD) is a measure of how much sunlight aerosol particles prevent from reaching the surface. Satellite-based AOD measurements show that air quality in South and East Asia is the most polluted globally, with AOD values in the Indo-Gangetic Plain sometimes exceeding 1.0 — meaning more than half the direct sunlight is being scattered or absorbed before it reaches the ground.

The 'heat index' — also called apparent temperature or 'feels like' temperature — combines air temperature and relative humidity to reflect what the temperature feels like to the human body. A heat index of 41°C (105°F) or higher is considered dangerous and can cause heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke in people exposed to the sun or engaged in strenuous outdoor activity.

Hurricane Harvey (2017) was the most extreme rainfall event in US history, dropping an estimated 1 metre of rainfall over greater Houston — a water volume of approximately 127 billion tonnes. Harvey's record rainfall was enabled partly by the warm Gulf of Mexico (about 1°C above normal), which is consistent with climate change increasing the moisture content of storms.

Frost wedging (freeze-thaw weathering) is the mechanical process by which water expands 9% in volume upon freezing in rock cracks, splitting rocks apart. This is the primary physical weathering process in cold climates, responsible for carving the jagged alpine landscapes of mountains and producing the angular scree slopes beneath cliff faces.

South America's Amazon Basin contains approximately 20% of all freshwater flowing into the world's oceans. The Amazon River discharges roughly 209,000 m³ per second — about 20% of all global river runoff — and the forest generates its own rainfall: about half the moisture in Amazon rainfall comes from water previously transpired by trees within the basin itself.

The Madeira Archipelago (part of Portugal) in the northeastern Atlantic experiences a 'thermal inversion' almost year-round: moist air is trapped below a cap of warm subsiding air from the Azores High, producing persistent low cloud on the north-facing slopes while the south coasts bask in sunshine. Similar conditions prevail in the Canary Islands, Hawaii, and other subtropical island archipelagos.

source.name: Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere

text: The 2010 Pakistan Super Flood — triggered by blocking of the jet stream that prolonged monsoonal rains — submerged one-fifth of Pakistan's entire land area, killing 2,000 people and affecting 20 million. The same blocking event simultaneously caused the devastating Russian heatwave; these simultaneous extreme events on opposite sides of the hemisphere were linked by a stationary planetary-scale Rossby wave.

The coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth is the Siberian town of Oymyakon, Russia, where temperatures can drop below −60°C in winter; the average January temperature is −50°C. It shares the record for the coldest temperature recorded in any permanently inhabited settlement with nearby Verkhoyansk, which recorded −67.8°C on February 5, 1892.

Sferics (or atmospherics) are bursts of radio waves produced by lightning discharges that propagate around the globe within the Earth-ionosphere waveguide. Long before satellite monitoring, sferics were used to detect thunderstorms at great distances; today, global lightning-location networks like WWLLN use radio wave arrival times to pinpoint each stroke within milliseconds.

The Polar Cell is the smallest and weakest of the three atmospheric circulation cells in each hemisphere, operating between the poles and about 60° latitude. Cold air descends at the pole, flows equatorward along the surface as the polar easterlies, and rises at the subpolar low-pressure belt (~60°) to return poleward aloft — though its circulation is constantly disrupted by the wandering polar vortex.

Compound extreme events — when two or more hazards occur simultaneously or in rapid succession — cause disproportionate impacts compared to either event alone. Simultaneous hot and dry conditions are the most dangerous compound event for wildfires; coastal flooding worsened by concurrent heavy rainfall is another; and heat-drought combinations can devastate crops more severely than either stress alone.

The Beaufort Scale was extended in 1946 by the WMO to include Force 13–17 for measurement in tropical cyclones; however, most meteorological services still use only Beaufort 0–12, as the extended scale is not universally applied. Category 5 hurricanes on the Saffir-Simpson scale (≥157 mph winds) correspond roughly to Beaufort Force 17.

Methane hydrates — ice-like compounds in which methane molecules are trapped inside water ice crystal cages — are found in vast quantities on the ocean floor and in permafrost, holding an estimated 500–2,500 GtC of methane. The destabilisation of shallow Arctic shelf methane hydrates by warming ocean water is a potential climate tipping point, though the timescale and magnitude of any large-scale release remain highly uncertain.

Cold fronts typically move at 25–35 km/h and slope backward (back over colder air) as they advance, whereas warm fronts advance more slowly at 15–25 km/h and slope forward. The classic Norwegian Cyclone Model developed by Vilhelm Bjerknes and his Bergen school of meteorology in the early 20th century — describing how mid-latitude cyclones grow, develop fronts, and decay — is still taught worldwide.

The stratospheric ozone layer absorbs nearly all ultraviolet-B (280–315 nm) radiation, which causes sunburn, DNA damage, and skin cancer. With ozone depletion, UV-B reaching Earth's surface at southern latitudes increased by up to 100% during Antarctic spring; skin cancer rates in Australia and New Zealand rose significantly before the Montreal Protocol began to take effect.

source.name: NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory UV Monitoring

text: The economic cost of weather and climate disasters has risen dramatically over recent decades: inflation-adjusted losses from billion-dollar weather disasters in the US averaged about $18 billion/year in the 1980s but exceeded $120 billion/year in the 2010s. This increase is driven by a combination of greater exposure (more people and assets in hazard-prone areas), climate change increasing event frequency/intensity, and improved reporting.

source.name: NOAA Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters

text: Albedo modification through marine cloud brightening (MCB) is a proposed solar geoengineering technique that would spray sea salt aerosols into low-level marine clouds to increase their droplet number and reflectivity. Field experiments have been proposed and debated globally; unlike stratospheric aerosol injection, MCB would be regionally targeted and reversible within days.

source.name: National Academies of Sciences Solar Geoengineering Report

text: The global warming 'hiatus' or 'pause' from approximately 1998–2013, when surface temperature increase appeared to slow, was later attributed largely to natural variability — particularly a strong El Niño in 1997–98 that inflated the starting temperature, and subsequent La Niña conditions — plus increased heat uptake by the deep ocean. Adjusted analyses using more complete observational data have largely erased the apparent pause.

source.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information

text: Wildfire smoke contains a complex mixture of gases and particles including carbon monoxide, ozone precursors, and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that can travel thousands of kilometres and dramatically reduce air quality. The 2020 US West Coast wildfires produced smoke so thick that air quality in San Francisco exceeded the worst recorded levels in Beijing, China, and was hazardous for over two weeks.

The global mean wind speed at 10 m height over the ocean has increased by about 1.5 m/s since 1990 according to satellite altimetry data, significantly increasing ocean wave heights. These stronger winds and taller waves affect global shipping routes, coastal erosion, and the mixing and oxygenation of upper ocean layers.

The Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW) programme of the WMO maintains over 30 global observing stations — including iconic sites like Mauna Loa, Hawaii and Cape Grim, Tasmania — that continuously monitor greenhouse gases, ozone, aerosols, and reactive gases. These long-term records are the foundation of our understanding of atmospheric composition change.

Permafrost peatlands — primarily in Siberia and Canada — store approximately 1,700 GtC of organic carbon, roughly twice the current atmospheric CO₂ content. These deposits accumulated over thousands of years as dead plant material failed to fully decompose in waterlogged frozen conditions; climate warming is now thawing them and stimulating decomposition, releasing CO₂ and methane.

source.name: USGS National Climate Change and Wildlife Science Center

text: Subarctic and Arctic soils experiencing thermokarst collapse can release mercury that has been sequestered in frozen ground for millennia. Permafrost contains an estimated 1,656,000 tonnes of mercury — almost twice the amount in all other soils, ocean, and atmosphere combined — and its release into waterways could have severe consequences for aquatic ecosystems and human health.

The first successful forecast of a hurricane by computer was made in 1954 when the NOAA forecasters used a primitive numerical model to predict the track of Hurricane Carol. Today, computer models like the Global Forecast System (GFS) and the ECMWF model can predict a hurricane's track 5 days in advance with an error of less than 300 km — a dramatic improvement from the 600–700 km errors of the 1980s.

The Arctic Ocean is the shallowest of the world's five oceans, with an average depth of only 1,038 m (3,407 ft); by comparison, the Pacific Ocean averages 4,000 m. This shallowness means terrestrial influences — river discharge, coastal erosion, and sediment transport — have a proportionally larger effect on Arctic Ocean chemistry and circulation than in deeper ocean basins.

A 'heat burst' is a rare meteorological event in which descending air from a dying thunderstorm heats and dries dramatically as it compresses, producing a brief, localized surge of very hot, dry, gusty winds at the surface — sometimes raising temperatures by 10°C or more in minutes, often in the middle of the night. A heat burst in Kopperl, Texas, on June 15, 1960, raised the temperature from 38°C to 68°C (160°F).

The Inuit (Eskimo) languages do not literally have 50+ words for snow, but the Yupik language of Alaska does use a rich array of morphemes related to snow and ice that can describe fine distinctions in snow conditions — 'aput' (snow on the ground), 'qana' (falling snow), 'piqtaq' (blowing snow), and many others. This linguistic richness reflects the critical importance of snow conditions to traditional subsistence living.

The global mean surface temperature responds to volcanic forcing with remarkable speed: in the two years following the 1991 Pinatubo eruption, global temperatures dropped by approximately 0.5°C. This fast volcanic response validates climate models and confirms the strong relationship between radiative forcing and temperature change, helping scientists calibrate climate sensitivity estimates.

Glacial erratic boulders — rocks transported far from their original source by glaciers and deposited when the ice melted — provided early 19th-century scientists with key evidence for the theory of an Ice Age. Swiss naturalist Louis Agassiz proposed in 1840 that glaciers once covered vast areas of Europe based on erratic boulders, glacial striae (scratches), and moraines found far from existing glaciers.

The global mean surface temperature in the Eocene Epoch (~56–34 million years ago) was approximately 8–14°C warmer than today, with CO₂ concentrations estimated at 1,000–2,000 ppm. There were no polar ice caps, tropical forests extended to the polar regions, and sea levels were approximately 70 metres higher than today — providing a window into what high-CO₂ worlds look like over geological timescales.

The wind chill factor describes how cold the combination of low temperature and wind feels to exposed skin, which loses heat much faster in windy conditions. At an air temperature of −20°C with a 50 km/h wind, the wind chill is equivalent to −37°C — meaning exposed skin can freeze within 10 minutes. Canada and the US adopted a new wind chill index based on controlled human subject experiments in 2001.

source.name: Environment and Climate Change Canada Wind Chill

text: The Mediterranean Sea — described as a 'sea within a sea' — loses more water by evaporation than it gains from rivers and rain, creating a net inflow of surface Atlantic water through the Strait of Gibraltar. This drives a unique circulation: Atlantic water flows in at the surface while a dense, saltier outflow exits deeper; the resulting 'Mediterranean Outflow Water' can be traced throughout the North Atlantic.

Kelvin waves in the ocean are large-scale waves confined to the equator or coastlines, propagating eastward along the equatorial Pacific at speeds of about 2–3 m/s. During the development of El Niño events, downwelling Kelvin waves triggered by westerly wind bursts over the western Pacific deepen the thermocline as they propagate eastward, warming the eastern Pacific and weakening the Walker Circulation.

The Arctic tundra biome — stretching across northern Canada, Alaska, Russia, and Scandinavia — is the world's largest treeless biome, shaped by extreme cold, permafrost, and high winds. As temperatures rise, shrubs are expanding poleward in a process called 'shrubification' that darkens the tundra surface, reduces albedo, and accelerates warming in a positive feedback loop.

Anticyclogenesis — the strengthening or formation of a high-pressure system — is associated with sinking air, which warms adiabatically and suppresses cloud and precipitation formation. The Bermuda-Azores High is a semi-permanent anticyclone that steers hurricanes; when it is stronger or positioned further north, hurricanes are deflected away from the US East Coast.

Rain gauges are the oldest meteorological instruments; a graduated bronze rain gauge was used in Korea as early as 1441 CE during the reign of King Sejong the Great. The standardised rain gauge used in modern networks is the cylinder 203 mm (8 inch) in diameter, with a smaller measuring tube that magnifies readings tenfold for accuracy.

The 'snowball Earth' hypothesis proposes that Earth was almost or completely frozen over at least twice during the Cryogenian Period (approximately 720–635 million years ago). Evidence includes glacial deposits at tropical latitudes and the sharp rise in atmospheric oxygen following deglaciation; the escape from this state may have involved a massive buildup of volcanic CO₂ over millions of years while photosynthesis was suppressed under ice.

Global glacier mass balance has been negative (losing mass) in every year since comprehensive global monitoring began in the 1970s, with the rate of loss accelerating. Mountain glaciers and ice caps (excluding Greenland and Antarctica) lost an average of approximately 270 Gt per year between 2006 and 2016, contributing about 0.7 mm/year to sea level rise.

The Coriolis parameter (f) — the mathematical measure of how strongly the Coriolis effect deflects moving air — is greatest at the poles (f = ±1.46 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) and zero at the equator. This is why tropical weather systems near the equator cannot develop rotation and become cyclones: without Coriolis effect, the pressure gradient force drives wind directly from high to low pressure without creating the spiraling inflow of a tropical cyclone.

Coastal fog known as 'garúa' (or 'camanchaca' in Chile) plays a critical ecological role in the hyperarid Atacama Desert and Peru's coastal deserts, where it provides the only significant moisture input in some locations. Fog-harvesting nets — mesh structures that condense fog into water — have been deployed in fog-rich desert communities from Chile to Morocco as a low-cost water supply technology.

The ENSO forecast skill has improved dramatically: whereas seasonal ENSO forecasts showed little skill more than 6 months ahead in the 1980s, today operational models routinely produce useful forecasts 9–12 months in advance. The 'spring predictability barrier' — a seasonal drop in forecast skill when forecasts are initialised in spring — remains a persistent challenge.

source.name: NOAA Climate Prediction Center ENSO Outlook

text: The 1970 Bhola Cyclone struck the Bay of Bengal on November 12, 1970, and remains the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history, killing approximately 300,000–500,000 people in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). The inadequate disaster response by the Pakistani government contributed to political unrest that ultimately led to the Bangladesh Liberation War in 1971.

The global mean residence time of CO₂ in the atmosphere is commonly cited as 'hundreds of years,' but this obscures complexity: carbon exchange with the ocean and land biosphere removes about 50% of each year's emissions within decades, while the remaining ~20% persists for centuries to millennia before being absorbed by deep ocean dissolution and rock weathering. This long tail of warming commitment is central to climate policy.

Aerosol indirect effects on climate are the most uncertain component of anthropogenic radiative forcing. When aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei, they increase cloud droplet number and reduce droplet size, making clouds brighter (first indirect effect) and potentially suppressing precipitation, extending cloud lifetime (second indirect effect) — overall a cooling effect, but difficult to quantify precisely.

The Beaufort Gyre and the transpolar drift stream are the two major surface circulation patterns in the Arctic Ocean; the transpolar drift carries sea ice from Siberia across the Arctic to the Fram Strait between Greenland and Svalbard, where it exits into the North Atlantic. This transport exports significant volumes of sea ice and freshwater that influence North Atlantic deep water formation.

Evaporation cooling explains why a dry breeze feels refreshing on a hot day: as moisture evaporates from skin, it absorbs latent heat and cools the surface. At 100% relative humidity — when the air is already saturated — no evaporation occurs and the body cannot cool itself by sweating; this is why humid heat is so much more physiologically dangerous than dry heat at the same air temperature.

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Heat Safety

text: The discovery that ancient climates could be reconstructed from oxygen isotope ratios in marine microfossils — by Cesare Emiliani in the 1950s — revolutionised palaeoclimatology. Heavier oxygen-18 preferentially stays in ocean water when light oxygen-16 evaporates to form snow; ice ages, when large ice sheets sequester light oxygen, show as spikes in the ocean sediment δ¹⁸O record.

Nunavut, Canada's newest territory, experiences one of the fastest-warming climates on Earth — temperatures have risen 3–4°C since 1948. Traditional Inuit ecological knowledge documents changes in sea ice predictability, unusual weather patterns, and shifts in animal migration routes that science is only beginning to capture through instrumental records.

Tornadogenesis — the process by which a tornado forms from a supercell thunderstorm — is still not fully understood despite decades of research and storm-chasing. The leading hypothesis involves the tilting and stretching of horizontal vorticity (spin) generated in the wind shear layer near the ground into the vertical by the storm's updraft, but observational confirmation of the exact mechanism at tornado scale remains elusive.

The Holocene Climatic Optimum, also called the Holocene Thermal Maximum, was a period approximately 9,000–5,000 years ago when Northern Hemisphere summer temperatures were 1–2°C warmer than 20th-century averages due to Milankovitch forcing that increased summer sunlight at high latitudes. This period saw the retreat of Arctic sea ice, retreat of Northern Hemisphere glaciers, and drier Saharan conditions as vegetation expanded.

The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, established in 1975, is the world's largest marine protected area covering 344,400 km². Climate change is now the reef's greatest threat, with ocean warming causing bleaching events of increasing frequency and severity; modelling suggests 99% of coral reefs worldwide would experience annual bleaching if warming reaches 2°C above pre-industrial levels.

source.name: IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere

text: The 'wet season' and 'dry season' classification applies to regions where annual rainfall is highly concentrated in a few months, particularly in the tropics and subtropics. Darwin, Australia's northern capital, receives less than 20 mm total in the combined June–August dry season but over 1,500 mm during the November–April monsoon season — a ratio of 75:1 between the wettest and driest months.

The term 'weather bomb' is used colloquially for a bomb cyclone but is not an official meteorological term. In contrast, 'explosive cyclogenesis' has a precise definition: a mid-latitude cyclone whose central pressure drops by at least 24 hPa in 24 hours, normalized to 60° latitude. These events are most common over the western North Atlantic and western North Pacific in winter.

The concept of 'natural variability' is central to climate science — it refers to fluctuations in the climate system not caused by external forcing (like greenhouse gas emissions), arising from internal processes like ENSO, the PDO, and ocean circulation changes. Separating the anthropogenic signal from natural variability requires long records, climate model ensembles, and statistical attribution methods.

The World Meteorological Organization's Commission for Instruments and Methods of Observation (CIMO) oversees the standardisation of weather observing practices globally, ensuring that a thermometer reading in Beijing is comparable to one in Buenos Aires. Without international standardisation — of instrument exposure, station siting, and observation times — building accurate global climate records would be impossible.

Typhoon Tip (1979) remains the most intense tropical cyclone ever recorded, with a central pressure of 870 hPa and maximum sustained winds of 305 km/h. It also holds the record for the largest tropical cyclone by diameter — at its peak, it spanned approximately 2,220 km in diameter, nearly half the width of the continental United States.

The Antarctic ozone hole was discovered by British Antarctic Survey scientists Jonathan Shanklin, Joe Farman, and Brian Gardiner in 1985 using ground-based spectrometers. The finding was so unexpected that NASA scientists initially dismissed satellite data showing the same feature, assuming it was instrument error; the discovery accelerated international negotiations that led to the Montreal Protocol.

The cloud-to-ground lightning return stroke travels at about one-third the speed of light (approximately 100,000 km/s), while the stepped leader that precedes it is much slower — about 200 km/s. What we see as a single flash typically consists of 3–5 return strokes in rapid succession, each following the ionised channel carved by the previous stroke.
