The Dew Point Depression — the difference between air temperature and dew point temperature — is a useful indicator of precipitation potential: when it drops to 3°C or less, precipitation is likely. Forecasters use the surface and upper-air dew point depression alongside instability indices to assess convective potential and fog likelihood.

The first automated weather station in Antarctica was installed at Automatic Geophysical Observatories in the early 1980s and now over 120 AWS units operate on the Antarctic continent and ice shelves. These unattended stations use satellite data links to transmit data globally within minutes of collection, providing crucial observations from one of Earth's most weather-hostile and data-sparse environments.

Tropical forests are 'evapotranspiration machines' that keep themselves cool through continuous moisture cycling; the Amazon's average daytime surface temperature would be about 3°C hotter without the cooling effect of forest evapotranspiration. Deforestation converts this cooling effect into sensible heat — heating the air — and can reduce regional rainfall by reducing moisture recycling.

The rate of global mean sea level rise has accelerated: it was about 1.3 mm/year in 1901–1971, increased to 1.9 mm/year in 1971–2006, and accelerated further to 3.7 mm/year in 2006–2018. The acceleration is driven by both increasing ocean thermal expansion and accelerating ice sheet mass loss from Greenland and Antarctica.

El Niño events increase the global mean surface temperature anomaly by about 0.1–0.2°C in the year following the peak, while La Niña events cool it by a similar amount; these oscillations are superimposed on the longer-term anthropogenic warming trend. Attribution scientists must account for ENSO's influence when interpreting annual temperature records.

source.name: NOAA Climate.gov ENSO and Global Temperature

text: The GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite) series, operated by NOAA, hover approximately 35,786 km above the equator in geostationary orbit, viewing the same disk of Earth continuously. The latest GOES-16 and GOES-17 satellites produce full-disk images every 10 minutes and mesoscale imagery every 30–60 seconds, revolutionising the monitoring of rapidly developing severe weather.

The concept of 'hysteresis' in the climate system means that returning to a previous state after crossing a tipping point is much harder — and may require far lower temperatures — than crossing the threshold in the first place. Ice sheet hysteresis is a major concern: once an ice sheet retreats past certain bedrock geometries that lead to runaway melting, re-glaciation requires temperatures far below the threshold that caused the original retreat.

Nitrous oxide (N₂O) is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 273 times that of CO₂ over 100 years, and it also destroys stratospheric ozone. Agricultural soils — where nitrogen fertilisers are applied — are the largest source, accounting for about 70% of anthropogenic N₂O emissions; livestock manure and biomass burning contribute most of the rest.

The global freshwater cycle is highly sensitive to changes in atmospheric circulation: the wet-get-wetter/dry-get-drier principle describes how regions already receiving substantial rainfall tend to get more as warming increases atmospheric moisture, while already-dry regions get drier. However, the actual patterns are more complex, with changes in storm tracks and regional circulation departing from this simple rule in many regions.

Cumulus clouds — the iconic cotton-ball clouds — are convective clouds formed by rising thermals of warm moist air; their flat bases mark the lifting condensation level (LCL) where the rising air cools to its dew point. The LCL can be estimated simply: for every 8°C of temperature-dew point spread, the cloud base lies approximately 1,000 m above the surface.

Dead reckoning — estimating current position from a previously known position by advancing that position using speed, heading, and elapsed time — was used by early meteorologists to track storm movement before modern observing systems. Today, ensemble weather models produce 'spaghetti plots' of numerous possible storm track solutions, visually representing the uncertainty in track forecasts.

The Interannual and decadal variability of Arctic sea ice is large enough to temporarily reverse the long-term decline: 2012 set a record low September minimum, but 2013 showed a partial recovery of about 1.5 million km² from the previous year's record. Scientists stress that such year-to-year variations, driven by atmospheric circulation patterns, do not reverse the underlying downward trend driven by global warming.

source.name: NSIDC Arctic Sea Ice News & Analysis

text: The global average temperature has now warmed in every decade since 1980 relative to the previous decade, and the 10 warmest years on record have all occurred since 2010. This unbroken sequence of record-warm decades is the clearest statistical signal of anthropogenic warming in the observational record.

Ground-based Doppler weather radar works by measuring the Doppler shift in frequency of microwave pulses reflected back from precipitation. Modern dual-polarisation radar — which transmits pulses both horizontally and vertically — can distinguish rain from hail, identify large hail, and estimate rainfall rates more accurately than single-polarisation systems.

source.name: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory Radar

text: Tropical cyclone intensity has increased globally over recent decades, with the proportion of storms reaching Category 3 and above rising. A 2020 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found the probability of a given storm reaching major hurricane intensity has increased by about 25% over the past four decades, consistent with theoretical predictions from thermodynamics.

source.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

text: Foehn wind events in the Alps can elevate temperatures by 15–25°C over a few hours, causing rapid snowmelt and avalanche risk; they also create high fire danger in valley floors. In Switzerland, the Foehn has historically been associated with increased rates of headaches, irritability, and even crime — effects sometimes attributed to high concentrations of positive air ions generated by the descending warm, dry air.

The 'heat health action plan' concept, developed in response to the 2003 European heatwave, involves activating emergency services, opening cooling centres, and alerting vulnerable populations when heat index thresholds are exceeded. France's implementation of heat health warning systems after 2003 is estimated to have prevented thousands of deaths in subsequent heatwaves.

source.name: World Health Organization Heat Action Plans

text: The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) migrates north and south with the seasons following the thermal equator, bringing wet seasons to tropical regions it passes over. In some years it does not migrate far enough north to reach the Sahel, reducing monsoon rainfall; understanding what controls the ITCZ's position is key to predicting drought in the world's most food-insecure regions.

Himalayan glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) are a growing hazard as climate warming enlarges proglacial lakes dammed by unstable moraines. When a moraine dam fails, a catastrophic flood wave travels downstream at velocities exceeding 20 m/s, devastating villages and infrastructure; Nepal experienced a major GLOF at Pokhara in 1985 that killed hundreds and destroyed a hydroelectric plant.

Drought is classified into meteorological drought (below-normal precipitation), agricultural drought (soil moisture deficit affecting crops), hydrological drought (reduced river flow and groundwater levels), and socioeconomic drought (when water scarcity affects economic activity). These cascading drought types can develop sequentially over weeks to months as an initial rainfall deficit propagates through soils, rivers, and groundwater systems.

source.name: NOAA National Integrated Drought Information System

text: The Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica — sometimes called the 'Doomsday Glacier' — is roughly the size of Florida and is considered the most vulnerable major glacier in the world because it rests on a bed that slopes inland and deepens toward the interior, making it susceptible to marine ice sheet instability. If it collapsed, sea levels would eventually rise by approximately 3 metres.

The term 'climate emergency' was adopted by the Oxford Dictionary as its word of the year in 2019, reflecting a global cultural shift in framing; over 2,000 jurisdictions representing over 1 billion people had declared climate emergencies by 2022. The IPCC AR6 itself used the phrase 'code red for humanity' in media communications around its 2021 publication.

The Tibetan Plateau generates powerful lee cyclogenesis (lows forming in the lee of the plateau) during the winter monsoon, as cold air masses from Siberia are channelled around the plateau's eastern flanks and cyclonic development is triggered in the downstream regions. These cyclones are important weather systems for much of China, bringing snowfall and cold spells to southeastern China.

Winter inversions trap pollutants near the ground in mountain valleys and cities, creating the worst air quality events of the year. Salt Lake City, Utah, regularly experiences winter inversions where valley smog becomes so concentrated that the air quality index exceeds hazardous levels; cold, dense air is trapped beneath warm air above, and without wind to mix the atmosphere, pollution accumulates for days.

The jet stream influences the path and intensity of extratropical cyclones that bring weather to mid-latitude regions. When the jet meanders widely in large-amplitude Rossby waves, it slows down and can 'cut off' cold pools (cold-core lows) from the main flow, creating persistent, slow-moving weather systems that can cause extended flooding or drought.

source.name: Met Office UK Jet Stream Guide

text: The Köppen climate system's 'B' (arid) climates — covering about 30% of Earth's land area — are the most extensive single category. Within B climates, the boundary between desert (BW) and steppe (BS) is where annual potential evapotranspiration equals approximately half the annual precipitation, a threshold that is shifting poleward and inland as temperatures rise.

The monsoon affects more than 70% of global annual tropical rainfall and the water supply for over half the world's population. Its predictability on seasonal timescales — largely driven by sea surface temperatures in the Indian and Pacific oceans — makes it one of the most important signals for climate services providing early warning of flood and drought risk.

Rossby waves — large-scale meanders of the jet stream and ocean currents driven by Earth's rotation and the variation of the Coriolis force with latitude — were first described mathematically by Carl-Gustaf Rossby in 1939. In the atmosphere, Rossby waves are responsible for the large-scale pattern of highs and lows visible on weather maps and have wavelengths of thousands of kilometres.

The Galveston Hurricane of 1900, which struck the Texas coast on September 8, remains the deadliest natural disaster in US history, killing an estimated 6,000–12,000 people. The flat barrier island city had no seawall; in its wake, a 17-foot seawall was constructed and the entire city was raised 3–6 metres by pumping in fill — an early example of engineered adaptation to coastal hazard.

The 100-year flood (or 1% annual chance flood) is not a flood that occurs every 100 years, but one that has a 1% probability of being equalled or exceeded in any given year. As climate change intensifies rainfall extremes, historical 100-year flood events are becoming more frequent — what was a 1% annual chance event may now have a 2–5% chance in many parts of the world.

The Bergeron-Findeisen process (also called the Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen process) explains why ice crystals in mixed-phase clouds grow rapidly at the expense of supercooled water droplets: the saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower than over liquid water at the same temperature, so water vapour diffuses from droplets to ice crystals, causing ice to grow and droplets to shrink. This is the primary mechanism by which precipitation-sized particles form in mid-latitude clouds.

Mountain snow packs act as natural water towers, storing winter precipitation as snow and slowly releasing it as meltwater through spring and summer when demand is highest. Around 1.9 billion people — about a quarter of the global population — depend on mountain watersheds for their water supply; declining snow packs and earlier snowmelt under climate change threaten water availability for agriculture, cities, and hydropower.

Carbon dioxide has an asymmetric effect on outgoing longwave radiation: each additional increment of CO₂ causes less warming than the previous one because CO₂ absorbs in bands that are already partially saturated. However, at the molecular edges of these bands, the absorption is not yet saturated, and additional CO₂ continues to increase forcing — this is why climate sensitivity is positive even at elevated CO₂ levels.

The frequency and severity of heat stress events for outdoor workers — particularly agricultural workers in tropical countries — is increasing rapidly. Workers in countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and sub-Saharan Africa face the greatest risk; labour productivity in outdoor occupations may decline by up to 20% in the most affected regions by 2080 under high-emissions scenarios.

Lake Titicaca, the world's highest commercially navigable lake at 3,812 m above sea level in the Andes between Bolivia and Peru, experiences dramatic daily weather cycles. Mornings are typically clear and cold, afternoons bring convective clouds and thunderstorms driven by solar heating of the high plateau, and evenings can be frigidly cold under clear skies as the thin atmosphere loses heat rapidly.

The Walker Circulation has weakened over the 20th century, consistent with theoretical predictions of how warming sea surface temperatures reduce the east-west sea surface temperature gradient that drives it. However, the trend is superimposed on large multidecadal variability, making attribution to human-caused climate change challenging.

The hypsometric equation relates the thickness of an atmospheric layer to its mean temperature: warmer air is less dense and occupies more vertical space, so warm air masses produce thicker layers between pressure surfaces. Forecasters use 1,000–500 hPa thickness to distinguish rain from snow: thickness values below 528 decametres (~5,280 m) strongly favour snow at the surface.

The global average wind speed at 10 m above the surface (used as the standard reference height in meteorology) is approximately 6.6 m/s (14.8 mph) over land. Wind energy potential is proportional to the cube of wind speed, meaning a 10% increase in wind speed corresponds to a 33% increase in power output — making even modest changes in average wind speed highly significant for wind energy.

source.name: World Resources Institute Global Wind Atlas

text: The atmospheric general circulation transports roughly 5 × 10¹⁵ watts (5 petawatts) of energy poleward — primarily as sensible heat, latent heat, and potential energy — maintaining the temperature difference between tropics and poles against the relentless solar heating imbalance. The ocean transports an additional ~2 petawatts poleward, particularly in the tropics and subtropics.

The Paris Climate Agreement's temperature targets — 1.5°C and 2°C — refer to global mean surface temperature (GMST) averaged over multiple decades, not a single year. Individual years may temporarily exceed these thresholds due to natural variability (like El Niño), but the climate threshold is considered breached only when the multi-decadal running mean crosses it.

source.name: IPCC Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C

text: The concept of a 'climate normal' — a 30-year average used as a reference baseline — is updated every 10 years by the WMO; the current standard period is 1991–2020, replacing the previous 1981–2010 baseline. Each update shifts the baseline warmer, which can create the impression that records are less exceptional than they are relative to historical climate.

The Sargasso Sea, located in the western North Atlantic within the Bermuda Triangle region, is unique among seas in having no land borders — it is defined entirely by four ocean currents. It hosts large floating mats of Sargassum seaweed that provide critical habitat for juvenile sea turtles and fish, and its circulation concentrates marine debris into the North Atlantic Garbage Patch.

Black carbon (soot) — produced by incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels, and biomass — is the second largest human contributor to global warming after CO₂. Deposited on snow and ice, it darkens the surface and accelerates melting; black carbon from fires and diesel engines in South Asia is considered a significant driver of Himalayan glacier retreat.

The Antarctic surface mass balance — the difference between snowfall accumulation and melt and runoff — is currently slightly positive (more snow falling than melting), because climate change increases precipitation in the cold interior. However, this gain is vastly outweighed by dynamic ice loss at the margins through glaciers calving into the ocean, so the Antarctic ice sheet is losing mass overall.

The global mean land surface temperature has warmed about twice as fast as the global mean ocean surface temperature since 1850, and land temperature anomalies are more variable from year to year. This land-ocean temperature contrast is explained by the ocean's greater heat capacity and the cooling effect of evaporation over ocean surfaces.

The Beaufort scale's Force 0 (calm) is defined as wind speeds below 1 km/h with smoke rising vertically and the sea surface described as 'mirror-like.' Such perfectly calm conditions are extremely rare over the open ocean, where even on 'still' days small swells generated by distant storms create constant wave motion. True calm occurs most frequently over land on clear, cold winter nights.

The Ozone-depleting substances (ODS) banned by the Montreal Protocol — primarily CFCs and HCFCs — are also potent greenhouse gases; by eliminating them, the Protocol simultaneously slowed ozone depletion and avoided an estimated 0.5–1°C of additional warming that would have occurred by 2050. This co-benefit makes the Montreal Protocol the most impactful climate agreement ever implemented.

The world's highest thunderstorm frequency is found in Kampala, Uganda, which averages about 242 thunder days per year. The Congo Basin and Lake Victoria are also global maxima for lightning; these regions experience intense convective activity fuelled by moisture, surface heating, and orographic lifting at the edge of the Albertine Rift Valley.

Phenology — the study of cyclic and seasonal natural phenomena — provides some of the most compelling evidence for climate change. Cherry blossom peak bloom in Washington DC has shifted earlier by about 5 days per decade since the 1920s; UK springtime butterfly emergence, bird migration, and plant flowering dates have all shifted 2–6 days earlier per decade since the 1970s.

The 'albedo paradox' of the Arctic describes how reducing CO₂ to cool the Arctic would be partially offset by increased sea ice and snow albedo — a desirable negative feedback — but the darkening from soot deposited on snow could negate some of this benefit. Researchers estimate that if black carbon emissions from shipping were eliminated as Arctic routes open, it could prevent 20% of the additional warming from sea ice loss.

Deep convection in the Mediterranean occurs primarily in winter in three regions: the Gulf of Lions (northwest Mediterranean), the Adriatic Sea, and the Aegean Sea. Cold, dry Mistral and Bora winds blowing over the sea cool the surface water and increase salinity through evaporation until it becomes dense enough to sink to the bottom, ventilating the deep Mediterranean and contributing to the global thermohaline circulation.

The Andes Mountains in South America create the world's most dramatic climatic contrast over short horizontal distances: the western slopes facing the Pacific are among the world's driest places, while the eastern slopes facing the Amazon Basin receive up to 8,000 mm of rain per year. This extreme gradient is produced by the trade winds lifting moist air against the eastern Andes while the Pacific coast lies in the rain shadow of the mountains and under the influence of the cold Humboldt Current.

The term 'weather window' describes a period of sufficiently calm conditions for activities like offshore oil and gas operations, construction, fishing, or maritime rescue. Accurate extended weather forecasts are commercially critical for these industries; the global commercial weather services market is estimated at over $6 billion annually.

The 'isallobar' is a contour line connecting points of equal pressure change over a specified time period, typically 3 or 24 hours. Isallobar analysis helps forecasters identify regions of rapid pressure fall (isallobaric lows) that will become centres of surface convergence and precipitation, and regions of pressure rise (isallobaric highs) associated with divergence and clearing.

Ocean deoxygenation — the loss of dissolved oxygen from seawater due to warming (warmer water holds less oxygen) and increased stratification — has reduced the ocean's oxygen content by about 2% over the past 50 years. The expansion of oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) threatens deep-sea organisms and commercially important fish species that are being squeezed into shallower, oxygenated layers.

source.name: IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere

text: The Pacific Northwest coast of North America experiences one of the world's most dramatic precipitation gradients: the Olympic Peninsula in Washington State receives over 4,000 mm of rain annually on its western side, while the city of Sequim on its eastern side — in the rain shadow — receives only about 400 mm, one of the driest spots in the Pacific Northwest.

The ITCZ's asymmetric position north of the equator year-round — rather than straddling it evenly — is linked to the slightly greater area and land mass of the Northern Hemisphere that makes it warmer on average. Climate modelling shows that asymmetric hemispheric heating drives the ITCZ toward the warmer hemisphere, a fundamental principle shaping the distribution of tropical rainfall.

Svalbard's Longyearbyen — at 78°N, one of the northernmost permanent settlements in the world — recorded its first ever above-zero January temperature (+3.2°C) in 2016, a temperature that would have been considered impossible just decades ago. The archipelago now has the fastest-warming capital city of any country on Earth.

The Cryogenian Period (720–635 million years ago) may have seen Earth completely ice-covered in 'Hard Snowball' episodes, with sea ice extending to the equator. Evidence includes: glacial deposits and carbon isotope excursions in equatorial rocks, and the subsequent rapid deposition of 'cap carbonates' — thick layers of limestone laid down as rising CO₂ (from millions of years of volcanic outgassing) caused explosive post-glacial warming.

A microburst is a downdraft with a diameter of 4 km or less that can produce strong divergent winds at the surface; dry microbursts in the desert Southwest occur without rain reaching the surface (the rain evaporates before landing), and the cooled air descends violently. During the period 1964–1985, microbursts were responsible for 26 major aircraft accidents and 620 fatalities before they were understood.

The Black Summer bushfire smoke plumes from Australia in 2019–20 travelled around the Southern Hemisphere and were detectable in the stratosphere for over a year. The smoke absorbed solar radiation, warmed the stratosphere locally by 2–3°C, and generated unusual circulation anomalies — including strengthened westerly winds that contributed to record warm temperatures over Australia in early 2020.

The Kuroshio Current — the Pacific equivalent of the Gulf Stream — flows northward along the coasts of the Philippines, Taiwan, and Japan, transporting enormous quantities of heat. Its extension into the open North Pacific drives extratropical cyclone development and strongly influences precipitation over Japan, Korea, and China; its variability on decadal timescales is linked to the Pacific Decadal Oscillation.

Radiocarbon (carbon-14) dating requires correcting for variations in atmospheric ¹⁴C production, which is affected by solar activity and Earth's magnetic field. Changes in ocean circulation also affect the radiocarbon age of marine organisms; coral skeletons and deep-sea sediments are used to reconstruct ocean circulation changes independently of radiocarbon dates that require calibration.

Wind turbines typically begin generating power at 'cut-in' wind speeds of about 3–4 m/s and reach their rated output at about 12–15 m/s; they shut down automatically at 'cut-out' speeds of about 25 m/s to prevent mechanical damage. The optimal wind turbine height has increased dramatically — modern offshore turbines with towers over 150 m can access stronger and more consistent winds.

The tropopause height varies with latitude and season: it is approximately 16–18 km in the tropics, drops to 10–12 km in mid-latitudes, and is only about 8 km high over the poles. As the climate warms, the tropopause is rising — by about 50–60 metres per decade — because the warmer troposphere expands vertically while a cooler stratosphere contracts.

Seasonal sea ice in the Arctic (which melts in summer) is far more dynamically active and ecologically significant than perennial sea ice. First-year ice (newly formed each autumn) now dominates the Arctic basin, having replaced the thicker, more resistant multi-year ice that once covered much of it. First-year ice is smoother, thinner, and more easily transported by winds than multi-year ice.

Flooding is the world's deadliest and most costly natural hazard, affecting more people annually than any other type of disaster. In 2021, devastating floods in Germany's Ahr Valley killed 188 people in a region that had not experienced catastrophic flooding in living memory; attribution studies found climate change made such extreme rainfall at least 1.2–9 times more likely.

Seasonal forecasts use statistical and dynamical methods to predict likely departures from normal temperature and precipitation over periods of 1–3 months. ENSO is the primary source of seasonal forecast skill globally; however, in regions far from the tropics or not strongly influenced by ENSO, seasonal forecast skill remains low — forecasting climate anomalies more than a season ahead is generally beyond current capability.

The carbon cycle includes both fast (years to centuries) and slow (millions of years) components. The fast carbon cycle involves exchanges among the atmosphere, land biosphere, and ocean surface; the slow carbon cycle involves the geological processes of volcanic outgassing, weathering of silicate rocks, and burial of organic carbon. Over millions of years, the slow cycle regulates CO₂ on geological timescales.

Mangrove forests — found in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones — are among the most carbon-dense ecosystems on Earth, storing 3–5 times more carbon per unit area than tropical rainforests, mostly in their deep organic-rich soils. They also provide critical coastal protection against storm surges, support fisheries, and filter sediment; mangrove area has declined by 20–35% since the 1980s due to coastal development.

Global sea surface temperatures are recorded by a combination of satellite instruments, ship intake thermometers, and Argo profiling floats. The Argo programme — approximately 3,900 floats drifting in the global ocean — has revolutionised ocean monitoring since the early 2000s; each float dives to 1,000–2,000 m depth, drifts for 10 days, then rises slowly measuring temperature and salinity before transmitting data via satellite.

The 'Great Dying' — the Permian-Triassic extinction event approximately 252 million years ago — killed about 96% of marine species and 70% of terrestrial vertebrates, making it the most severe mass extinction in Earth's history. It is linked to massive Siberian Traps volcanic eruptions that released vast quantities of CO₂ and methane, raising global temperatures by 10–15°C and acidifying and deoxygenating the oceans.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

text: The global ocean has absorbed about 25% of human CO₂ emissions since industrialisation, significantly slowing the pace of climate change. However, this uptake is declining in efficiency as the ocean warms and surface waters become saturated; the Southern Ocean, which absorbs around 40% of all ocean CO₂ uptake, has shown decadal variability in its sink strength linked to wind-driven upwelling.

Polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) — rare nacreous clouds forming in the stratosphere at temperatures below −78°C — are spectacularly iridescent due to diffraction of sunlight by their uniform ice crystals. They form primarily in the Antarctic winter stratosphere and are crucial for ozone destruction chemistry, providing surfaces for heterogeneous chemical reactions that release reactive chlorine from anthropogenic CFCs.

Climate feedback parameters quantify how much additional warming results from each feedback mechanism. The combined feedback parameter of all fast feedbacks (water vapour, lapse rate, surface albedo, clouds) is approximately −1.1 W/m²/°C, meaning feedbacks amplify the initial CO₂ forcing by about 3-fold. Without feedbacks, climate sensitivity would be about 1.2°C per CO₂ doubling instead of the assessed ~3°C.

The term 'paleotempestology' refers to the study of ancient tropical cyclone activity using geological proxies including lake sediments, speleothems (cave deposits), and coastal marsh sediments that preserve signatures of storm surge events. Records extending back 3,000–5,000 years show that Atlantic hurricane activity varies on centennial timescales, often in response to El Niño and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation patterns.

Dryland areas — defined by a ratio of annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration below 0.65 — already cover over 40% of Earth's land surface and are expanding under climate change. Drylands support 2.7 billion people, many of whom are among the world's most food-insecure; models project drylands will expand by up to 23% by 2100 under high-emissions scenarios.

Global CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and cement reached a record high of approximately 36.8 GtCO₂ in 2023 despite global renewable energy expansion. The gap between current emissions trajectories and those needed to limit warming to 1.5°C requires cutting global emissions roughly in half by 2030 — a pace of decarbonisation unprecedented in economic history.

The isotopic composition of precipitation varies with temperature: colder temperatures during glacial periods produce snow with more depleted (lighter) oxygen and hydrogen isotopes. Speleothems (cave stalagmites and stalactites) record these isotopic variations in their calcite layers with annual precision, providing high-resolution paleoclimate archives that preserve records of monsoon intensity, drought, and temperature changes.

North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) formation requires a specific combination of low temperature, high salinity, and sinking at the ocean surface. As Greenland melt and Arctic river runoff add fresh water to the North Atlantic, the density of surface water decreases, potentially disrupting NADW formation and weakening the AMOC. Paleoclimate records show that past AMOC collapses caused severe cooling of 5–10°C in Western Europe.

'Sunny day flooding' or 'nuisance flooding' — coastal tidal flooding that occurs even in fair weather during spring high tides — has increased by 300–900% in frequency at US Atlantic Coast cities since 2000, driven by sea level rise. Miami's Biscayne Boulevard, Charleston's historic waterfront, and Annapolis' town dock now flood regularly during king tides.

The insolation at Earth's surface is modified by the solar zenith angle, atmospheric path length, and reflective properties of the surface. At the Saharan noon on the summer solstice, direct beam solar radiation can reach approximately 1,000 W/m² at the surface — equivalent to ten 100-watt light bulbs per square metre — explaining why solar panel installations in such regions are highly productive.

source.name: NASA Surface Meteorology and Solar Energy

text: Wind-driven churning of the ocean's mixed layer enhances heat and gas exchange between the ocean and atmosphere. When tropical cyclones pass over the ocean, their intense winds mix cold water from below to the surface, cooling the sea surface temperature and reducing the storm's fuel supply in a natural negative feedback — though fast-moving storms outpace this cooling mechanism.

Hurricane Katrina (2005) was the costliest tropical cyclone in US history, causing approximately $125 billion in damage (2005 dollars) and killing around 1,800 people. The storm surge — not the wind — caused most deaths, with levee failures flooding 80% of New Orleans. Climate change increases future risk by raising sea levels (amplifying storm surge) and potentially intensifying storm winds.

Sea surface salinity (SSS) provides a direct measure of the water cycle: fresh precipitation reduces SSS, while evaporation increases it. The salt cycle in the ocean amplifies the atmospheric water cycle signal, making high-salinity regions more saline and low-salinity regions fresher over time — a phenomenon called 'the ocean as amplifier of the global water cycle' that is intensifying with warming.

The global dimming phenomenon — a reduction in the amount of solar radiation reaching Earth's surface from the 1950s to 1980s due to increasing atmospheric aerosols from industrialisation — may have masked early greenhouse gas warming. Global brightening — increasing solar radiation at the surface since the 1980s as clean air regulations reduced aerosol emissions — may have contributed to accelerated warming from the 1980s onward.

Tree phenology data from Japan's Imperial Court records of cherry blossom festivals dating back to 812 CE have been used to reconstruct spring temperatures in Kyoto over more than 1,200 years. The 2021 cherry blossom peak bloom date of March 26 was the earliest in this 1,200-year record, illustrating how historical records can extend instrumental climate data.

The aerosol-cloud interaction involves aerosols acting as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN): more CCN produce more but smaller cloud droplets, making clouds brighter (the Twomey effect) and potentially longer-lived. Ship tracks — bright linear cloud signatures visible in satellite imagery from the exhaust of ships at sea — are a vivid example of the Twomey effect operating in real-time in marine stratocumulus clouds.

The term 'flash flood' refers to a rapid, sudden rise of water in a stream or low-lying area due to heavy rain, levee or dam failure, or sudden snowmelt. Flash floods are the #1 weather-related killer in the United States, averaging about 150 deaths per year; they can develop within minutes to hours, and driving into floodwaters is responsible for the majority of flood-related deaths.

Tropical cyclone track predictability is significantly higher than intensity predictability: 5-day track errors have been halved over the past 30 years, but intensity forecast errors have improved much more slowly. The challenge of intensity forecasting lies in the storm's inner-core dynamics — including rapid intensification events, where central pressure drops by more than 35 hPa in 24 hours — which depend on processes at scales too small for current models to resolve.

The Milankovitch cycles — periodic variations in Earth's orbital eccentricity (~100,000 years), axial tilt (~41,000 years), and precession (~23,000 years) — are the 'pacemakers' of the ice ages. At the last glacial-interglacial transition (~18,000–10,000 years ago), Milankovitch forcing increased Northern Hemisphere summer insolation, initiating ice sheet retreat that was amplified by CO₂ and albedo feedbacks.

The global mean surface temperature is measured by multiple independent research groups using different datasets, methodologies, and quality-control procedures: NASA GISS, NOAA GlobalTemp, HadCRUT (UK Met Office/CRU), Berkeley Earth, and Copernicus ERA5 reanalysis. All show a consistent long-term warming trend, and their agreement despite methodological differences provides strong evidence that the trend is real.

The Beaufort scale was developed empirically for open ocean conditions; its descriptions of wave height and sea state are well calibrated to wind speed offshore but are poor guides at coastal margins and in semi-enclosed seas where wave heights may be much smaller than predicted by the wind speed alone due to limited fetch. Fetch — the unobstructed distance over which wind blows across water — is critical for wave development.

The Lorenz attractor — the butterfly-shaped mathematical object generated by Edward Lorenz's simplified atmospheric convection equations — is the most famous example of a strange attractor in chaos theory. It demonstrates how a deterministic system can produce trajectories that never exactly repeat and are exquisitely sensitive to initial conditions, providing the mathematical foundation for understanding why deterministic weather prediction has fundamental limits.

The role of clouds in the current and future climate is summarised by the 'cloud feedback' parameter: low clouds predominantly cool the planet (high albedo), while high clouds warm it (greenhouse effect). Evidence from paleoclimate records, climate models, and observations now consistently indicates that the net cloud feedback is positive — clouds will amplify warming — with low cloud reductions being the primary contributor.

The global freshwater withdrawal for agriculture, industry, and domestic use totals approximately 4,000 km³ per year — roughly 4% of global river runoff. Agriculture accounts for about 70% of this withdrawal, primarily for irrigation; in water-stressed regions, groundwater is extracted far faster than it is replenished, with serious long-term consequences for food production and water availability.

The most snow ever measured at a weather station in a single season is 28.96 metres (95 feet) at Mount Baker Ski Area, Washington State, USA, during the 1998–99 season. The world record for 24-hour snowfall at a single location is 1.93 metres (76 inches) recorded at Silver Lake, Colorado, USA, on April 14–15, 1921.

Monsoon rains in the Sahel have partially recovered since the devastating 1970s–1980s drought years, in what is called the 'Sahel greening.' This recovery is attributed partly to increased rainfall linked to rising Atlantic sea surface temperatures and partly to land management improvements. However, rainfall is more variable and concentrated in intense events, increasing flash flood risk even as average rainfall recovers.

The Southern Hemisphere westerly winds have been strengthening and shifting poleward since at least the 1970s, driven by both stratospheric ozone depletion (which cooled the Antarctic stratosphere and increased the polar vortex) and greenhouse gas increases. This shift is associated with increased upwelling of warm deep water around Antarctica and changes in the Southern Ocean carbon sink.

Biochar — charcoal produced by pyrolysis of organic material and added to soils — is proposed as a long-term carbon sequestration method: unlike fresh organic matter, biochar degrades very slowly in soil and can persist for centuries to millennia. Studies suggest biochar application can also improve soil water retention and fertility, offering co-benefits for agriculture.

The 'carbon budget' — the total amount of CO₂ that can be emitted while limiting warming to a given temperature threshold — is the foundational concept linking emissions to climate outcomes. The remaining carbon budget for a 50% probability of staying below 1.5°C was approximately 500 GtCO₂ from the start of 2020; at 2022 emission rates, this budget will be exhausted in about 9–10 years.

Speleothem records from Borneo and China show that the East Asian and tropical Indo-Pacific summer monsoon was intensified during the Medieval Warm Period (~950–1250 CE) and weakened during the Little Ice Age (~1400–1850 CE), demonstrating that monsoon strength is sensitive to changes in global mean temperature — and therefore will be affected by contemporary warming.

Antarctica receives the least precipitation of any continent — averaging just 150–200 mm of water equivalent per year — qualifying as a polar desert. Despite this, it has accumulated ice more than 4,700 metres thick in places because of the extreme cold that prevents melting; ice accumulates over millions of years from sparse snowfall with almost no loss.

Cumulonimbus incus — the 'anvil cloud' — is a cumulonimbus thunderstorm cloud that has reached the tropopause, where stable stratospheric air prevents further upward growth, causing the top to flatten and spread downwind in the characteristic anvil shape. The anvil points in the direction the storm is moving and shows the position of the highest and most intense part of the thunderstorm's outflow.

The Coriolis effect not only deflects air and ocean currents but also affects the draining of water from bathtubs and sinks — but in real plumbing, this effect is so tiny that it is overwhelmed by the shape of the basin and initial water motion. Laboratory demonstrations with carefully controlled conditions have confirmed the effect, but it is negligible for ordinary water usage.

The global fire season has lengthened by approximately 19% between 1979 and 2013, exposing more land to conditions conducive to burning. Climate change is driving this trend through longer and more intense heatwaves, earlier snowmelt, and increased drought frequency. Fire-affected land area is projected to increase by 20–50% over the 21st century depending on emissions pathway.

The Indian Ocean is the warmest of the world's major oceans, with mean sea surface temperatures consistently around 26–29°C over much of its extent. It is also the most climatically influential: its warming trend is driving increased extreme rainfall in South Asia and East Africa and intensifying the Indian Ocean Dipole mode, affecting a region home to one-third of humanity.

source.name: IPCC Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere Chapter 6

text: The Meiyu-Baiu rainy season — called Meiyu in China and Baiu in Japan — is caused by the stationary front between cold, dry continental air and warm, moist air from the Pacific and Indian oceans. Exceptionally heavy Meiyu rains in 2020 caused the worst flooding in the Yangtze River basin in decades, affecting 70 million people and causing $35 billion in damage.

The tipping point of the West Greenland ice sheet may be at around 1.5°C of global warming above pre-industrial levels; beyond this threshold, positive feedbacks could trigger irreversible and complete melting on a timescale of millennia, contributing approximately 7 metres to global sea level. A 2021 study in Nature Climate Change found we may already be close to this threshold.

Climatologists use 'fingerprint detection' to attribute observed climate changes to their causes by comparing distinctive patterns in observations to the patterns predicted by climate models. The spatial pattern of warming (greater at the poles, greater over land), the increase in daily minimum temperatures faster than maximums, and the cooling of the stratosphere alongside tropospheric warming are all distinct fingerprints of greenhouse gas forcing.

The global ocean's average temperature at depth has been rising for decades even without direct contact with the warmer atmosphere, because of heat transported downward from the warming surface layer. The deep ocean (below 2,000 m) is warming at a rate of about 0.002°C per decade — small in absolute terms but enormous when multiplied by the ocean's vast volume, representing a huge amount of stored thermal energy.

Satellite altimetry — using microwave pulses from polar-orbiting satellites to measure ocean surface height — has continuously monitored global mean sea level since 1992, providing the definitive record of sea level change. The TOPEX/Poseidon, Jason-1, Jason-2, and Jason-3 satellites form an unbroken record of sea level rise with millimetre precision, showing a clear acceleration that matches predictions from ice loss and thermal expansion.

The concept of 'committed warming' or 'warming in the pipeline' refers to the additional temperature rise that will occur even if greenhouse gas concentrations were held constant today, because the climate system — particularly the ocean — has not yet reached equilibrium with current forcing. IPCC AR6 estimates approximately 0.1–0.3°C of additional committed warming above 2011–2020 levels.

The discovery of the 'ozone hole' over Antarctica was made possible by long-baseline monitoring with Dobson spectrophotometers — instruments that measure atmospheric ozone by comparing the intensity of ultraviolet light at different wavelengths. The first Dobson instrument was built by G.M.B. Dobson in the 1920s; the global network of Dobson instruments now provides a 70-year record of stratospheric ozone.

Hydropower generates about 15% of the world's electricity and over 60% of renewable electricity. Its output is highly sensitive to precipitation and snowmelt patterns, making climate change a significant risk to energy security in hydro-dependent countries. Droughts in Brazil, which relies on hydropower for 65% of electricity, and in the western United States have both forced grid operators to rely on fossil fuels.

The meridional temperature gradient — the difference in temperature between the tropics and the poles — drives the strength of the mid-latitude jet stream. As the Arctic warms faster than the tropics under climate change, this gradient is weakening, which may be causing the jet stream to slow and meander more widely, potentially linking climate change to an increase in persistent weather extremes at mid-latitudes.

Inland seas and large lakes create their own regional climates, moderating temperature extremes and generating lake breeze circulation systems analogous to sea breezes. The Great Lakes of North America moderate temperatures along their shores significantly: Chicago's lakefront is typically several degrees cooler in summer and warmer in winter than areas just a few miles inland.

source.name: NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory

text: Tropical cyclone rainfall is projected to increase significantly under climate change: models consistently show 10–30% more rainfall per storm as the warming atmosphere holds more moisture. More of this rainfall will also fall at greater distances from the storm centre as moisture-laden environments allow convective bands to extend further. Hurricane Florence (2018) dropped record rainfall partly attributed to climate change.

The 'hockey stick' controversy — the intense political and scientific debate surrounding Mann et al.'s 1999 reconstruction of Northern Hemisphere temperatures — has since been confirmed by multiple independent studies using different proxy data and methods. The National Research Council concluded in 2006 that the reconstruction was essentially correct, and subsequent work has further strengthened the finding of unprecedented modern warmth.

source.name: National Academies of Sciences Surface Temperature Reconstructions

text: Convective available potential energy (CAPE) is the thermodynamic energy available to a parcel of air lifted vertically, measuring thunderstorm potential. Values above 1,000 J/kg indicate significant thunderstorm potential; above 2,500 J/kg is considered extreme, capable of supporting supercells and tornadoes. A warming climate generally increases CAPE values, potentially intensifying convective storms.

The Amazon rainforest is approaching a dieback tipping point driven by deforestation, wildfires, and climate change. Currently around 17% of the Amazon has been deforested; models suggest a tipping point may occur between 20–25% deforestation, beyond which reduced evapotranspiration would dry the forest beyond its self-sustaining ability, potentially converting large areas to savanna.

The global mean temperature is measured as an anomaly (departure from a baseline), not an absolute value, because the actual surface temperature varies so dramatically from the tropics to the poles that an absolute global mean is less informative. The standard approach compares each location to its own historical baseline, so an anomaly map shows where it is warmer or cooler than normal rather than absolute temperature.

Tropical cyclone frequency is not projected to increase globally — models consistently predict a slight decrease or no change in total cyclone numbers — but the proportion of the most intense storms (Category 4–5) is projected to increase significantly. This intensification without frequency increase means the global average destructive potential per storm season may nonetheless rise.

The global ocean covers approximately 71% of Earth's surface and has a mean depth of 3,688 metres. Its total volume of approximately 1.335 billion km³ contains about 97% of all Earth's water. The ocean's specific heat capacity is about four times that of land surface material, giving it enormous thermal inertia that buffers the rate of global warming.

The Arctic is experiencing 'Atlantification' — an intrusion of warm, salty Atlantic water into the eastern Arctic Ocean that is eroding the cold, fresh surface layer and promoting sea ice loss in the Barents Sea. This process, linked to both natural variability and climate change, is contributing to the extreme warming observed in the Barents Sea, which has lost more than 95% of its winter sea ice extent since 1998.

Supercooled large drops (SLDs) — supercooled rain droplets and drizzle drops larger than 50 micrometres — are an especially dangerous form of aircraft icing because they can flow behind the leading edge protections on wings and freeze in areas not designed to handle ice. The 1994 American Eagle Flight 4184 crash near Roselawn, Indiana (68 fatalities) was caused by SLD icing and led to new FAA icing certification requirements.

Global mean surface temperature has already warmed by about 1.1–1.2°C since the pre-industrial period (1850–1900), and the warming rate over the past 50 years is unprecedented in at least the last 2,000 years. IPCC AR6 states with high confidence that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land, and that current CO₂ concentrations are higher than at any point in at least 2 million years.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers

text: The 'wet adiabatic lapse rate' — about 4–6°C per 1,000 metres — describes how saturated air cools more slowly than dry air (dry adiabatic lapse rate ~10°C/km) because condensation releases latent heat. This difference is why mountains force air to rise, cool, condense, and precipitate on the windward side, then descend, warm, and dry on the leeward side — the foundation of orographic precipitation.

The Angstrom exponent characterises aerosol size distribution in the atmosphere: fine-mode aerosols (like smoke and pollution) produce large Angstrom exponents, while coarse-mode aerosols (like sea salt and dust) produce small values close to zero. This parameter, derived from multi-wavelength optical measurements, is used to distinguish pollution events from natural dust and sea spray using satellite data.

The Bering Sea, between Alaska and Siberia, is one of the most biologically productive seas in the world, supporting vast populations of walleye pollock, crab, halibut, and seabirds. Sea ice extent in the Bering Sea reached historically low levels in 2018–2019, causing catastrophic declines in snow crab populations, seabird breeding failures, and changes in whale distribution that have upended Alaska's fishing industry.

The Insolation Variability — changes in solar radiation received at the top of the atmosphere due to Milankovitch orbital cycles — provides the 'pacing' for glacial-interglacial cycles, but the magnitude of insolation change is far too small to explain the observed temperature swings of ~8°C. CO₂, methane, and ice-albedo feedbacks amplify the initial Milankovitch forcing approximately 8–10 fold.

The Pacific Ocean's 'warm pool' — a region of consistently warm water (>28°C) in the western tropical Pacific — is the largest reservoir of warm ocean water on Earth and the powerhouse of the global atmospheric circulation. The warm pool is expanding eastward under climate change, which is altering the base state of the ENSO system and shifting rainfall patterns across the tropics.

Fog seasons, historically reliable in many coastal cities, are changing under climate change. San Francisco's summer fog season has shortened — fog frequency declined about 33% over the 20th century — affecting the cooling function fog provides to coastal redwood forests and agriculture. Meanwhile, some inland valleys are experiencing more winter fog as warmer conditions alter evaporation and boundary layer dynamics.

Subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) prediction — forecasting 2–8 weeks ahead — is sometimes called the 'predictability desert' because it sits between the 2-week deterministic weather forecast limit and the seasonal climate prediction timescales dominated by ENSO. The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the primary source of predictability in this time range, and improvements in MJO prediction are gradually extending useful forecast lead times.

Biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) released by forests — primarily isoprene and monoterpenes from trees like oaks and conifers — react with atmospheric pollutants to form secondary organic aerosols that can seed clouds. The blue haze over the Great Smoky Mountains and the Blue Mountains of Australia is caused by fine aerosol particles formed from BVOC oxidation scattering short-wavelength (blue) light.

The world's largest coral reef is the 2,300-km Great Barrier Reef; the second largest is the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System (700 km) running from Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, and Honduras. Both reefs face overlapping threats from ocean warming (bleaching), acidification, runoff, and overfishing; the Mesoamerican reef lost approximately 80% of its coral cover between 1980 and 2006.

Thermohaline circulation transports heat poleward equivalent to roughly 1.3 petawatts in the Atlantic — approximately 100 times the total global electricity consumption — and plays a critical role in the global climate. Because it is driven by density differences between cold, salty deep water and warmer, fresher surface water, its sensitivity to freshwater forcing from melting ice makes it a potential climate tipping element.

The 'greening' of the Arctic — an expansion of shrub and grass vegetation into previously bare or lightly vegetated tundra as temperatures rise — has been detected by satellite since the 1980s. This greening feeds back positively on warming by increasing the absorption of solar radiation; however, in some areas 'browning' is occurring due to drought stress from increased evapotranspiration exceeding moisture supply.

Natural climatic cycles, including the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation, and the North Atlantic Oscillation, operate on multidecadal timescales and can temporarily enhance or offset global warming trends. These modes of natural variability make attributing specific decades of faster or slower warming challenging, requiring statistical methods that account for internal variability.

The 2022 Pakistan floods, caused by record monsoon rainfall supercharged by a preceding severe heatwave, submerged one-third of the country, killing over 1,700 people and causing $30 billion in damage — roughly equivalent to Pakistan's entire annual development budget. Attribution studies found climate change made the event 50% more likely and more intense, while pre-existing extreme heat had dried soils reducing their ability to absorb the deluge.

Sudden oak death, caused by the water mould Phytophthora ramorum, has killed millions of oaks and tanoaks across coastal California and Oregon. Its spread is facilitated by the specific combination of mild temperatures and abundant moisture — climate conditions that have expanded under changing precipitation patterns. This is one of many examples of climate change altering the geographic range of plant diseases.

source.name: USDA Forest Service Sudden Oak Death

text: The polar night — the period when the sun does not rise above the horizon at high Arctic and Antarctic latitudes — creates months of continuous darkness at the poles in winter. At the poles themselves, this night lasts approximately 6 months; at Longyearbyen (78°N), it lasts from October 26 to February 15. Despite the darkness, meteorological processes continue and significant weather events including storms and blizzards occur throughout polar winter.

Convective inhibition (CIN or CINH) is the thermodynamic 'cap' that prevents thunderstorm development by requiring parcels to overcome a stable layer of air before they can rise freely. A strong CIN 'lids' the atmosphere and allows heat and moisture to build all day; if a storm system disturbs the lid in the afternoon, the release of accumulated instability can produce violent severe weather.

The global atmospheric methane growth rate reached a record high of 15.3 ppb/year in 2020 — the largest annual increase since measurements began in 1983. The cause is debated but likely involves increased wetland emissions from warmer temperatures, increased fossil fuel extraction, and reduced atmospheric hydroxyl radical (OH) levels that would normally destroy methane.

The Indian Heat Wave of May 2022, which set temperatures above 45°C across large parts of India and Pakistan, was the worst in recorded history for the region in March and April. Attribution scientists found it would have been 'virtually impossible' without climate change, and projected such events will occur every 4–5 years by mid-century under moderate warming scenarios — compared to once every 50 years historically.

The Atacama Desert's extreme aridity results from multiple reinforcing factors: it lies in the rain shadow of the Andes, it is dominated by the descending arm of the Hadley circulation, and it is cooled by the cold Humboldt Current offshore which suppresses convection. The Atacama receives so little moisture that some bacteria found in its soils do not require liquid water to survive — they extract moisture directly from minerals and atmospheric humidity.

Lake Vostok, buried beneath 4 kilometres of ice in Antarctica, is the largest known subglacial lake on Earth, approximately 250 km long and 50 km wide. It has been isolated from the atmosphere for at least 15 million years, potentially harbouring microbial life adapted to extreme cold, darkness, and pressure. Its very existence was suspected from airborne radar surveys in the 1970s and confirmed by drilling in the 1990s.

The ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 (δ¹³C) in atmospheric CO₂ has been declining — a process called 'Suess effect' — because fossil fuels are depleted in ¹³C relative to the atmosphere, and as we burn more of them we dilute the atmospheric ¹³C ratio. This isotopic signature is one of the clearest chemical proofs that the increase in atmospheric CO₂ comes from fossil fuels rather than natural sources.

The Pineapple Express is a specific type of atmospheric river that originates near Hawaii and carries moisture from the tropical Pacific to the US West Coast and British Columbia. It typically brings several days of heavy rainfall and warm temperatures, often causing floods and mudslides in California; the term entered widespread use after a particularly destructive 1997 event.

The Younger Dryas ended approximately 11,700 years ago with a dramatic warming of about 10°C in Greenland within 50 years — some ice core records suggest the transition occurred in as few as 1–3 years. This abrupt end to the last major cold period, caused by the resumption of AMOC after a freshwater shutdown, provided the warm stable climate in which human civilisation and agriculture developed.

The atmospheric residence time of a greenhouse gas is the key determinant of its long-term climate impact. CO₂ — with a complex multi-century atmospheric lifetime — is the most important long-term climate forcer; methane, with its 12-year lifetime, is potent in the near term but degrades; halocarbons like CFC-12 persist for over 100 years; while water vapour cycles through in ~9 days as a rapid feedback.

The 2017 Atlantic hurricane season was the most costly in recorded history (at the time), with three Category 4 or 5 hurricanes — Harvey, Irma, and Maria — making landfall in succession within weeks. Hurricane Maria caused near-total destruction in Puerto Rico; the official death toll was revised from 64 to approximately 3,000 in 2018 after a study found excess mortality from the aftermath.

The concept of 'climate justice' recognises that those most vulnerable to climate change — small island developing states, low-lying coastal nations, and least developed countries — have contributed least to historical greenhouse gas emissions. The 0.4 billion people living in the 50 least developed countries are responsible for less than 1% of cumulative global CO₂ emissions but face some of the most severe climate impacts.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG2 Summary for Policymakers

text: Deep learning and artificial intelligence are transforming weather forecasting: Google DeepMind's GraphCast and NVIDIA's FourCastNet models trained on decades of weather data can produce 10-day global weather forecasts in seconds rather than the hours required by physics-based numerical models — and in some skill metrics are competitive with the world's best operational models. These AI models may fundamentally change the economics and speed of weather forecasting.

Hurricane names have been used on a rotating list basis since 1960; before that, Atlantic storms were identified by their year and order. The World Meteorological Organization maintains six rotating lists of Atlantic hurricane names; a name is permanently retired when the storm was so deadly or costly that future use would be confusing. Retired names include Katrina, Harvey, Irma, Maria, and Dorian.

source.name: NOAA National Hurricane Center Name Retirement

text: The Thwaites Glacier's ice shelf — which currently acts as a buttress restraining the flow of ice into the ocean — has a system of parallel fractures that could cause it to collapse in pieces within 3–5 years according to research published in 2022. Without this buttress, the glacier would flow faster, potentially doubling Thwaites' contribution to global sea level rise.

The 'sea ice paradox' describes the observation that Antarctic sea ice was increasing even as Arctic sea ice was declining dramatically. This paradox has since been largely resolved: the increasing trend observed through about 2014 was driven by strengthening westerly winds and changing ocean circulation; since 2016 Antarctic sea ice has dropped sharply, and 2023 saw Antarctic sea ice extent reach the lowest on record by a large margin.

The Dobson Unit (DU) is the standard unit for measuring total column ozone: 100 DU is equivalent to a 1-millimetre-thick layer of pure ozone at surface temperature and pressure. The global average total column ozone is about 300 DU; during the spring ozone hole season in Antarctica, values below 220 DU are observed and the minimum can drop below 100 DU in severe years.

The 'last ice area' (LIA) — the region in the Canadian Arctic Archipelago north of Greenland projected to retain summer sea ice longest as the Arctic warms — may be the final refuge for ice-dependent species like polar bears and ringed seals. However, recent research found that ice in this region is also becoming younger and thinner than expected, raising concerns about its long-term stability.

Hailstones form within the updrafts of large thunderstorms as ice pellets are repeatedly cycled upward through supercooled water layers, accumulating alternating clear and opaque layers of ice. The largest hailstone ever measured in the United States fell in Vivian, South Dakota, on July 23, 2010: it weighed 878 grams (1.94 pounds) and had a diameter of 20 centimetres (8 inches).

source.name: NOAA National Weather Service Hail Records

text: The 2019–2020 period of unusually warm global ocean temperatures pushed atmospheric CO₂ concentrations to 421 ppm in May 2021 — the highest level in human evolutionary history and likely the highest for at least 3–5 million years, when sea levels were 5–20 metres higher and global temperatures 2–3°C warmer than pre-industrial levels.

Climate change is shifting the geographic ranges of disease-carrying insects: the Aedes aegypti mosquito (vector for dengue, Zika, and yellow fever) and Aedes albopictus are expanding their range poleward and to higher altitudes as warmer winters no longer kill them off. The global burden of dengue fever has grown 30-fold over the past 50 years, with climate-driven expansion of mosquito habitat being a significant contributing factor.

Mega-droughts — droughts persisting 20 years or longer — have been identified in paleoclimate records for the American Southwest during the Medieval Warm Period (~900–1300 CE). A 2022 study in Nature Climate Change found that the Western US megadrought that began in 2000 is the driest 22-year period in at least 1,200 years — a multi-decadal event made 42% more likely by climate change.

source.name: Nature Climate Change Western US Megadrought

text: The polar amplification of warming has made the Arctic the world's fastest-warming region; temperature records in the Arctic are being broken with increasing frequency. The town of Verkhoyansk in Siberia — previously best known as one of the coldest inhabited places on Earth — recorded 38°C (100.4°F) on June 20, 2020, a temperature never before observed north of the Arctic Circle.

The Northern Annular Mode (NAM), also called the Arctic Oscillation (AO), describes the dominant pattern of atmospheric pressure variability in the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. In its positive phase, a strong polar vortex keeps cold Arctic air locked in the north and sends milder, wetter conditions into Europe; in its negative phase, cold air spills southward into Europe, North America, and East Asia.

The aerosol-climate feedback involves complex interactions: dust from expanded deserts could either cool or warm depending on composition and overlying cloud; smoke from more frequent wildfires absorbs sunlight and warms the atmosphere above; and declining sulphate aerosols from cleaner energy sources are contributing to accelerated warming. These competing effects make the future aerosol forcing trajectory one of the most uncertain aspects of climate projections.

The world's lowest precipitation ever recorded in a full calendar year is 0 mm, at Arica, Chile, over multiple years. The driest inhabited place on Earth — also Arica — averages just 0.76 mm per year. Its extreme aridity results from the combined effects of the cold Humboldt Current, subsiding Hadley circulation air, and the rain shadow of the Andes.

Glaciovolcanism — the interaction between ice and volcanic activity — is a significant risk in Iceland, where subglacial eruptions can rapidly melt ice and generate powerful glacial outburst floods (jökulhlaups). The 1996 Gjálp eruption beneath Vatnajökull glacier melted 3 km³ of ice and produced a jökulhlaup that peaked at 50,000 m³/s — equivalent to 40 times the average discharge of the Amazon River.

The global stratospheric aerosol layer — a permanent, thin veil of sulphate particles in the lower stratosphere at 15–25 km altitude — is produced continuously by volcanic sulphur dioxide emissions and sporadic injections from eruptions. In the absence of major eruptions, the stratospheric aerosol optical depth is about 0.003; after the 1991 Pinatubo eruption it reached 0.15 — a 50-fold increase.

source.name: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory Stratospheric Aerosols

text: Atmospheric blocking — the persistence of large-scale high-pressure systems that deflect the normal progression of weather systems — is associated with some of the most extreme weather events on record including the 2003 European and 2010 Russian heatwaves, the 2018 Japanese and Korean heatwaves, and the 2021 Pacific Northwest event. Blocking frequency and persistence may be increasing under climate change though this remains debated.

The term 'climatic teleconnection' describes statistical relationships between climate anomalies in widely separated regions of the globe, connected through atmospheric waves or ocean-atmosphere interaction. The famous ENSO teleconnection links tropical Pacific sea surface temperatures to drought in Australia, floods in Peru, and altered hurricane activity in the Atlantic — all simultaneously.

Cryoconite holes — small water-filled pockets in glacier ice, formed when dark dust particles absorb sunlight and melt downward — are among the most extreme habitats on Earth, yet they harbour diverse communities of bacteria, algae, tardigrades, and rotifers. The darkening of glaciers from cryoconite deposition increases melt rates by reducing glacier albedo.

The Global Carbon Budget — published annually by the Global Carbon Project — tracks the sources and sinks of carbon in the Earth system. In 2022, approximately 40.6 GtCO₂ was emitted from fossil fuels and land use change; of this, about 18 GtCO₂ was absorbed by land ecosystems, 10.5 GtCO₂ by the ocean, and the remaining 12 GtCO₂ accumulated in the atmosphere.

The Benguela Current, flowing northward along the Atlantic coast of southern Africa, is driven by southeast trade winds that push surface water offshore, drawing up cold, nutrient-rich water from depth. This upwelling system supports one of the world's richest fisheries; fog is pervasive along the Namibian coast where the cold current meets warm, moist air.

The global water table is falling in the world's most heavily irrigated regions: the Central Valley of California, India's Punjab, and the North China Plain are all experiencing significant groundwater depletion. A 2023 study in Nature found that one-third of the world's largest groundwater systems are being depleted faster than they can recharge, threatening food production for billions of people.

Snow grains (also called 'diamond dust') are tiny ice crystals that fall from clear or nearly clear skies in very cold, calm conditions, typically at temperatures below −15°C. They are common in the interior of Antarctica and the high Arctic and create spectacular optical effects including sun dogs, halos, and light pillars — ice crystal optical phenomena caused by light refracting through the oriented hexagonal crystals.

The global monsoon system — encompassing not just the Asian monsoon but also the West African, North American, Australian, and South American monsoons — covers about two-thirds of the global population and half of global precipitation. Changes in the global monsoon under warming include more intense but potentially less frequent rainfall events and shifts in onset and withdrawal dates.

Aerosol effects on precipitation remain one of the most challenging aspects of cloud physics and climate science. Polluted air with high aerosol concentrations produces many small droplets that are slow to coalesce into rain — potentially suppressing precipitation in some regions while enhancing it in others by changing cloud lifetime and intensity. Untangling aerosol effects from dynamical changes in rainfall patterns is an active research area.

The Beaufort Sea's annual sea ice cycle — growing from September to March and melting from March to September — now produces younger, thinner ice on average. Since the 1980s, multi-year ice (ice surviving at least one summer) has declined from about 45% of Arctic sea ice to less than 25%, making the remaining ice more mobile, less saline, and more easily melted.

The concept of 'overshoot' in climate policy refers to scenarios where global temperatures temporarily exceed the 1.5°C Paris Agreement target before declining — requiring large-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR) to draw temperatures back down. Most 1.5°C-consistent scenarios in IPCC AR6 involve some degree of overshoot, reflecting the difficulty of staying under the target without removing CO₂ from the atmosphere.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG3 Summary for Policymakers

text: The Beaufort Scale's intermediate Force 6 (strong breeze, 39–49 km/h) is described as long waves beginning to form, white foam crests more extensive everywhere, and some airborne spray. On land, large branches in motion and umbrellas used with difficulty. This force is familiar to coastal residents and is where recreational boating starts to require caution.

The Indonesian Throughflow — a current carrying warm, fresh Pacific water into the Indian Ocean through the Indonesian archipelago — transfers approximately 10–15 Sv (sverdrups) of water and 1 petawatt of heat between the world's two largest ocean basins. It plays a key role in redistributing heat globally and influences the Indian Ocean warming trend and monsoon variability.

The Horn of Africa experienced five consecutive failed rainy seasons between 2020 and 2022 — the most prolonged drought in 40 years — driven by La Niña conditions that reduced Indian Ocean rainfall. The drought pushed over 22 million people into severe food insecurity across Ethiopia, Kenya, and Somalia, with climate change assessed to have increased the probability of such prolonged drought 100-fold.

source.name: World Weather Attribution Horn of Africa Drought 2022

text: Clammy, cold 'sea smoke' fog forms when very cold air flows over much warmer open water, causing rapid evaporation from the water surface that immediately condenses in the frigid overlying air. Sea smoke is common in the Great Lakes in late autumn before ice forms and in the Arctic wherever open water remains amid sea ice, appearing as rising wisps or columns above the surface.

The Baffin Island Ice Cap and other Arctic Canadian ice caps are among the fastest-retreating glaciers in the world, losing approximately 20 Gt of ice per year. LiDAR surveys show that some ice caps on Baffin Island are currently smaller than at any time in the past 40,000 years, and that ice originally established during the Neoglacial period (~3,000–5,000 years ago) has been fully lost.

Wave height in the open ocean depends on three factors: wind speed, wind duration, and fetch (the distance over which the wind blows). The fully developed sea state for a 50-knot wind requires about 1,200 km of fetch and 42 hours of sustained winds to generate its maximum significant wave height of approximately 15 metres; shorter fetch or duration produces smaller waves.

The 'urban canyon' effect in cities — tall buildings channelling and accelerating wind through narrow streets — produces local wind gusts significantly stronger than the regional background wind. In extreme cases like downtown Dallas, Texas, or Canary Wharf in London, ground-level winds can exceed the background by 200–300% due to downwash from building corners and funnelling through street corridors.

The global warming 'detection and attribution' science has advanced to conclude with very high confidence that human activities are the primary driver of warming since the mid-20th century. IPCC AR6 states 'it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land' — the strongest language yet used by the IPCC on human causation, reflecting more evidence and better methods.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers

text: The Clausius-Clapeyron relation also explains the 'thermodynamic' increase in extreme precipitation: for every degree of warming, the atmosphere's water holding capacity increases by ~7%, and in storms where moisture supply is the limiting factor, precipitation intensity increases by a similar amount. Observed increases in extreme daily rainfall events globally are tracking this theoretical prediction.

The stratospheric ozone layer's protective function was calculated theoretically by Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland in 1974, who showed that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released at the surface would drift into the stratosphere and release chlorine atoms that would catalytically destroy ozone. Their work earned them the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 alongside Paul Crutzen.

The term 'climate refugee' or 'climate migrant' describes people displaced by climate change impacts including sea level rise, drought, flooding, and extreme heat. The World Bank projects 216 million people could become internal climate migrants by 2050 under high-emissions scenarios in South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, East Asia, Pacific, and North Africa — with the largest numbers in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa.

Ice fog — composed of tiny suspended ice crystals rather than water droplets — forms when temperatures drop below about −30°C and water vapour condenses and freezes directly in the air. Common in the Arctic and sub-Arctic, ice fog can produce extremely poor visibility and accumulates on power lines, trees, and aircraft, creating a sparkling, fairy-tale appearance while causing practical hazards.

The global mean precipitation is projected to increase by 1–3% per degree of global warming, but this global average masks enormous regional variation. Wet regions generally get wetter and dry regions drier; monsoons intensify; and precipitation extremes increase faster than mean precipitation because of the thermodynamic increase in atmospheric moisture capacity.

The El Niño event of 1997–98, the strongest on record until 2015–16, caused global economic losses estimated at $45 billion and contributed to the warmest year on record at that time. It produced severe droughts in Australia, Indonesia, and parts of Africa; flooding in Peru and Ecuador; and altered weather patterns globally — demonstrating the profound reach of Pacific ocean temperature anomalies.

The global surface temperature increase of 1.1–1.2°C since pre-industrial times is accompanied by a rise in global mean sea level of approximately 20 cm, a decline in Arctic sea ice extent of approximately 40% in September, and widespread glacier retreat affecting every continent. These concurrent changes across multiple independent indicators provide overwhelming evidence of a system undergoing rapid, coherent climate change.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers
