text: Omega-3 fatty acid content in polar fish is declining because warming oceans are reducing the abundance of cold-adapted marine algae that produce these essential nutrients, replacing them with warm-adapted species with lower omega-3 content. This is one of many pathways through which climate change affects human nutrition — in this case threatening the health benefits of eating oily fish.

The Indian Ocean monsoon system is one of the oldest known in Earth's geological history; geologists have found evidence of summer monsoon-type precipitation dating back over 23 million years. The Asian monsoon intensified dramatically about 8 million years ago as the Tibetan Plateau reached its current elevation, and has been modulated by ice age cycles ever since.

The concept of 'net zero' emissions — balancing the amount of greenhouse gas produced with the amount removed from the atmosphere — has become the central goal of climate policy for most nations. Achieving net zero by 2050 globally is considered necessary to limit warming to 1.5–1.7°C; as of 2023, over 140 countries covering about 90% of global GDP had announced net-zero targets.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG3 Summary for Policymakers

text: The Loess Plateau in China — a region blanketed in windblown silt (loess) that accumulated during Pleistocene Ice Ages — provides one of the world's longest continental paleoclimate records, with loess-palaeosol sequences (alternating dust layers and soil horizons) extending 8–10 million years. The thickness of loess layers reflects glacial wind intensity, while palaeosols indicate warmer, moister interglacial periods.

Geostrophic wind — the theoretical wind that blows parallel to isobars when the Coriolis force exactly balances the pressure gradient force — is a useful approximation to the actual wind in the upper atmosphere, where friction is minimal. At the surface, friction slows the wind and causes it to cross isobars at 10–30° toward lower pressure, resulting in the spiral inflow seen in surface cyclones.

The global average annual cycle of CO₂ measured at Mauna Loa peaks around May each year (when Northern Hemisphere plants have not yet grown enough to absorb the winter's CO₂ buildup) and reaches a minimum around September-October (after the growing season's peak absorption). The amplitude of this seasonal swing has increased by about 15% since the 1960s, reflecting the response of land ecosystems — mainly boreal forests — to warming.

The Great Smog of London in December 1952 — caused by a temperature inversion trapping coal smoke and car exhaust under a blanket of cold, still air for five days — killed an estimated 4,000–12,000 people and is considered the worst air pollution event in UK history. It directly led to the Clean Air Act of 1956, which banned coal burning in domestic fireplaces in designated areas and transformed London's air quality.

A 'superbloom' occurs in the Sonoran and Mojave Deserts when unusually heavy winter rains germinate millions of dormant seeds simultaneously, carpeting the desert floor in wildflowers. The conditions required — specific timing of moisture, minimum temperatures, and solar radiation — occur only a few times per decade. A spectacular superbloom occurred in California's Antelope Valley and Death Valley in 2023.

The general circulation of the atmosphere maintains the global energy balance through the transport of sensible heat (warm air moving poleward), latent heat (moisture moving poleward and condensing), and potential energy. In the atmosphere, latent heat transport is approximately equal to sensible heat transport in the tropics, while sensible heat dominates in mid-latitudes and is carried primarily by extratropical cyclones.

The South Asian monsoon onset, which normally brings the first monsoon rains to Kerala around June 1, has become more variable in recent decades, with onset dates ranging from late May to mid-June. This variability in a season that determines water supply for over 1 billion people is a significant economic and humanitarian challenge; improving 2–4 week forecasts of monsoon onset is a major research priority.

The Scripps CO₂ Program, founded by Charles David Keeling in 1956, operates the world's longest continuous atmospheric CO₂ record from Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, and other global stations. Keeling's meticulous calibration methods — his obsessive attention to instrument consistency — are the reason the record is trusted as an accurate measure of global atmospheric CO₂ change over seven decades.

The 'carbon budget' for 1.5°C warming, as assessed by IPCC AR6, was approximately 400–500 GtCO₂ remaining from the start of 2020. At the rate of emissions in 2022 (approximately 40 GtCO₂/year), this budget would be exhausted in approximately 10–12 years — placing the 1.5°C limit firmly within the near-term policy window, not some distant future constraint.

Anticyclonic gloom — persistent low cloud and fog that develops under high-pressure systems in winter — is a feature of several European cities that are prone to prolonged grey, damp, cold spells without reaching freezing temperatures. The phenomenon is particularly common in the Po Valley of northern Italy, where anticyclonic conditions trap cold, stable air in winter, trapping pollution and creating dense valley fogs.

The interannual variability of sea surface temperature in the Northern Indian Ocean has increased significantly since the 1980s, with more frequent and intense marine heatwaves. A 2021 Nature study found Indian Ocean warming drove a 52% increase in tropical cyclone intensification rates in the Arabian Sea between 1982 and 2019 — threatening coastal populations from Oman to India who historically experienced fewer intense storms.

Global mean sea level is projected to rise by 0.28–1.01 metres by 2100 under different emissions scenarios according to IPCC AR6, with higher outcomes possible if the West Antarctic ice sheet becomes unstable. Under a very high-emissions scenario (SSP5-8.5), global mean sea level rise could reach 2 metres by 2100 if low-probability, high-impact ice sheet dynamics occur.

The IPCC was founded in 1988, and its First Assessment Report (1990) stated with certainty that greenhouse gases were increasing and would cause warming — yet by 2021's Sixth Assessment Report, the evidence had strengthened from 'certain warming will occur' to 'unequivocal that human influence has already warmed' the climate system. This progression over 30+ years of assessments represents one of science's most sustained, collaborative, and consequential research efforts.

The future of Earth's climate depends critically on human choices in the coming decades. IPCC AR6 projects that limiting warming to 1.5°C requires reaching net-zero CO₂ emissions by around 2050 globally, while warming of 4°C or more is possible in high-emissions scenarios by 2100. The range of possible futures is wider than at any point in the observational record, making the decisions made by this generation perhaps the most consequential in human history for the long-term state of Earth's climate.

source.name: IPCC AR6 WG1 Summary for Policymakers
